1        INTRODUCTION
RINA Consulting, Inc. (RINA) has been retained by the Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) of the
Government of Suriname (GOS) to conduct a Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA)
of the Mining Sector financed by the World Bank Group’s (WBG) International Bank for Reconstruction
and Development (IBRD). The development of this SESA is part of an overarching goal to strengthen
the environmental and social standards, and impact management under the Country Partnership
Strategy (CPS) between the WBG and the GOS.
As part of this consultancy, RINA will prepare the following:

1.1   BACKGROUND
The SCSD project consists of three components:
 Component 1: Strengthening the mining sector governance, transparency, accountability, and
  administration.
 Component 2: Investing in Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and value chains in targeted
  emerging industries.
 Component 3: Project management and evaluation.
The first component of the SCSD project (SCSD - C1) is focused on technical assistance and seeks to
specifically strengthen the mining sector governance, transparency, accountability, and administration.
This component focuses on supporting improvements to the legal, regulatory, and institutional
framework governing mining in Suriname. The purpose is to improve social and environmental impact
management and to align Suriname’s framework to international best practice by providing its institutions
with knowledge and tools to carry out their mandated functions. Specific activities planned in the SCSD,
in addition to the development of the SESA, include the following:
1. Strengthening the legal, regulatory, and institutional frameworks governing the mining sector
   through support towards the revision of relevant legislation and regulations and the establishment
   of the Minerals Institute, which will integrate and strengthen mining cadaster, geological data
   management, and mining inspectorate functions. This includes defining a roadmap and
   implementing institutional reforms; supporting the development of required legal and regulatory
   frameworks; and supporting the establishment and operationalization of the Minerals Institute,
   including the collection of production and export statistics and setting up a Minerals Statistics
   Database.
2. Sector administration capacity building to assist the GOS, in particular staff from the Ministry of
   Natural Resources, the Minerals Institute, and other relevant ministries including the Ministry of
   Finance, to build the required technical skills and managerial capabilities to regulate and monitor
   the mining sector.
3. Strengthening revenue assessment, collection, and forecasting through support to the Extractive
   Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI) and setting up systems to improve revenue collection in a




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                      Page 10
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL


      transparent and accountable manner. This includes the development of documentation systems and
      standardized procedures for the submission and analysis of monitoring reports, in conformity with
      the Mining Decree and specific investment agreement commitments, as well as for the calculation
      of mining royalties and establishment of export controls.
4. Building independent oversight capacity and stakeholder consultation mechanisms, by providing
   support to non-state actors involved in the EITI process in Suriname (including Indigenous and tribal
   peoples’ representatives, non-governmental organizations, community-based organizations,
   technical experts, and other civil society representatives), to strengthen their participation in
   increasing transparency and disclosure in the mining industry.
5. Enhancing environmental, health, and social performance of the mining sector, including:
      a) Preparation of a SESA covering mining, which will entail a comprehensive sector-wide
         examination of potential impacts, both positive and negative, of future development in the mining
         sector, and the identification of gaps in regulations, institutional capacity, and public consultation
         mechanisms, and areas that can be strengthened.
      b) Capacity support to enhance social and environmental impact management, including technical
         assistance for the implementation of select reforms recommended by the SESA. This support
         will be consistent with international standards such as the WBG’s on Environmental, Health,
         Safety and REDD+ guidelines, and will promote improved mining practices that aim to reduce
         impacts on forest, reduce the sector’s vulnerability to climate change risks, help mitigate climate
         change - through improved water efficiency and substitution of inputs/enhanced energy
         efficiency, to reduce GHG emissions in existing and future mining operations - and improve
         Indigenous and tribal community engagement.
This document is the Scoping Report for the SESA study for the Mining Sector of Suriname, described
in item 5(a) above. It should be noted that according to the Terms of Reference (ToR) for this
consultancy, the Inception Report or Work Plan was prepared simultaneously and should be read in
combination with this Scoping Report. Both the Inception report and this Scoping Report will be
presented before the stakeholders for consultation in the events to take place between October 24 and
November 5, 2022, for review and comments.

1.1.1     Background Documents
Various instruments were prepared by the GOS as part of SCSD lending requirements. These prior
studies have been reviewed and incorporated as references as part of the desktop review of this Scoping
stage. The studies are listed below.
 Country Partnership Strategy (WBG, April 2015);
 SCSD Environmental and Social Management Framework – ESMF (WBG, June 2019a);
 SCSD Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Planning Framework – ITPPF (WBG, February 2019b);
 SCSD Rapid Social Assessment – RSA (WBG, June 2019c); and
 SCSD Resettlement Policy Framework – RPF (WBG, June 2019d).
In addition, the SCSD project has strong and compelling links with Suriname’s National Development
Plan (Nationaal Ontwikkelings Plan - NOP) 2022-2026 (NDP), which outlines the development trajectory
for Suriname for upcoming years. For the development of this scoping report, RINA reviewed the NDP
2022-2026 to understand the objectives related to the development of the mining sector.

1.2     ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITATIONS
The SESA Scoping process was subject to a number of assumptions and limitations, which should be
considered when reading the information presented in this report. The Consultant is confident that these




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                           Page 11
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL


assumptions and limitations do not compromise the integrity of the SESA Scoping report. The relevant
assumptions and limitations are as follows:
         Limited Geographic Information Systems data to spatially analyze limits of possible impacts;
         The SESA Scoping report provides a general context about the potential impacts: additional
          specialized studies may be necessary following the identification of impacts that will need further
          detailed analysis during the SESA phase;
         The SESA Scoping process provides expert analysis and should not be categorized as a full
          SESA study.

1.3       STRUCTURE OF THE SCOPING REPORT
The structure of the scoping report was designed to aid in framing the content and methodology of the
SESA. The scoping report consist of the following sections:
         Introduction: Introduces the scope of the consultancy and background documents used as
          references.
         Scoping of the SESA: Provides an overview of the SESA Scoping process.

2 SCOPING OF THE SESA
The SESA will entail a comprehensive mining sector-wide examination of potential impacts, both positive
and negative, of future potential investments in the mining sector, and identify gaps in regulations,
institutional capacity, and public consultation mechanisms that can be strengthened. For this purpose,
the SESA requires a strategic look at environmental and social aspects, and continuous stakeholder
consultations. The SESA will provide guidance to the MNR and NIMOS on systematically integrating
environmental, socio-economic, health and safety concerns in policy, regulation and planning, project
development, operations, maintenance, and decommissioning of mining sector activities. Furthermore,
the SESA will provide a benchmark for cumulative environmental and social effects with other ongoing
sector programs and plans. The SESA will ensure that the concerns and expectations of different
stakeholders are taken into account in the decision-making process for equity and sustainable
development of Suriname’s mining sector.
As a summary, the development of the SESA will follow 6 Stages. The general approach to be used is
presented in Figure 2-1.




                        Figure 2-1:   Technical Approach and Methodology for SESA

   Source: RINA, 2022



The first stage of the SESA requires the development of a Scoping Report (this document) to frame the
content and methodology with substantial stakeholder inputs. To frame the SESA study, scenarios of
the mining sector’s development have been proposed and will be presented in the relevant section of
this report. The purpose of presenting these scenarios is to initiate dialogue with the stakeholders.
To this end, the following process is proposed in accordance with the ToR of this Consultancy:
 Identify the preliminary environmental and social characteristics of those areas most likely to be
  affected by future mining activities, identifying sensitive ecosystems, protected areas, areas of high
  biodiversity value, areas inhabited by Indigenous peoples, Maroons, fishermen, etc. This will include
  the identification of available and relevant Geographic Information Systems (GIS) data for the mining
  sector.
 Assemble preliminary desktop information relevant to the scope of the SESA, including but not
  limited to: current projects, plans and trends in the applicable mining sectors, including artisanal and
  small-scale mining (ASM), and to present the forecasts of future mining development scenarios to

 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL


    be developed subsequently, and scenarios for sector development including constraints and
    opportunities.
 Identify the preliminary environmental and social risks and vulnerabilities to be considered and
  assessed (e.g., potential Indigenous and tribal community land use, water quality, air quality,
  geology and soils, biodiversity, marine resources, socio-economic, coastal activities, etc.).
 Ensure that the SESA be a participatory process, and that the Scoping Report be
  consulted/validated with stakeholders according to the stakeholder consultation plan presented in
  the Inception report. For this purpose:
     o   Key stakeholders in the mining sector have been preliminary mapped. These stakeholders will
         be consulted, their interests, concerns and incentives will be analyzed. The specific plan for
         stakeholder consultations is presented in the Inception Report. The aim of the Inception report
         is to make sure that stakeholder’s interests, concerns and advice are considered in the SESA.
     o   The Scoping Report and Inception Report will be presented to the stakeholder in the first
         validation meeting(s). They will provide input to both reports prior to finalization.

   3 APPLICABLE STANDARDS
   The SESA is a Strategic Environmental Social Assessment process that uses analysis and public
   participation that engages various stakeholders in a dialogue on environmental and social issues they
   consider priorities and that are or may be affected by mining sector reforms. Stakeholders include
   government, public and private organizations, and vulnerable sectors such as local communities,
   Indigenous and tribal peoples, women and youth, and makes sure their voices are heard. Specific
   activities and general implementation of the SESA will be directed by the WBG Operational Policies,
   international standards, and best practices. These policies and standards are described below.

   The GOS has not established air quality levels standards in its legal or regulatory framework, therefore,

   quality, should prevent or minimize impacts by ensuring that:
              Emissions do not result in pollutant concentrations that reach or exceed relevant ambient quality
               guidelines and standards2 by applying national legislated standards, or in their absence, the
               current World Health Organization (WHO) Air Quality Guidelines (see Table 1.1.1), or other
               internationally recognized sources3;...”

3.2.2      Noise and Vibration Guidelines
The WBG General EHS Guidelines requires that noise impacts should not exceed the Decibel A Scale
(DbA) levels presented in Table 3-3, or result in a maximum increase in background levels of 3 decibels
(dB) at the nearest receptor location off-site. The GOS still needs to establish noise levels standards in
its legal or regulatory framework.

                                       Table 3-3:       WBG’s Noise Level Guidelines
                                              Noise Level Guidelines (a)
                                                                                  One Hour LAeq* (dBA)
                             Pollutants                                        Daytime            Nighttime
                                                                             07:00 - 22:00      22:00 - 07:00
 Residential; institutional; educational (b)                                      55                 45
 Industrial; commercial                                                            70                        70
Source: WBG, 2007
Notes:
(a) Guidelines values are for noise levels measured out of doors. Source: Guidelines for Community Noise. (WHO, 1999).
(b) Noise monitoring should be carried out using a Type 1 or 2 sound level meter meeting all appropriate IEC standards

In addition, during construction and decommissioning activities, noise and vibration may be caused by
the operation of pile drivers, earth moving and excavation equipment, concrete mixers, cranes and the
transportation of equipment, materials, and people. Some recommended noise reduction and control
strategies to consider in areas close to community areas include:
          Planning activities in consultation with local communities so that activities with the greatest
           potential to generate noise are planned during periods of the day that will result in least
           disturbance.
          Using noise control devices, such as temporary noise barriers and deflectors for impact and
           blasting activities, and exhaust muffling devices for combustion engines.

           Avoiding or minimizing project transportation through community areas.

3.2.2.1       Occupational Permissible Noise and Vibration Exposure Levels
The WBG General EHS Guidelines provide noise limits for various working environments (see Table
3-4). These guidelines require that:
           No employee should be exposed to a noise level greater than 85 dB(A) for a duration of more
            than 8 hours per day without hearing protection;
           No unprotected ear should be exposed to a peak sound pressure level (instantaneous) of more
            than 140 dB(C).
           The use of hearing protection should be enforced actively when the equivalent sound level over
            8 hours reaches 85 dB(A), the peak sound levels reach 140 dB(C), or the average maximum
            sound level reaches 110dB(A).
           Prior to the issuance of hearing protective devices as the final control mechanism, use of
            acoustic insulating materials, isolation of the noise source, and other engineering controls
            should be investigated and implemented, where feasible.
           Periodic medical hearing checks should be performed on workers exposed to high noise levels.

The WBG General EHS Guidelines defines vibration as the exposure to hand-arm vibration4 (from
equipment such as hand and power tools) or whole-body vibrations5 (from surfaces on which the worker
stands or sits), which should be controlled through wise selection of equipment, installation of vibration
dampening pads or devices, and by limiting the duration of exposure. In addition, the limits for vibration
and action values, (i.e., the level of exposure at which remediation should be initiated), are provided by


*******

4
    Vibration transmitted through hand: holding a vibrating tool, 5 - 1500 Hz, ISO 5349-1. (CCOHS, 2005) or vibration workers
      experience when using tools such as chain saws, jackhammers, grinders, drills, etc. Excessive Hand-Arm Vibration can lead
      to what is commonly referred to as Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS). (Larson Davis, 2022a)
5
    Vibration transmitted through a supporting area to whole body: sitting in a chair, standing on vibrating ground 0.5 - 80 Hz; ISO
      2631-2 Sea sickness 0.1- 0.5 Hz, ISO 2631-1. (CCOHS, 2005) or Whole-body vibration (WBV) is the vibration transmitted
      through the seat or feet of a worker while operating machinery or standing on vibrating platforms. Some work environments
      where WBV is of concern include mining, farming, construction, trucking, sailors, helicopter pilots, and industrial equipment.
      (Larson Davis, 2022b)

    Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
    of Suriname
    Scoping Report - FINAL


the ACGIH6. The exposure levels should be checked on the basis of daily exposure time and data
provided by equipment manufacturers.
While the government of Suriname has not developed an occupational workplace exposure standard
for WBV, it is useful to make a comparison to an accepted standard in order to work out how much HAV
and WBV exposure is likely to cause a risk to workers. This is done by using daily vibration exposure
A(8) or vibration dose value (VDV), as developed by the American Conference of Governmental
Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH) and the European Union (EU). The ACGIH has developed Threshold Limit

3.3      FREE, PRIOR AND INFORMED CONSENT (FPIC)

FPIC is a standard protected by global human rights’ legislation. It reaffirms the right to self-
determination and the freedom to seek one's own economic, social, and cultural growth. The FPIC
principle focuses on the Indigenous Peoples’ \right to self-determination over land and resources on the
premise of safeguards that those rights cannot be affected or impacted or even diminished without
consultation and Free, Prior, and Informed Consent. Considered an emerging standard in the dialogue
on Indigenous Peoples rights, Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) is becoming part of customary
international law. It is especially applicable for the safeguard of property. FPIC aims to ensure the
inclusions, disclosure and respect for Indigenous and Tribal Peoples in any and all decision-making
process that involves them, their land or any other property.
Elements of FPIC can be defined as follows:
     free: no coercion, intimidation or manipulation;
     prior: consent is obtained in advance of the activity associated with the decision being made, and
      includes the time necessary to allow Indigenous and Tribal Peoples to undertake their own decision-
      making processes;
     informed: Indigenous Peoples have been provided all information relating to the activity and that
      that information is objective, accurate and presented in a manner and form understandable to
      Indigenous and Tribal Peoples;
     consent: implies that Indigenous Peoples have agreed to the activity that is the subject of the
      relevant decision, which may also be subject to conditions.”
Although Suriname has not ratified the Labour Organization Convention (ILO) 169, it has voted in favor
of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) which was adopted




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                               Page 25
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL


by the General Assembly on Thursday, 13 September 2007 which specifically mentions FPIC in its
Articles 10, 11, 19, 28 and 29, and the obligation to consult in its Articles 19 and 32
The requirement of consultation and FPIC procedures is clearly explained in the Environmental
Framework Act that was published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Suriname on May 07, 2020.
The act clearly defines FPIC as:
     an internationally used abbreviation for the Free Prior Informed Consent principle from the
     international law, in relation to Indigenous and tribal people, and comprises of the manner in which
     the government should engage Indigenous and tribal people in decision-making related to activities
     in their living area. Only based on proper information, common processes of decision-making and
     free will, can the Indigenous and tribal people take well-informed decisions regarding the allowance
     of any form of economic activities in their living area. In situations where a direct interest exists for
     the Indigenous and tribal people within their living area and whereby permits and or concessions
     are granted to persons or decisions are taken on the use of their living area, the approval of the
     Indigenous and tribal people is required before decisions are taken by the government. In cases
     these involve government projects included in policy programs approved by the people’s
     representative body, the Indigenous and tribal people must be consulted in advance before any
     right is granted to third parties (p. 2)

The Act further includes the obligation for the National Environmental Authority that NMA procedures
“ensure that the FPIC principle is applied in decision-making processes that regard the living area of
the Indigenous and tribal people” *p.6 Article 3 Duties and competences of the NMA Paragraph 1.m.)

4 LEGAL, REGULATORY AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK IN
  SURINAME’S MINING SECTOR
4.1        INTRODUCTION
This section provides a description of the relevant regulations set by the GOS for social planning and
environmental protection relevant and applicable to the mining sector. Therefore, the legislative,
regulatory and institutional requirements guiding the mining sector development project, are discussed
in more detail below.
In addition, Suriname is signatory to a number of international conventions that address environmental
and social issues. These international conventions are the key drivers behind for the development of
legislation in most countries, including Suriname.
The GOS have different ministries and institutions responsible for the management of the environment
and natural resources, and social themes.

4.2        LEGAL, REGULATORY AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK
The legal and regulatory framework of Suriname is composed of the national Constitution, Laws or Acts
of Parliament (also called Wet Landsverordening prior to 1975), Decrees (Decreet)7, Government State
Orders (Staatsbesluiten). In addition, there are regulations namely, Presidential Resolutions,
Presidential Orders, Ministerial Orders (beschikkingen) and District Ordinances (verordeniningen). The
regulatory framework is also supported by international agreements, treaties, conventions, etc. The
following sections describe in detail the legal and regulatory framework of Suriname.

4.2.1       National constitution and laws
Suriname is governed in accordance with its National Constitution (GOS, 2000) established in 1987 and
last amended in 1992. Article 41 states that the “natural riches and resources are the property of the
nation and should be used in economic, social and cultural development. The nation has the inalienable
right to take full possession of its natural resources in order to utilize them for the economic, social and
cultural development of Suriname.”
The Suriname Constitution sets specific social objectives related to environmental aspects, which
include:
           Article 6 (a) – “the identification of the potential for development of its own natural environment
            and the augmentation of the capacity to increasingly expand that potential”; and
           Article 6 (g) – “creating and improving the necessary conditions for the protection of nature and
            for the preservation of the ecological balance”.
In addition, the Constitution also states that all workers have the right to safe and healthy working
conditions (Article 28), and everyone has a right to health (Article 36). Finally, Article 42 affirms that the
law shall guarantee that the method in which trade and industry are conducted, shall not be contrary to
the national objectives and the public’s interest, notably public order, health, morality and state security.

    Decrees date from the period of 1980 – 1986 and have the same status as past or present Laws

In 2020, the ‘Milieu Raamwet S.B. 2020 no. 97 (Environmental Framework Act8 (EFA) S.B. 2020 no.
97)’ was established for the protection and sustainable management of the environment in Suriname
and the implementation and carrying into effect of obligations deriving from the membership of Suriname
to international agreements, notably the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the UN
Convention on Biological Diversity, the Paris Agreement, the Stockholm Convention (Conventions on
persistent organic pollutants (POPs), and the Rotterdam Convention *Prior Informed Consent (PIC)
Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade. Another important
matter is the investigation, prosecution and trial of offences defined in this Act as environmental
offences. (UNEP, 2022)
The Act is composed of 77 articles divided into 11 Chapters: General provisions (I); The National
Environment Authority (II); Duty of Care (III); Environmental Strategy (IV); Activities and Environmental
Consequences (V); Control of Pollution – Environmental Pollution and Standards (VI); Waste and
Hazardous Substances (VII); Legal Protection Mechanisms (VIII); Environmental offences and
Sanctions (IX); Provisions on Enforcement and further provisions (X); Transitional and Final Provisions
(XI). (UNEP, 2022)
The Act establishes the National Environment Authority (NMA) as a statutory body. It shall be the
successor to the Environmental Coordination Office of the Presidential cabinet. The National Institute
for Environment and Development in Suriname (NIMOS) will transition into the NMA.
In July 2020, the institutional structure for environmental management changed with the change of
Government. The structural change included the establishment of a new Ministry for Spatial Planning
and Environment (ROM). The Ministry of ROM aims to coordinate all environmental activities in the
country.
The legal positioning of the Ministry of ROM became a priority, and a formal working group was
established to amend the Environmental Framework Act (EFA). The amendment proposes that the
Ministry become primarily responsible for coordinating Environmental Policy while the NIMOS is being
transformed into the National Environmental Authority. A Presidential Resolution (PB. 31) was
promulgated to facilitate the transition period scheduled to start August 15, 2020. Although the
Environmental Framework Act was adopted in 2020, the legislation that would allow for its regulations
for further implementation of the Act has yet to be approved. As such, the National Environmental
Authority still needs to be installed. In addition, a Bill to amend the EFA has now been prepared. The
date for the Act to enter into force along with its provisions has yet to be confirmed but was It is now
expected that the amendments will be discussed in Parliament toward the end of 2002 or early 20239.
It is stipulated in the EFA that the NMA shall prepare the National Environment Strategy and be the main
focal point for environmental protection in Suriname. It shall also ensure that the FPIC principle is applied
in decision-making processes affecting the habitat of the Indigenous and tribal peoples. Key chapters
include (UNEP, 2022):
           Chapter III defines a duty of care for the environment. This duty means that everyone knows or
            can reasonably suspect that his or her actions or omissions shall have adverse consequences
            for the environment, must omit such action insofar as this can be reasonably required.
           Chapter IV requires the NMA to elaborate the environmental strategy as incorporated in the
            National Development Plan for Strategy into a national environmental policy plan. The Act sets
            out the priorities of such policy. One priority is the inventory, protection and regulation of
            endemic flora and fauna and traditional and medicinal knowledge. The national plan shall be
            elaborated in environmental programs, which shall also be established at district level. The NMA
            shall publish an environmental report every four years. The Act establishes an Environment

        Fund. Activities for which an environmental impact assessment is required shall be defined by
        a State Decree. This Act sets out the procedures for such an environmental impact assessment.
       Chapter V, the NMA shall be informed about government activities that may affect the
        environment and shall carry out an environmental impact analyses for such activities or policies
        or a strategic impact analysis for economic sectors such as forestry, water and agriculture.
       Chapter VI is about environmental pollution and rehabilitation of the environment. The NMA
        shall define polluting activities and be responsible for environmental authorizations.
       Chapter VII indicates that the NMA shall establish standards and procedures for waste
        treatment, reuse and recycling as well as the processing of waste. The NMA establishes rules
        for handling with hazardous substances. It is also charged with monitoring activities in this area
        prevention of environmental pollution.
       Chapters VIII and IX are about environmental offences. Penal law shall be the ultimate resort
        for such offences. Article 47 defines environmental offences and for this purpose indicates
        various other laws including, amongst others the Agriculture Act, the Forestry Act and the Water
        Resources Act.
In the past years, NIMOS has done some preparatory work by drafting subsidiary legislation necessary
for the implementation of the Environmental Framework Act. The following regulations have been
prepared in this regard:
1. A draft regulation to determine the activities subject to an EIA
The implementation regulation gives an overview about the activities for which an EIA is or is not
required. The list includes activities related to different kinds of projects and indicates to which category
(A, B) they belong. According to the determined category, NMA (transitions from NIMOS) shall decide
whether the execution of an EIA shall take place. The regulation further indicates that project activities,
which fall under category C, do not require an EIA, but are still obliged to apply for an environmental
license.

2. A draft regulation to implement Environmental Impact Assessment
This draft regulation has now been combined with the draft regulation to determine the activities subject
to an EIA whereas, the proponent of an activity is obliged to ask compulsory advice from NMA for the
submission of an application for a license whether an EIA is required. The regulation sets further
provisions regarding the determination of the scope of the required EIA, specifications for the
qualification of persons to conduct an EIA, minimum requirements for the Environmental Impact Reports
(EIR) including the submission and assessment of the EIRs.

3. A draft regulation on Pollution Control
This implementation regulation lays down provisions concerning the prevention of environmental
pollution by means of inter alia introducing a licensing system. For an effective monitoring of compliance
with the provisions under or pursuant to the Environmental Act, the regulation also determines the
pollutants, their values, quantities and other technical details in connection with the measurability of
environmental pollution. Regarding existing sources of pollution, it is obliged to register these sources
with NMA. The regulations further provide provisions regarding spills and accidental releases.

4. A draft regulation on Hazardous Substances
The implementation regulation lays down provisions concerning hazardous substances to prevent
environmental pollution by means of inter alia introducing a licensing system. For an effective monitoring
of compliance with the provisions under or pursuant to the Environmental Act, the regulation also
determines the hazardous substances as well as the provisions concerning inter alia the license, the
transport, the use, the treatment and the registration of such substances.




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                         Page 29
   Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
   of Suriname
   Scoping Report - FINAL


 Additional regulations regarding administrative and institutional matters, as well on waste, hazardous
 substances and audits still need to be drafted.

 Other relevant environmental legislation in Suriname includes:
        The ‘Hinderwet G.B. 1930 no. 40 z.l.g. bij S.B. 2001 no. 63 (Nuisance Act G.B. 1930 no. 40 as
         amended by S.B.2001 no. 63)’ defines the permit requirements to control noise and air pollution
         for industrial development projects. The permits are issued and enforced by local District
         Commissioners (Buursink, 2005; SRK, 2007);
        The ‘Natuurbeschermingswet, 1954 no. 26 z.l.g. bij S.B. 1992 no. 80 (Nature Conservation Act
         1954 G.B. 1954 no.26 as amended by S.B. 1992 no.80)’ defines the procedures to establish
         and manage conservation areas. According to the Act, the only allowable activities in the
         protected areas are activities of scientific, educational or cultural importance. Conservation
         areas can be established by State Order and managed by the Forest Service (LBB) who
         delegated this responsibility to the Nature Conservation Division (NDC).
        The ‘Jachtwet 1954 G.B. 1954 no. 25 z.l.g. bij S.B. 1997 no. 33 (Game Act 1954, G.B. 1954 no.
         26 as lastly amended by S.B. 1997 no. 33)’ provides rules for protecting fauna and the regulation
         of hunting. Under this Act, animals are designated as protected animals and receive legal
         protection.
        Jachtbesluit 2002 S.B.2002 no. 116 (Game State Order 2002 S.B. 2002 no. 116) provides for
         hunting seasons, bag limits and hunting permits.
        The ‘Wet Bosbeheer S.B. 1992 no. 80 (Forest Management Act S.B.1992 no. 80)’ provides a
         framework for forest management, exploitation and related sector activities to guarantee
         sustainable utilization of forest resources. The Act classifies forests in Suriname in three ways:
         permanent, temporary (maintained for the time being), or one-time exploitation forest (land
         intended for other future use where tree cover will be completely cleared). Resource exploitation
         in public forests (domain land) is allowable with a permit or forest concession granted by the
         Ministry of Land Policy and Forestry Management (GBB), which issued regulations for logging,
         deforestation, and processing-related activities.

4.2.3       Sectoral and cross-sectoral policies
The following sectoral and cross–sectoral policies are also considered relevant in relation to concerned
environmental and socio-economic settings of the mining sector:
       Suriname’s National Development Plan 2021 – 2026 (NDP10): The general objective of the
       development plan is to build and maintain a national economy that is free from foreign domination
       with the participation of the citizens, and from which citizens benefit. The NDP looks to the future
       and identifies several policy areas as well as long- and short-term goals (GOS, 2022c). With regard
       to the gold sector (Chapter A6), the NDP mentions that forecasts indicate that the gold price will rise
       (significantly) in the future, thus making gold mining more lucrative. However, the danger is that
       unstructured small-scale gold mining will accelerate with disastrous consequences for the already
       severely degraded environment (GOS, 2022c).
       For the gold mining sector, the NDP includes a strength, opportunities, weaknesses and threats
       (SWOT) analysis for the gold mining sector, which is presented in


       A6.14.1: Informal gold sector must be reordered (planned in 2022).
       1. A6.14.2: Allocate specific areas for small-scale gold mining (planned in 2023).
       2. A6.14.3: Check which concession rights have been issued and see what the possibilities are to
          revoke them in the event of inactivity (planned in 2024).
       3. A6.14.4: Establish and roll out a rehabilitation plan for degraded areas (planned in 2024).
       4. A6.14.5: Exploring options for setting up Surinamese gold business/company (planned in 2024).
       5. A6.14.6: Mining law amendment. (Amendment to Mining Act II). A new law should set clear
          rules for rehabilitation, those informal gold sectors and issuance policies (planned in 2025)11.
       6. A6.14.7: Implementation of gold mining without the use of toxic substances (the knowledge is
          already in Suriname), with in particular a phasing out of the use of mercury (planned in 2023).

       For the later strategic action item A6.14.7, the NDP has set a plan to reach it, as shown in Figure
       4-1.

      Based on Surinam’s National Goals, in 2018 Surinam received funding from the Global Environment
      Facility (GEF)13 to improve the management of mining, especially artisanal and small-scale gold
      mining (ASGM), and promote environmentally responsible mining technologies (excluding the use of
      mercury), in order to reduce negative effects on biodiversity, forests, water and local communities,
      while reducing greenhouse gas emissions (known as the “EMSAGS Project”) (European
      Commission, 2021). The key organizations involved in this initiative are the UNDP (implementing
      agency14), the MNR and NIMOS (executing agencies). The mid-term review report for the project
      carried out between August and December 2021 (UNDP, 2022), indicates that the project is offtrack
      and no real progress has been achieved on any of the main outcomes expected for this initiative,
      which include:
           Outcome 1, "Institutional capacity, inter-institutional coordination and availability of funding
               increased for improved management of ASGM”;
           Outcome 2, "Policy and planning framework for the management of the environmental
               impacts of ASGM mining strengthened";
           Outcome 3 "Uptake of environmentally responsible artisanal small-scale gold mining
               practices increased”; and
           Outcome 4, "Knowledge availability and sharing increased at the national and regional scale
               on environmentally responsible ASGM”.
      .

1. National Biodiversity Strategy: Suriname developed a National Biodiversity Strategy (NBS),
   which establishes the national vision and strategic directions to conserve and sustain rich
   biodiversity and biological resources. Moreover, the NBS sets out its goals for sustainable
   management of the nation’s natural resources and supports the equitable sharing of biodiversity
   related to services and benefits. The NBS provides a framework for the development of a
   Biodiversity Action Plan, which will identify the activities, tasks, outcomes, milestones, and
   implementation of a strategic program. The use and management of biodiversity remains a critical

    element in the maintenance and development of traditional societies for an emerging modern
    economy in Suriname.
2. National Oil Spill Contingency Plan of Suriname (NOSCP) 2016: The National Oil Spill
   Contingency Plan outlines Suriname's National Policy and Response Organization to a national
   level event as well as what is expected of the Responsible Party in ensuring a rapid, cooperative
   and effective response to an oil spill incident. The primary objective is to protect human health and
   safety, minimize social and environmental impacts, and ensure that the socio-economic and
   environmental conditions are restored. The Plan has been developed in conjunction with the
   Nationaal Coordinatie Centrum voor Rampenbeheersing (NCCR), the Maritime Authority Suriname
   (MAS), National Security, the National Institute for Environment and Development in Suriname
   (NIMOS), RAC/REMPEITC Caribe, Staatsolie Maatschappij Suriname N.V. (Staatsolie), and Oil
   Spill Response Ltd (OSRL). Following international and regional best practice, ISO 155441 and the
   International Maritime Organization (IMO) Manual on Assessment of Oil Spill Risk and
   Preparedness (2010 Edition), this plan establishes the roles, duties and responsibilities of the
   above-mentioned organizations in the response to a national level oil spill incident.
The NOSCP aims to ensure that any response operation recognizes the following as primary objectives:
        Protecting human health and safety
        Minimizing any social and environmental impacts
        Ensuring that the socio-economic and environmental conditions are restored, as near as is
         practicable, to pre-spill conditions.

Since 1919, the International Labor Organization has maintained and developed a system of
international labor standards aimed at promoting opportunities for women and men to obtain decent and
productive work, in conditions of freedom, equity, security and dignity (ILO, 2022). The ILO Governing
Body has identified eight “fundamental” Conventions, covering subjects that are considered to be
fundamental principles and rights at work: freedom of association and the effective recognition of the
right to collective bargaining; the elimination of all forms of forced or compulsory labor; the effective
abolition of child labor; and the elimination of discrimination in respect of employment and occupation.
The ILO has also designated another four Conventions as governance (or priority) instruments, thereby
encouraging member States to ratify them because of their importance for the functioning of the
international labor standards system. (ILO, 2019). Of these, Suriname has ratified eight (out of ten)
fundamental conventions, three (out of four) governance conventions and 22 (out of 176) principal
technical conventions. These and other relevant ILO conventions are presented in Table 4-5.

4.2.5     National institutional framework for environmental and social management
Suriname’s mining sector is governed by the Mining Decree (1986) and regulated by the Ministry of
Natural Resources, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Regional Development and the Ministry of
Trade, Industry and Tourism. The legal and fiscal framework for the oil, gas and mining sectors is also
supported by other legislation, including the Corporate Income Tax Act and Dividend Tax Act. (EITI,
2022). Applications for mining rights are processed by the Geological Mining Service (GMD) and are
reviewed and approved by the Ministry of Natural Resources in accordance with the Mining Decree.
Suriname does not have a public mining license register, however some information about issued
licenses is included in EITI Reports (EITI, 2022). EITI Suriname is administered by the Suriname Multi-
Stakeholder Group (MSG), which is hosted by the Ministry of Natural Resources. The MSG is chaired
by the Minister of Natural Resources. (EITI, 2022)
On the other hand, the environmental approval process is to be administered under the new
Environmental Framework Act 2022, through the yet to be operational National Environment Authority
(in Dutch: Nationale Milieu Autoriteit, NMA), an institution transitioned from the National Institute for
Environment and Development in Suriname (in Dutch: National Instituut voor Milieu en Ontwikkeling in
Suriname, NIMOS), thus forming the new National Environment Structure in Suriname. Through this
structure, the provisions included in the Environmental Framework Act will be implemented and applied
in an efficient and effective manner. (NIMOS, 2022b).
The key institutions can be summarized as follows:

4.2.5.1    Ministry of Natural Resources - MNR
The aim of the Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) is to ensure an integral sustainable and efficient
management and development of the production of the natural resources present in Suriname, taking
into account the environment, safety and rights of local communities. The organizational structure of the
MNR has recently changed. The Ministry now consists of four (4) directorates, as further detailed in the
organizational structure, namely (MNR, 2022a):




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                      Page 59
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL




    1. Directorate General Administration NH
    2. Directorate of Water
    3. Directorate of Energy
    4. Mining Directorate
The organization has been expanded to include directorate and departmental tasks. The determining
organizational objectives for this are:
    1. Planning, monitoring and control of the spending of the budget and other resources.
    2. Optimization of the operational execution of tasks.
    3. Application of integrated management in the various policy areas.
    4. Application of advancing technology within the various policy areas.
    5. Continuous quality improvement and quality maintenance of the execution capacity.
    6. Entry into regional and international partnerships.
    7. Sustainable professional and personal development of staff.
Based on the objectives described above, the organization chart of the MNR is presented in Figure 4-2.




                                  Figure 4-2:   MNR organizational structure

physical planning, nature conservation and forest management. The institutional coordinating function
of the Ministry of Land Policy and Forest Management is, among others, related to: (i) proper land

4.2.5.3   Ministry of Regional Development and Sport
The Ministry of Regional Development and Sport is responsible for the development of rural areas and
the provision services outside Paramaribo. Duties in each of the ten districts are managed by district
admirations, headed by District Commissioners.

4.2.5.4   Ministry of Spatial Planning and Environment - ROM
In July 2020, the institutional structure for environmental management changed with the change of
Government. The structural change included the establishment of a new Ministry for Spatial Planning
and Environment (ROM). The Ministry of ROM aims to coordinate all environmental activities in the
country. Legal positioning of the Ministry of ROM became a priority, and a formal working group was
established for amending the Environmental Framework Act. The amendment proposes the Ministry to
become primarily responsible for coordinating Environmental Policy while the NIMOS will transition into
the National Environmental Authority (NMA). According to the Presidential Resolution (PB. 31), .Starting
August 15, 2020, the Ministry of ROM and NMA transition into their new roles within 18 months, the
Ministry of ROM and NIMOS had 18 months for the transition, which was scheduled to initiate August
15. . However, the transition has not yet been completed and it is expected that this period will be
extended.

4.2.5.5   The Ministry of Transport, Communication and Tourism (MTCT)
The Ministry of Transport, Communication and Tourism (MTCT) is responsible for the transport sector
(water, air and road transport), as well as public transport and its supervision. In addition, the ministry
has the task to facilitate the water and air traffic sector, in particular with regard to the safe and efficient
handling of persons and goods, pilotage and the management of all ports. Furthermore, the ministry is
also in charge of the telecommunications sector and tourism in general as well as the further
development of the tourism sector in particular.

4.2.5.6   Ministry of Public Works
The Ministry of Public Works is, among other things, responsible for the preparation and implementation
of various Civil Engineering and Construction Works, traffic technical facilities, the issuance of
construction and allotment permits, and also of green areas, street maintenance and waste processing.
The Road Authority (RA) is currently the only Parastatal organization under the Ministry of Public Works.
The RA is known as the institution that has the necessary knowledge and experience with regard to,
among other things, the rehabilitation of roads and the maintenance of verges. The Road Authority was
established by the law of 25 July 1995, in which the following tasks are described:
    1. Management and maintenance of primary roads and river crossings
    2. Advising the government on the repair and maintenance of roads and fixed river crossings.
Currently, the RA maintains and manages 859.79 km of Primary roads. The activities of the RA are
divided into the maintenance of the primary roads in and outside Paramaribo. Furthermore, the
maintenance of verges and adjacent bridges that are connected to the primary roads, culverts, traffic
facilities, road furniture, underground infrastructure and all other work that falls within the tasks of the
institute established in 1995.

4.2.5.7   Bauxite Institute Suriname
The Bauxite Institute Suriname was established on February 17, 1981, by Decree E-9 S.B. 1981 no. 14
as a legal entity “sui generis” established to control the entire bauxite happening in Suriname in order
to enable the Government to obtain a fair share from the proceeds of bauxite and its derivatives. The

4.2.5.8     National Coordination Centre for Disaster Management - NCCR
NCCR is a division of the Ministry of Defense that develops national policies on disaster management
and acts as coordinator and facilitator in crisis and disaster management during crises and disasters.

4.2.5.9     Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI) Suriname
EITI Suriname is administered by the Suriname Multi-Stakeholder Group (MSG), which is hosted by the
Ministry of Natural Resources. The MSG is chaired by the Minister of Natural Resources. (EITI, 2022)
Suriname was found to have made meaningful progress in implementing the 2016 EITI Standard in
March 2021, following its first Validation. The Validation identified 19 corrective actions to be addressed
by the country’s next Validation, expected to commence in April 2023. (EITI, 2022)

4.2.5.10    National Institute for Environment and Development in Suriname (NIMOS)
NIMOS was established on March 15, 1998, as the executive body of the National Environmental
Council (which no longer exists). NIMOS is an autonomous government foundation, supervised by a
Foundation Board and consists of the following 7 board members. The board is appointed for 2 years
by the President of the GOS. The day-to-day management and overall coordination of NIMOS is
undertaken by the General Director. Currently NIMOS has 27 staff members, of which 20 are employed
on a permanent basis and the remaining on a project basis. (NIMOS, 2022b)


NIMOS consists of several offices, each tasked with specific responsibilities, namely (NIMOS, 2022b):
    1. Administration
    2. Environmental & Social Assessment
    3. Environmental Monitoring & Enforcement
    4. Environmental Legal Services
    5. Environmental Education & Public Outreach
    6. Environmental Planning & Information Management
    7. Environmental Funding & Investments (not operational).
    8. Environmental Research (not operational).


The mission of NIMOS is to “initiate the development of a national legal and institutional framework for
environmental policy and management in the interest of sustainable development” that is to be driven
by the following goals (NIMOS, 2022b) :
    1. Achieving National Environmental Legislation in the broadest sense of the word.

    2. Preparing and implementing Environmental Protection legislation.
    3. Coordinating and monitoring of Compliance.
Under the new Environmental Framework Act, NIMOS will be in responsible to develop the State of the
Environment Report that will be used to inform policy and decision making of the NMA (NIMOS, 2022b).
In addition, the new Act will require the development of Implementation Regulations to facilitate its

    2. EIA Procedure,
    3. Environmental Permit,
    4. Hazardous Substances,
    5. Environmental Fund,
    6. Rules and Procedures for the Environmental Controllers.
NIMOS has also developed Generic Environmental Assessment Guidelines as well as specific
Guidelines. These Guidelines carefully explain the procedures as how they should be carried out if the
Environmental Framework Law and the Environmental Regulations were in place (NIMOS, 2022b).
The EIA process described by NIMOS is divided in 5 phases, namely (NIMOS, 2022b):
1. Screening phase: This is the phase in the EIA process, in which NIMOS decides whether an
   Environmental Impact Assessment is needed or not. If yes, NIMOS will indicate the nature and
   extent of the analysis. NIMOS acknowledges three categories of EIA:
    a. Category A: an EIA is mandatory.
    b. Category B, either:
          i.    An EIA is required (Category B, path 3);
         ii.    Another environmental document is needed (e.g., Environmental Management Plan)
                (Category B, path 2);
         iii.   No EIA is needed, but some environmental information is required before a decision can
                be taken (Category B, path 1).
    c.     Category C: No EIA is required, but the project proponent will have to keep with the minimal
           guidelines.
    2. Scoping phase: In this phase the Terms of Reference (ToR), sometimes also called Scoping
       report, for the EIA-study has to be prepared.
    3. Assessment phase: In the assessment phase, the EIA-study is to be carried out by a qualified
       consultant or consultancy firm by order of the project proponent.
    4. Review phase: During the review process, the submitted Environmental Impact Statement (EIS)
       is reviewed by NIMOS.
    5. Decision-making phase: After the EIS is reviewed, NIMOS should send the environmental
       advice regarding approval or denial of the project to the permitting agency.
Meanwhile NIMOS has the following sector specific EIA Guidelines in use, namely:

4.2.5.11     National Environment Authority– NMA
With the approval of the Environmental Framework Act (EFA), the National Environmental Authority (in
Dutch: Nationale Milieu Autoriteit) is established and responsible for enforcing this law. With this
institution, the National Environmental Council (NMR), which has not been operational for many years,
ceased to exist and the Environment Coordination within the President's Office has been renamed NMA,
while NIMOS will cease to exist and will transition into the NMA. In practice, the situation has developed
differently than prescribed by the EFA; the staff of Environmental Coordination is employed by the new
Ministry of ROM and NIMOS is incorporated into the NMA, a process that is now underway.
The NMA will be responsible for administering the Environmental Impact Assessment process and
Pollution Control. The NMA is to be responsible for the implementation and enforcement of the
Environmental Framework Act.

4.2.5.12     State Oil Company Suriname (Staatsolie Maatschappij Suriname N.V)
The State Oil Company Suriname is involved with the development of Suriname’s hydrocarbon potential
over the full value chain, to generate electricity, and to develop renewable sustainable energy resources.
It is further engaged with assessments of hydrocarbon potential, promotion, contracting, and monitoring
activities of other oil companies on behalf of the State.

4.2.5.13     Staatsolie Hydrocarbon Institute N.V. (SHI)
Since its establishment in December 1980, Staatsolie has acted as the state vehicle through which the
government oil policy was executed and whereby foreign companies could only explore for and produce
oil through service contracts with Staatsolie. The regulator’s role was further developed through the
establishment of the Petroleum Contracts division in 2000, followed by the establishment of SHI in 2020.
SHI is an agent of the Government of the GOS and performs a regulatory role for the exploration and
drilling activity (exploration and production)

4.2.5.14     Minerals Institute
The government of Suriname wants to promote a regulated and responsible expansion of the mining
industry, including improved control over informal goldmining. However, weak institutional capacity in
the public sector and the absence of an adequate legal and regulatory framework have inhibited
prospects for growth. Moreover, weak corporate governance in the small-scale mining activity and the
lack of social and environmental standards have diminished the sustainability and positive social impacts
of the sector. The current mining policy aims to create a Minerals Institute – through the merger of the
Geological Mining Service (GMD), the Bauxite Institute of Suriname (BIS) and the Suriname Gold Sector
Regulation Commission (OGS15) - and to enact a new mining law since these currently are uncapable

5 ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL CHARACTERISTICS
This section describes the biophysical and socio-economic environment indicating area where possible
impacts can occur from the mining sector.

5.1     INTRODUCTION
Suriname is endowed with many natural resources including soil, water, forests and mineral ores. The
fertile soil of the young coastal plain, combined with the large freshwater swamps and rivers in the north
are favorable for large scale agriculture. The largest part of the country (almost 88 % of total land area)
consists of tropical rainforest, marginally used by local people for non-timber forest products. The
cultivated land represents 8% of the total land area, whilst the remaining 4% consists of other non-
forested natural areas (savannahs, swamps and wetlands). The cultivated area is used for forestry
(3.7% of total land area), agriculture (3.2 %), and settlements, mining and hydropower reservoirs (1.3
%). Taking into account the low historical deforestation rate (between 0.03 and 0.04 % per year),
Suriname is identified as a country with a High Forest Cover, and Low Deforestation rate (HFLD-
country). (Berrenstein, 2016).

5.2     PHYSICAL ENVIRONMENT

5.2.1   Climatic Conditions
Suriname is located north of the equator on the northeastern coast of South America, between 40-60
north latitude and 540-580 west longitudes. Suriname has a tropical climate with abundant rainfall,
uniform temperature, and high humidity. The country shows a smooth orography, with height ascending
as we move southwards from the only coast in the north (Figure 5-1). This difference in altitude leads to
diverging coastal and interior climates. (IADB, 2021)

5.2.1.1   Temperature
The average daily temperature in the coastal region is 27.6°C, with an average daily variation of 4°C.
There is relatively little variation in temperature between the seasons in the coastal region. January is
the coldest month with an average temperature of 27.5°C, and October is the warmest with an average
temperature of 29.2°C. The annual variation of the average temperature is 2-3°C. The interior has similar
figures, with an even smaller annual variation of average temperatures (IADB, 2021). The average
annual temperature in 2019 was 28.0 ºC with an average minimum temperature of 23.9 ºC and an
average maximum temperature of 31.5 ºC (GBS, March 2020).

5.2.1.2   Rainfall or Precipitation
Suriname has two wet and two dry seasons. The beginning of the seasons is not simultaneous for all
areas. Most of the precipitation is measured during the rainy season. The Inter Tropical Convergence
Zone (ITCZ) is responsible for precipitation (GBS, March 2020).
In 2019 the average yearly precipitation was 1,617.5 mm (GBS, March 2020), The average annual
rainfall in Suriname is 2,200 mm; however, localized rainfall varies over the terrain where the coastal
plains receive on average 1,500 -1,750 mm and the central region receives 2,500 - 3,000 mm. Suriname
experiences two wet seasons: a major wet season between May and July when most of the country
receives 250 - 400 mm per month, and a minor wet season from November to January, which brings
around 150 - 200 mm of rainfall per month. The country also experiences two short dry seasons: a short
dry season from February-April with mean monthly rainfall of 100 mm and a long dry season from August
to December with less than 100 mm of rainfall per month. Suriname is south of the hurricane belt and
therefore evades this threat. (SWRIS, 2022). The average temperature and precipitation per month are
presented in Figure 5-2.
Precipitation amounts vary across the country. On average, Paramaribo receives 1,756 mm of rainfall
annually, Bigi Pan in the northwestern coast receives 1,796 mm/year, Kwamalasamutu in southern
Suriname receives 2,392 mm/year, and Tafelberg in central Suriname receives 1,851 mm/year.
Variation in monthly rainfall results in two wet and two dry seasons in the northern part of Suriname. In
the south, one wet and one dry season are distinguished (IADB, 2021).

In the whole country, the rainfall varies from less than 1,750 to greater than 3,000 millimeters annually.

Inter-annual variations in climate are caused by the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO)16. El Niño
episodes bring dry conditions throughout the year, and bring warmer temperatures between June and
August, while La Niña episodes bring wetter conditions throughout the year and cooler temperatures
between June and August. The observed mean in relative humidity is 81%. (SWRIS, 2022)

5.2.1.3       Evaporation
The annual evaporation is about 1,700 mm (1931-1960). About 67% of the precipitated water on the
Suriname rivers basins returns to the atmosphere by evapotranspiration and approximately 33% is
drained off into the Atlantic ocean. (SWRIS, 2022)

5.2.1.4       Wind
Winds in Suriname generally move in a northeasterly direction. Maximum average wind speed ranges
from 30-42 km/h on the coast to about 30 km/h in the interior. Wind is highest during the dry seasons,
with up to 40 km/h in March, and a second stronger peak in September and October. Wind speeds are
relatively high along the seashore and decrease as one moves inland. Wind speeds of 20 to 30 km/h
generally occur during the day and drop dramatically during the evening and night, especially in the
interior (IADB, 2021).

Although Suriname falls outside of the hurricane belt, the weather is occasionally affected by tails of
hurricanes. Local gales (in Surinamese called “sibibusi”) appear before storms, generally at the end of
the rainy seasons. During such gales maximum wind speeds of 20-30 m/s have been recorded. Such
gales occur over the whole country and may destroy trees and houses. No information is available on
the frequency of such gales. (GOS, 2016)

5.2.1.5    Humidity
Relative humidity is very high for all of Suriname, 80% or higher, and has a latitudinal gradient, with the
maximum values found at the coast and slightly lower values further inland. Daily humidity is on average
80-90% in the coastal regions. It is lower in the central and southern regions of the country, with an
average of 75%. In forested areas, air humidity depends, among other things, on the penetration of solar
radiation. Variations of relative humidity are between 70-100% in forested areas and between 50-100%
in open areas (IADB, 2021). In 2019 the average humidity was between 74% and 80% (GBS, March
2020).

5.2.1.6    Air quality
In general, the air quality in Suriname deteriorates during dry conditions and improves during the wet
season. During rainy seasons, rain suppresses dust particles in the atmosphere and alleviates air
pollution. Dust emissions are further reduced by damp soil conditions. During the dry season, dust
emissions generally increase as the soils become desiccated (SWM, 2019).

5.2.2     Climate change adaptation
In the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) of 1992, climate change
was defined as "a change of climate, which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity, which
changes the composition of the global atmosphere, and which is observed on top of the natural climate
variability over comparable intervals of time." The negative effects of climate change are not limited to
sea level rise, but affect all components of the environment: wind, precipitation and temperature. These
three components of the climate can cause alone or jointly, disasters, but there are also natural
disasters, such as earthquakes, infectious diseases and plagues, the risk of which must be assessed
as adequately as possible (GOS, 2017).

5.2.2.1    Sea Level Rise
Rapidly rising global temperature, melting of polar ice caps, rising of the sea water level and changes in
climate patterns and natural ecosystems are now becoming a daily concern (GBS, March 2020).
Suriname is a country with a low-lying coast where over 80% of the population resides, and where the
major economic activities and infrastructure are concentrated. These areas are and can suffer extensive
losses and damages from the effects of climate change (UNDP, 2019).
For people, sea level rise is one of the major impacts of climate change, and although more detailed
and accurate estimates of the impact of the rise in the sea level are needed (GOS, 2017), some studies
indicate that a 1m sea level rise (SLR) would significantly impact 7% of the population of Suriname,
particularly considering that most of this population is located in the coastal areas of the country
(Dasgupta et all, 2007). Figure 5-4, shows the extension of ocean waters without sea level rise (ASLR
= 0m) and see level rise scenario (ASLR = 1m).
For a young nation with less than 600,000 inhabitants, of which the majority lives in flat coastal areas
and heavily relying on natural ecosystems, the climate change impacts can be potentially catastrophic
and is expected to be an enormous setback to the development of the country (Berrenstein, 2016).
Considering that the coastal plain is vulnerable to sea level rise, and that Paramaribo is approximately
between 0 and 3 m above sea level, the country has been included in the listed of ten vulnerable
countries with low-lying coastal plains that are threatened by sea level rise in this century (GBS, March
2020).

5.2.2.2       Droughts and Floods
Suriname is one of the most vulnerable countries in the world to the impact of flooding. The country is
prone to periodic flooding due to heavy rainfall, especially when combined with spring tides.
Approximately 87 percent of Suriname’s population lives along the 386 km long coastal plain (around
67 percent in Paramaribo), and flooding affects most of the population and an estimated 90 percent of
human activities. Flooding is exacerbated by poor drainage in the relatively highly populated urban areas
on the coast, such as the capital city of Paramaribo. In addition, the coastal zone is also susceptible to
erosion and some parts are prone to coastal flooding (WBG, 2022a).
Suriname has not experienced major natural disasters, and these have remained relatively limited,
without large numbers of casualties. These natural disasters include the 2004 drought in the interior,
where villages could no longer be reached via the river and had to get food aid, the floods of 2006 and
2008 in the interior, then in the coastal plain, and the wind gusts (strong local whirl winds) reporting 29
events between 2015 and 2019 (GBS, March 2020). Other flooding events in the country were recorded
in 2021 with an estimated 10,100 people affected (OCHA, 2022).
The WBG is financing the Saramacca Canal System Rehabilitation Project17 (approved in 2019) which
aims to support the country to reduce flood risk in the greater Paramaribo area and improve the
Saramacca Canal System. It will improve the resilience against flooding by improving the ability of the
Saramacca Canal to discharge water efficiently and safely, while improving vessel transport and
strengthening the government’s capacity to manage and operate the canal’s drainage system.

5.2.2.3       Disaster Response and Relief
For disaster and emergency response, the government of Suriname has the stablished National
Coordination Center for Disaster Relief (NCCR). The role of the NCCR is to coordinate the various
services (Police, Fire department, National Army, NGOs and other parties) so that assistance can be

provided in a very effective and organized manner for areas within the Surinamese territory affected or

5.2.2.4       Carbon Sink Country
Suriname is a negative carbon-emitting country yet is committed to playing its part in the global fight
against climate change. It provides a key ecosystem service to the world. About 94% of Suriname’s
territory remains forested, storing about 11 gigatons of carbon and absorbing (carbon sink country) more
than 8.8 million tons of forest carbon annually (UNDP, 2019).
Despite its limited budget, the country has made progress towards climate-resilient and compatible
development through a number of green policies and initiatives – in particular, actions to protect and
use its forests sustainably (UNDP, 2019). These and others are included in its second Nationally
Determined Contribution (NDC) of 2022 also known as the national climate pledge and were submitted
in December 2019 in fulfilment of obligations under the Paris Agreement on climate change (GOS,
2019b).

5.2.3       Soil and Land Management
The current land degradation in Suriname is largely a result of mining activities. A distinction must be
made between: a) land degradation accumulated over a long period of time as a result of the bauxite
production, with little or no recovery of the environmental damage, particularly the land degradation and
b) the continuing impact of the current mining activities in the gold sector. In 2017, Suriname planned to
formulate a strategy and action plan for the limitation and restoration of land degradation based on
research and consultations with stakeholders with the focus on mined areas. Regarding the large-scale
agricultural activities while maintaining the environmental legislation to be adopted, strategies will be
developed with stakeholders to reduce land degradation. Crucial in this respect is agreeing on standards
and mechanisms for monitoring, controlling and reporting (GOS, 2017).

5.2.3.1       Geology, geography and soils
Suriname covers about one tenth of the Precambrian Guiana Shield18, a deeply weathered, rainforest-
covered hill and mountain land stretching from the Amazon River in Brazil to the Orinoco in Venezuela
(BOSMA, 1984) (see Figure 5-5). Geologically, the Guiana Shield is an ancient Precambrian land mass,
4 billion to 590 million years old, comprised of varied formations of sedimentary and igneous origin
especially granites and gneisses (Huber, 1995). The age and history of the Guiana Shield uplift provide
important clues to the origin and evolution of topographic formations such as drainage divides and
waterfalls particularly relevant to the distribution patterns of aquatic fauna. For example, the Kaieteur
Falls with an approximate height of 226m in Guyana isolates the only known habitats of the catfish
species Lithogenes villosus, considered relict taxa. We also note that there are gaps in knowledge about
the geology and biogeography of the Guyana Shield (LUJAN & ARMBRUSTER, 2011).
Eroded material from the Guiana Shield was deposited in the subsiding areas to the north. The oldest
outcropping sediments in this coastal area have been deposited during three distinct periods resulting
in three different formations (BOSMA, 1984):
 The Zanderij Formation, consisting of medium to coarse sands to sandy clays, which have been
  deposited by braided rivers at the foot of the Guiana Shield in the form of alluvial fans;
 The Coropina Formation, consisting of fine sandy to clayey marine sediments, which have been
  deposited north of (and on top of) the sediments of the Zanderij Formation. The marine clays were
  deposited as extensive clay flats and the marine sands as ridges, which were later severely eroded.

     The Guiana Shield forms the northern part of the Amazonian Craton, the core of the South American continent, and is separated
      from its southern counterpart, the Central Brazilian shield, by the Amazon–Solimões basin.

    The remaining surface deposits of this formation are found as “islands” surrounded by the sediments

 The Mara and Coronie Formations. The Mara Formation consists of marine clays and peat that were
  deposited in the eroded areas in between the remnants of the Coropina Formation, and in gullies
  that had been cut into the former Old Coastal Plain. The Coronie Formation in the coastal plain is
  predominantly of marine origin, but along the main rivers’ sediments have been deposited in fluviatile
  and estuarine environments. The deposits consist of mudflats of marine clays and ridges of sands
  and shells. The finer sediments (clay, silt and fine sand) originate from the Amazon basin, while
  coarser sands come from the Hinterland.

The Suriname part of the shield consists of three distinct belts of low- and high-grade metamorphic
rocks, separated by vast areas composed of granitoid and meta volcanic rocks. The basement is locally
overlain by remnants of the sub-horizontal Precambrian Roraima sandstone formation and is cut by
Proterozoic and Permo-Triassic dolerite dikes. In the coastal area to the north, it is covered by Mesozoic
to Holocene sediments (BOSMA, 1984).
The Precambrian crystalline basement of Suriname consists of two high-grade metamorphic gneiss
belts of Archean and Lower Proterozoic age, a likewise Lower Proterozoic volcanic -sedimentary
greenstone belt, and a granitoid-volcanic complex in-between. The basement carries a few remnants of
a once extensive cover of flat lying Middle Proterozoic and Permo Triassic dolerite dikes. The basement
was essentially formed during the Trans-Amazonian Orogenic Cycle from about 1,800 to 2,000 million
years ago (Ma). Younger, largely vertical movements culminated during the Nickerie Metamorphic
Episode at about 1,200-1,300 Ma. This episode may be attributable to a continental collision along the
westernmost margin of the Guiana Shield (at the present position of Colombia and Venezuela) (Vletter,
1984).
Suriname can mainly be distinguished by three landscapes (or geographic regions) as described below
and shown in Figure 5-6 [ (SWRIS, 2022); and (GOS, 2016)]:
1. The Coastal Plain: the coastal plains are about 21,000 km2 and can be divided into:
    a. The young coastal plain (lower plain): consists of soft fluvial clays and of sand ridges. This area
       is lower than 6 m above mean sea level. In this area percolation and surface drainage are very
       slow, because of the clay and peat soils. Most water is removed by evapotranspiration.
    b. The old coastal plain (upper plain): consists of silt clays, loams, sandy loams and fine sand. This
       area lies between 6 and 12 m above mean sea level. In this area percolation and surface
       drainage are very slow.
        The coastal plain area plays an important role in the maintenance of drinking water reserves
        because the greatest amount of rainfall percolates into the ground here, recharging the
        freshwater aquifers. The soils of the Young Coastal Plain are the most fertile zone of Suriname
        and has contributed to the development of large-scale agricultural activities. The soils of the Old
        Coastal Plain (generally composed of clay, sandy-clay or clayey-sand) offer good opportunities
        for agricultural development, in particular, horticulture. (Berrenstein, 2016)
2. The Cover Landscape or Savannah Belt consists of white coarse sands and coarse sandy clays.
   This area is about 8,500 km2 and lies between 15 and 20 m above mean sea level. In this area,
   groundwater flow is the main contributory to discharge. The period of time to peak in this area is
   about 6.5 to 15 hours. This area reacts more quickly to rainfall. The savannah belt is an important
   source of recharge for the aquifers.
3. The Interior Highlands or Precambrian shield or basement. This occupies about 80% Suriname’s
   landscape. Infiltration and percolation in this area is very small. Surface runoff is very high, and the
   drainage density is high. Time to peak period is about 13 to 28 hours with a concentration time of
   51 to 72 hours.

Source:     (GOS, 2016)



The coast of Suriname is part of the coastal system, which extends from the mouth of the Amazon River
in Brazil to the mouth of the Orinoco River in Venezuela. It is a muddy coastline where mud, including
fine sands, from the Amazon Basin are being deposited. The coast is subjected to active
geomorphological development, which is determined by a system of cyclic accretion and erosion. Both
are linked to the presence of shoreface-attached mudflats and mud banks, which continuously migrate
to the west (GOS, 2016).
The Global Lithological Map (GLiM) 19 developed by the University of Hamburg was used to extract the
soil types of Suriname (see Figure 5-7). The soils over the major area of Suriname consist of
metamorphic rocks in the interior highland geographic region, followed by siliciclastic sedimentary rocks
mainly along the coastal plain and savannah belt regions). Acid plutonic rocks, acid volcanic rocks, basic
plutonic rocks, and other rocks are distributed in lower proportions around the interior highland
geographic region (GLiM, 2022). The siliciclastic sedimentary rocks are clastic non-carbonate
sedimentary rocks that are almost exclusively silica-bearing, therefore, mining activities in these silica
bearing soils requires special protection measures for exposed personnel.
A more detailed graphical depiction of Suriname’s geology and mineral resources is presented in Figure
5-8.
