5.2.4     Water Resources
Water is an important and valuable resource (raw material), and its value will increase in the future, It is
also one of the important resources of Suriname. A compelling standard for regional and zoning plans
will be the protection of the quality of both soil and surface water. Therefore, the mapping of existing
water resources, and the planning of new ones is of utmost importance. The drainage of areas is a key
issue in planning a livable and healthy environment, and in the development of regional and zoning
plans. Storage of water will become a standard component of all regional plans. Laws and regulations
regarding the use and extraction of water will be incorporated into the new planning legislation (GOS,
2017).
The pollution of Suriname's water resources is one of the most threatening issues in the development
process: this relates to the pollution of waterways, such as rivers and creeks, often through illegal
production activities such as gold mining (GOS, 2017).

5.2.4.1    Water Sources and Quality
In Suriname, water resources are abundant and can be found as surface or groundwater. The total
outflow into the Atlantic ocean consist of 80% of the basement area runoff (126,500 km2), 8% of the
savannah area and 8% of the coastal plain areas (21,000 km2). (SWRIS, 2022)
The main fresh water source is the abundant annual rainfall, which, together with the topography, soil
types and land cover has resulted in many streams and large wetlands. Seven main rivers, originating
in the Interior of the country, annually convey about 4,800 m3/s of fresh water into the Atlantic Ocean,
which is about 30% of the annual rainfall. The Marowijne and the Corantijn Rivers contribute 70% to the
total discharge. Of the remaining rainfall, the largest part evaporates and only a small part percolates to
the aquifers, recharging ground water reserves. The hilly to mountainous interior has a dense network
of streams, while the low-lying coastal area has extensive swamps and fewer streams. Some of these
swamps have salt or brackish water. Surface water resources (rivers, creeks and swamps) are mainly
used for irrigation (e.g., for rice and banana cultivation) and for the generation of hydropower.
Groundwater is mainly used for potable purposes. However, excessive extraction in some areas results
in increased intrusion of saltwater. (Berrenstein, 2016)

5.2.4.1.1 Surface waters
The basement area is the major source of surface water, and the savannah belt is the major source of
groundwater runoff. (SWRIS, 2022) The main surface waters in Suriname are presented in Figure 5-9.

            Rivers
            Suriname has seven major streams draining toward the Atlantic Ocean (see Table 5-1). The largest are
            the Marowijne and Corantijn rivers that form the country’s borders, respectively, in the east and the west.
            These two rivers flow northward and drain almost 58% of the country. The Coppename and the
            Suriname rivers also flow northward and together drain about 24% of the country. The smallest rivers
            are the Nickerie, Saramacca, and Commewijne rivers, which drain 16% of the country’s waters. The
            final 2% of the country consists of coastal areas with direct drainage into the Atlantic Ocean. The
            Suriname river drains on average about 4,800 m3/s (756 mm/year) freshwater into the Atlantic ocean.
            The main rivers are tidal and contain brackish water in the coastal area. (SWRIS, 2022).

            All four major rivers and their near-coastal subsidiaries have estuarine characteristics. The large
            volumes of tidal water and the strong tidal currents give these river estuaries a more or less funnel-
            shape and a wide mouth. They are characterized by mixing up of fresh and muddy saline water, and by
            relatively large tidal variations. In the river estuaries considerable quantities of marine mud are moved
            upriver with the intruding tide. Sedimentation of this mud occurs on the riverbed and as flats at the inside
            of river bends. The opposite outer bend, on the other hand, may be eroded by undercutting of the
            riverbank. (GOS, 2016)
            Swamps and Wetlands
            The coastal area of Suriname, in particular the young Coastal plain, is very low and flat with elevations
            of between the 0-10m. The “coastal belt” is about 5 km wide in the east and about 50 km wide in the
            west. Swamps cover about 60 percent of the coastal plain. In many areas, water is fresh during the wet
            seasons from precipitation falling directly on the swamps. During dry seasons, the swamps revert to
            brackish conditions. The four largest swamps are the Nani swamp, Coronie swamp, Coesewijne swamp
            and Surnau swamp. (SWRIS, 2022)




            Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                          Page 81
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL




The Nanni swamp supplies irrigation water for about 18,000 ha of agricultural lands, mostly for rice
crops. The total area of the swamp is about 1,550 km2. The only source of water available for the swamp
is rainfall and inflow from the Zanderij formation and the Old coastal plain. A water balance shows that
in a year with average rainfall, the discharge is 12.5 m3/s. In an extreme wet year discharge increases
to 16.8 m3/s., and in an extreme dry year the discharge can fall to 9.5 m3/s. (SWRIS, 2022).
The total area of the Coronie swamp is about 700 km2. The area of the Coesewijne swamp depends on
its water level and during the rainy season it may extend over 800-900 km2. (SWRIS, 2022)
Reservoirs
The artificial lake, the Brokopondo reservoir22, is the largest artificial open freshwater resource in
Suriname. It is located in the Suriname river at Afobaka, 194 km upriver. It covers an area of 1,560 km2.
The purpose of this reservoir is to provide electricity for the aluminum smelter at Paranam (operational
in 1964). Controlled discharge at Brokopondo provides a mean yearly flow of approximately 250 m3/s.
(SWRIS, 2022)

5.2.4.1.2 Groundwater and aquifers
The coastal plain area plays an important role in the maintenance of drinking water reserves because
the greatest amount of rainfall percolates into the ground here, recharging the freshwater aquifers.
These aquifers are the main resource for potable water in the coastal areas (mainly around the capital).
Ninety-five percent of the country’s total supply of potable water comes from ground water. The ground
water resources of Suriname are used for public supply and to lesser extent industry. Suriname contains
two hydrologically distinct provinces, the Interior Precambrian Shield of crystalline rocks, comprising 80
percent of the country, and the coastal plain basin, comprising the remaining 20 percent. There is an
abundance of good quality groundwater contained in the coastal basin. Groundwater in the young
coastal plain is not renewable, however, groundwater in the old coastal plain and savannah belt area is
renewable. (SWRIS, 2022)
The aquifers of Suriname are in the coastal basin, which are built up of unconsolidated sediments
consisting of a sequence of clay, sands, sandy clay, clayey sands, gravel, with more or less kaolin
content, and thin bed organic compound. These aquifers, which have been classified based on the
geological ages, are the Nickerie, Onverwacht, A-sand, Coesewijne, Zanderij, Coropina and Demerara.
The most important freshwater aquifers from where water is withdrawn are (SWRIS, 2022):
 A-sand aquifers: no recharge; depths from 130-190 m
 Coesewijne aquifers: no recharge; depths from 70-110 m, and
 Zanderij aquifers: recharge from Savannah area; depths from 15-60 m

5.2.4.2       Water Use and Accessibility
While improving water quality is critical to prevent disease, improving the accessibility and availability of
drinking water is equally important, particularly for women and girls who usually bear the primary
responsibility for carrying water, often over long distances. Overall, 98.2 % of the population in Suriname
has access to improved drinking water sources, 99% in urban region, 98 % in rural coastal and 91% in
the rural interior region. (GBS, March 2020).
The source of drinking water for the population varies by district. In Paramaribo, 88% of the population
uses drinking water that is piped into their dwelling or into their yard or plot. For Nickerie this is 81% and
for Wanica and Para this is 72%. The households in the districts of Commewijne (27%), Brokopondo
(33%) and Sipaliwini (6%) have the lowest access to piped water into their dwelling. The second most
important source of drinking water is rainwater collection. In Sipaliwini 73% of the households use
rainwater. In Brokopondo and Sipaliwini, 8% of the households use surface water (rivers and ponds) as
sources of drinking water, which is considered an unsafe source29. (GBS, March 2020).
In general, the water quality in Suriname is good, but the quality of surface water in both urban and rural
areas is under severe pressure by mining and industrial activities, poor waste processing and insufficient

5.3     BIOLOGICAL ENVIRONMENT AND BIODIVERSITY

5.3.1    Ecosystems
The natural terrestrial ecosystems of Suriname are shown in Figure 5-13 and can be characterized as
follows (Berrenstein, 2016):
 Mangrove forest and brackish herbaceous swamps are estuarine and influenced by coastal
  changes and tidal action, consisting of mangrove forests, locally interrupted by salty to brackish
  lagoons and low vegetation of succulent salt plants and brackish herbaceous swamps. Mangrove
  forests protect the coastline and riverbanks against erosion and stimulate accretion, serve as
  nursery grounds for many species of marine fish and shrimps, and contain a high degree of
  biodiversity. The estuarine zone of Suriname is a wetland of international importance as it contains
  the feeding and nesting sites for Caribbean coastal birds and feeding grounds for migratory birds
  from North America. Along the coastline, mainly in the eastern part of the country, sand and shell
  beaches are found. These beaches are nesting places of international importance for four species
  of sea turtles.
 Freshwater herbaceous swamps dominate the Young Coastal Plain and part of the Old Coastal
  Plain. These wetlands play an important role in supplying freshwater to the estuarine zone, thus
  contributing to the maintenance of the brackish condition of these waters. The swampy areas are
  inundated throughout most of the year, allowing a peat layer to accumulate on top of the mineral
  soil.
 Low swamp forest is a low swamp forest, including palm swamp forest, covering about 3% of
  Suriname. If no forest fires occur, it develops into high swamp forest.
 Swamp forests are high swamp forests and creek forests. High swamp forests are found in the
  shallow freshwater swamps of the coastal plain where strong fluctuations in surface water levels
  occur, being the climax vegetation in the ecological succession of wet areas. Creek forests are found
  along creeks and are enriched by a large number of species from the surrounding high dryland
  forest.
 Marsh forest is a seasonal swamp forest found on poorly drained soils. During the rainy seasons,
  the soil may be totally inundated. In the dry seasons, the soil does not desiccate. Species diversity
  is intermediate between that of the high swamp forests, and the high dryland forests. Marsh forests
  are usually rich in palms.
 High dryland forest covers about 80% of Suriname, which is found at 400-600 meters above sea
  level. These are upland forests with the presence of a high and dense canopy at 25-45m with
  emergent trees up to 50-60m. Tree species diversity is high (between 100-300 species per hectare),
  it is an important habitat for large mammals and houses at least 500 bird species.
 Mountain forests are upland forests found above 400m. These forests are frequently covered in
  clouds, which reduces the solar radiation and plant productivity. Temperatures are lower and the
  average humidity is higher than in high dry land forest of the lowlands. Epiphytes (such as mosses,
  ferns, orchids and bromeliads are abundant in both numbers and species. The flora and fauna of
  these montane forests is quite different from those of the lowland forests.
 High and low xerophytic forests are found in savannah areas. This type of forest commonly grows
  on excessively drained soils and on permeable soils resting on impermeable subsoils, hard pans
  and rocks. As a result, there is a water shortage in the soil during dry seasons. This vegetation type
  can also be found in the hilly/mountainous areas in the interior, especially where laterite caps,
  conglomerates, dolerite and granite rocks and sandstones are covered with a thin layer of soil,
  where they are also known as mountain savannah forest.
 Open savannah can be considered as remnants of the extensive Pleistocene climate savannah,
  that once covered Suriname almost entirely. Savannah ecosystems only survived where they were
  frequently burnt. At present, ten different types of savannahs have been distinguished in Suriname.




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                     Page 90

    Most savannahs are found scattered over the savannah belt. In the absence of fire, savannah
    vegetation eventually develops into forest.

5.3.1.1   Coastal and Marine resources
The GOS reports that there are serious concerns related to coastal and marine resources, since these
are being subject to depletion, including marine water, beaches and coastlines, marine protected areas,
mangroves, fisheries and aquaculture, and other coastal and marine resources. Particularly marine
water and coastal areas are under increasing environmental stress from pollution, overfishing, and
degradation of coastlines (GBS, March 2020)
Suriname’s marine area is subdivided in four zones (GBS, March 2020):
    1. The Continental Inner or Brown water Zone: The water reaches a depth of about 30 m and
       is brown due to the heavy load of mud; along the coast, there are extensive mud banks that
       move slowly to the west, and sand banks that either also move along or have fixed locations
       near the mouths of major rivers;
    2. The Continental Mid or Green-water Zone: The water is between 30 and 60 m deep and is
       still a bit muddy, but much less so than in the previous zone; the water has a greenish tint due
       to the abundance of algae, and is thus biologically very productive;
    3. The Continental Outer or Blue-water Zone: The water is between 60 and 100 m deep and is
       clear, not muddy; the water has a blue tint due to the limited presence of algae, and is
       biologically less productive than the previous zone;
    4. The Deep Sea Blue-water Zone: The water is blue and deeper than in the previous zone; this
       zone starts where the continental slope begins to drop off (this slope starts at about 100 m
       depth, and levels off at several thousand meters below the surface of the sea).

5.3.1.2   Sensitive ecosystems
Despite being quite resilient and fast growing, mangrove ecosystems are considered sensitive globally
due to the key roles of the plants themselves in coastal ecological and geomorphological processes.
The six mangrove species are present in Suriname (MBG, 2022), including red mangrove (Rhizophora
harrisonii, Rhizophora mangle, Rhizophora racemose), white mangrove (Laguncularia racemosa) and
black mangrove (Avicennia germinans and Avicenia schaueriana) species. The conservation of
Suriname mangroves seems relatively ensured, as the vast majority of their coastal distribution is
currently protected by four MUMAs and one Nature Reserve (see below) along the Suriname coast
(Figure 5-15). In addition, GOS received international funding to setup a Mangrove Biodiversity
Monitoring System in 2019 with 12 permanent monitoring stations, and this work was able to determine
that mangrove cover in Suriname is estimated to have increased by approximately 1% over the period
1988-2018 (SBB, 2019).

5.3.3      Forest Management
In 2017, the government identified that the pristine natural forest (14.8 million hectares of tropical forest),
which is largely still in the ‘heart’ of the Suriname would be divided into different categories, each with
its own economic potential. The wood production forest (4.5 million ha) accounts for 30.4 percent of the
total tropical forest. Of the production forest, 62 percent had already been produced in 2015. The
integration of the national development planning and the regional planning should result in structure and
zoning plans, which should facilitate the sustainable use and management of forests: strengthening
regulatory and supervisory institutions and the involvement of the local population are key principles in
this approach. Suriname actively participates in REDD+. The program can play an important role in the
activities that should be implemented to operationalize Suriname’s sustainable development strategy.
This international program focuses on the provision of technical assistance through the application of
innovative technology, analysis and reporting methods, as well as by mobilizing financing (GOS, 2017).

5.3.4      Deforestation
Despite Suriname’s wealth of forest cover, the negative impact from mining industries, the largest sector
of the country’s economy, has been evident, both from illegal (small- scale) and legal mining. Although
this sector has attracted most of the investments (national and international) in the country, consequently
raising the export trend and the development of related sectors35, it is also the cause of almost 70% of
the country’s annual deforestation(see Figure 5-16). In addition, other change drivers include
hydropower construction, agriculture (including slash and burn), and road construction. (Terra-i, 2014)
The Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 report for Suriname (FAO, 2020) indicates that about
97% of the country is still covered by forest, thus being equal with French Guyana as the most forested
country in the world. Indeed, Suriname has a very low deforestation rate, which does not show an
increase in recent years, ranging from 0.05% to 0.1% over the last decade (see Figure 5-18). Suriname
has a long history of sustainable forest management practices and forest protection. The Ministry of
Physical Planning, Land and Forest Management (Min. of RGB) is the Ministry that is responsible for
forest management in Suriname. Within this Ministry, the Foundation for Forest Management and
Production Control (SBB) is the institution responsible for sustainable forest management in the country.
As a forestry institution, SBB has the responsibility to report to the Global Forest Resources Assessment
(FRA) 2020. (FAO, 2020)
The designation of 2.3 million ha of the country (14% of the total land area) as protected areas, and the
development of the Celos Management System as a tool for the sustainable utilization of the 4 million
ha forest designated for sustainable production of forest products, within the so called "Forest Belt", are
evidence of the country's effort to keep the natural forest intact. (FAO, 2020)
In Suriname, the so-called Reduced Impact Logging (RIL) system is practiced and promoted in the
production forest, minimizing the damages to the forest as a result that the forest cover remains intact
even after timber has been harvested, by allowing natural regeneration. Nevertheless, the increased
timber production has its challenges, to monitor the application of this RIL-guidelines as mentioned in
the draft Code Of Practice for SFM, which might lead to unforeseen forest degradation (FAO, 2020).
Developments in sectors other than the forestry sector also leads to deforestation, for instance mainly
due to planned and unplanned mining, mostly gold mining, a fabricated hydropower lake, agriculture,
infrastructure construction etc. (FAO, 2020). The total area of deforestation due to ASGM for the period
of 2000 to 2016 is around 700.28 km2 (GOS, 2019a). The mining areas (gold and bauxite) are being
rehabilitated with tree planting; approximately 1,150 ha of the mining areas has been rehabilitated (FAO,
2020).

5.3.5   Biodiversity management
Suriname has already made a great investment in the preservation of its biodiversity by designating
territories as nature-parks or protected areas. The strategy to protect and manage these environmental
areas is the highest priority for biodiversity preservation. However, the government recognizes that it
does not mean that the preservation of this would be unimportant outside these environmental areas.
In particular, after considering the main factors threatening Suriname’s high biodiversity:
       Mining (specifically gold mining);
       Forestry (in particular non-regulated logging);
       Both the legal and illegal hunting and fishing and trade in protected animals; and
       Mechanical agriculture and the use of agrochemicals.

5.3.6   Protected Areas
Protected areas have been established based on the following legislative products (Ouboter, 2002):
 Police Penal Code of 1915 (amended in 1942): Estuary of the Coppename River; became
  Coppename Monding Nature Reserve in 1961, based on the Nature Preservation Law of 1954.

 Nature Preservation Law (Government Bulletin 1954, No. 26), amended in 1992: All present Nature
  Reserves.
 “Agricultural Act” of 1936 and Degree L-2 of 15 June 1982: Brownsberg Nature Park was given on
  long-term lease to the Foundation for Nature Preservation (STINASU) based on this act.
 Planning Act (Government Bulletin 1973, No. 89): Bigi Pan Multiple-Use Management Area was
  created based on this act.
 Forest Management Act (Government Bulletin 1992, No. 80): Provides the possibility for maintaining
  forests that could have special scientific, educational, cultural, or recreational value.
The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) reports that Suriname has 22 Protected Areas, of

5.3.7     Key Biodiversity Areas
Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) are sites that contribute significantly to the global persistence of biodiversity, on land,
in freshwater or on the seas. These sites have been identified over the last four decades by an international network

 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL


of NGOs, academic institutions and government organizations using a series of complementary approaches. Two
subsets of KBAs have been identified so far across virtually all countries worldwide (IBAT, 2022):
          Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs; over 13,000 sites identified by the BirdLife International
           Partnership)
          Alliance for Zero Extinction Sites (AZEs; 853 sites identified by the Alliance for Zero Extinction)
KBAs have been identified for birds by the BirdLife International Partnership, for Critically Endangered or Endangered
species restricted to single sites through the Alliance for Zero Extinction, and for other mammals, reptiles, amphibians,
fish, plants and invertebrates through the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF) hotspot profiling process.

5.4       SOCIO-ECONOMIC
This section presents the key and relevant socio-economic aspects of the current conditions in Suriname, in relation
to mining development. These and other aspects will be addressed in more detail during the SESA.

5.4.1       Demographics and Population
The great diversity of the population of Suriname comprises Indigenous tribes37 (Native Amerindians) and tribal people
(descendants of African slaves), Maroon diaspora, the European diaspora (Dutch descendants), Javanese diaspora
(descendants or Indonesia), Hindostani diaspora (descendants or India), creoles and others, while the greatest
contribution of all these ethnic groups is the preservation of cultural values, norms and traditions. The population
composition in percentage is as follows: Hindustani, 27.4%; Creoles, 17.7%; Maroons, 14.7%; Javanese, 14.6%;
Mixed, 12.5%, others (Chinese, Indigenous people, Lebanese, European, etc.) The percentage of Indigenous
population in Suriname is only 3.8%, mainly living in different parts of the country (GOS, 2020).
According to the geographical data sourced from the National Land Monitoring System of Suriname (GOS, 2022), the
Maroon and Amerindian populations are geographically concentrated in the districts of Sipaliwini, Para and
Brokopondo. All of them are in the interior zone of the country, far from the coastline. While the coastal strip of the
Atlantic Ocean is a fertile and cultivated plain area where most of the population lives, the interior is sparsely populated
and characterized by dense tropical forests.
Out of the 10 districts of Suriname, Sipaliwini hosts the largest number of Amerindians’ villages (23) and Maroons’
villages (138). This is followed by the districts of Para and Marowijne, which have 14 and 10 Amerindian villages
respectively, and the district of Brokopondo that has 30 villages inhabited by Maroons. The remaining districts of
Suriname host less than 5 villages inhabited by Amerindians and/or Maroons. A brief analysis of the number of villages
classified by culture per district and resorts, is presented in Table 5-11.
It is worth mentioning that the data consulted and hosted by GOS (2022) does not include the population residing in
the district of Paramaribo.

Dutch is the official language; however more than 16 other languages are spoken. Sranang Tongo (Surinamese, is

In 2019, the estimated population of Suriname reached a total of 598,000 inhabitants over a land territory of 163,820
km2 (approximately 3.65 inhabitants per km2). The sex distribution of the population accounted for 51.4% being female
(307,372 inhabitants) and 48.6% being males (290,628 inhabitants). In 2019, 19.3% had 2 household38 members,
17.3% had 3 household members and 17.5% had 4 household members. Only 3.9% had more than 9 household
members. Most households in Paramaribo and Wanica have a household size of 2 to four household members (GBS,
March 2020).

5.4.2       Education
In Suriname, the education system consists of pre-primary, primary, junior and senior secondary schools, which also
includes technical and vocational education as well as higher or tertiary (technical/ vocational) education (GOS,
2022a). Completion rates are 85 % at primary education level and progressively decreasing at the junior secondary
and senior secondary level to respectively 49 % and 24% (GOS, 2022a).Completion rates are higher for children living
in urban areas and those from to the richest quintiles compared to their peers from the rural areas and the poorest
quintile. The literacy rate in Suriname is about 98 percent, and on average, less than 10 percent never completed
primary education.
The Covid-19 pandemic has adversely impacted learning due to school closures and limitations in rolling out distance
learning. This learning loss will mainly weigh in on labor productivity going forward, putting the students from low-
income households in a disadvantageous position (WBG, 2022a).

For the rural and tribal communities in Suriname, primary education is the highest accessible level in their own region
and in some areas, there are secondary schools (Zanderij, Albina and Apoera). Only the Nickerie district provides
senior secondary education in addition to the capital city of Paramaribo (VIDS, 2020).

5.4.3       Health and Sanitation
Access to safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) is essential for good health, welfare and productivity
and is widely recognized as a human right39. Inadequate WASH is primarily responsible for the transmission of
diseases such as cholera, diarrhea, dysentery, hepatitis A, typhoid and polio. Diarrhea diseases exacerbate
malnutrition and remain a leading global cause of child deaths. Drinking water may be contaminated with human or
animal feces containing pathogens, or with chemical and physical contaminants with harmful effects on child health
and development. While improving water quality is critical to prevent disease, improving the accessibility and
availability of drinking water is equally important, particularly for women and girls who usually bear the primary
responsibility for carrying water, often over long distances. (GBS, March 2020).
The most significant environment-related diseases in Suriname are malaria, dengue fever and Leptospirosis. These
can be reduced through good public policies and making financial investments, expanding access to water, sanitation
facilities and hygiene education, ensuring that garbage is collected properly, promoting the use of clean household
fuels, and controlling the (insect and animal) vectors that transmit diseases. The total number of confirmed cases or
hospitalized cases reported between 2015 and 2019 for Malaria, Dengue, Leptospirosis Chikungunya and Zika are
presented in Table 5-12.

Suriname does not have wastewater treatment systems for municipal households nor treatment facilities for Industrial
facilities. The amount of wastewater is estimated to be equal to the amount of water delivered (GOS, 2019a).
Considering that an estimated that terms of water consumption consumed through the SWM network in 2019 (see
Table 5-4 in Section 5.2.4.2.1), the wastewater discharged without treatment in the districts supplied by the SWM is
estimated to be 28,323,000 m3. Part of the domestic sewage (feces and urine) from urban areas, is treated in septic
tanks (in 2010, 86% of homes in Paramaribo had septic tanks). The effluent of the septic tanks is collected in the street
sewers and drains indirectly to the river through the Saramacca canal or is pumped into the Atlantic Ocean through
pumping stations (GEF-CReW, 2010). The situation in the regional or rural areas follows a similar pattern to that of
Paramaribo and the greater Paramaribo area, with no existing infrastructure or treatment facilities for household or
industrial facilities.

   Health and gold mining activities
   Gold mining goes together with health threats due to water pollution from mercury and cyanide, poor working
   conditions and housing, and lack of health facilities Some problems that occur due to the small scale and illegal gold
   mining are degradation of forest lands by wildly, scattered excavation, inefficient mining practices, social disruption
   and destabilization of local communities (GBS, March 2020). This is of particular concern, given that “relatively high
   levels of mercury have been found in hair samples from women and children in interior areas of Suriname"… “levels
   similar to those found in previous cohort studies that have found negative neurodevelopmental impacts on children
   exposed during gestation and possibly during early childhood“ (Ouboter, et al., 2018).
   In terms of mercury, the GOS calculated the releases of mercury into the environment for each source category. The
   primary metal production accounts for 97% of the releases, as seen in Table 5-14 (GOS, 2019a). The GOS identified
   that the individual sub-categories contributing with the highest mercury releases to the atmosphere were:
         1. Gold and silver extraction with the mercury-amalgamation process (89%)
         2. Informal waste burning and Informal dumping of general waste (6%)
         3. Gold extraction and initial processing by other processes than mercury amalgamation (3%)
   The individual mercury releases sub-categories contributing with the highest inputs of new mercury were:
         1. Gold and silver extraction with the mercury-amalgamation process (70%)
         2. Gold extraction and initial processing by other processes than mercury amalgamation (27%).


   Community health and mercury
   Mercury releases to the environment from mining are described below:
          Air: Diffuse sources as small-scale gold mining from informally burned waste with fluorescent lamps, batteries
           thermometers, and during the amalgamation process of gold with mercury.
          Water: Surface run-off and leachate from mercury contaminated soil and waste dumps
          Land: Uncollected waste products dumped or buried informally, local un-confined releases from industry such as
           on-site hazardous waste storage/burial or spreading of sewage sludge with mercury content on agricultural land
           (sludge used as fertilizer).
          By-products and impurities: Metal mercury or calomel as by-product from non-ferrous metal mining (high mercury
           concentrations)
          Sector specific waste treatment / disposal: Hazardous industrial waste with high mercury content that is deposited
           in dedicated safe sites, and confined deposition of tailings and high-volume rock/waste from extraction of non-
           ferrous metals.

   It was estimated that approximately 62,159 kg of mercury is released into the environment each year due to ASGM,
   of which 16,267 kg was released to air, leaving 45,892 kg mercury released to land and water. Thus, mercury pollution
   from ASGM in Suriname can be linked to the fact that there is often no separate collection or treatment of tailings
   before release into the environment. (GOS, 2019a). In addition, some hot spots of mercury contamination related to
   mining may include:
         Tailings/residue deposits from artisanal and large-scale gold mining.
                   o    In the ASGM areas, tailings are not controlled and are directly deposited into the environment. Some
                        companies have taken control measures before waste is discharged into the environment.
                   o    For the large-scale companies, the waste is collected into a controlled tailing pond, the overflow is
                        discharged into the environment in a controlled matter.
         Tailings/residue deposits from other non-ferrous metal extraction.
   These hot spots need to be evaluated, in terms of location and extent, contamination path analysis, potential
   affectation of communities and sensitive ecosystems.

   5.4.4      Labor market
   The labor market is divided into three components, which, although connected, are very distinct because of their
   nature, size and challenges. There are two main institutions responsible for the production of labor market information
   in Suriname. 1) The Labor Market Directorate of the MOL collects and analyses data based on jobseekers who have
   registered at the Department for Direct Mediation in that Ministry. 2) The General Bureau for Statistics (ABS) collects
   data on the workforce during regular household surveys, as well as the population census carried out every 10 years.
   The most recent nationwide data are from the population census of 2012. More recent data, (available until 2016),
   have been derived from the household survey. However, data from the household surveys are only gathered for the
   districts of Paramaribo, Wanica, Commewijne and Nickerie. The data collected during the census are sex
   disaggregated.




   Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                                                 Page 110
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL


In 2018, the Gold Sector Ordinance (OGS40) identified that around 40,000 persons are directly and indirectly involved
with ASGM activities in Suriname, and 7342 persons are registered by OGS as employees directly involved with
ASGM activities. Nevertheless, the number of illegal ASGM miners and whether they hold a concessions rights
issued by the government under the Mining Decree are unknown and would require a special study. In addition, the
potential exposure of ASGM miners to mercury through different methods, such as mercury amalgamation of gold is
unknow, (GOS, 2019a). Considering that the majority of ASGM taking place in Suriname's Greenstone Belt, where
most gold deposits are located, is being undertaken by overall Brazilians (Garimpeiros), and to a lesser extent by the
Surinamese Maroons, (GEF, 2016), the potential Occupational Health and Safety issues from these activities have
not been considered in this sector and therefore need to be evaluated.

       7. Agriculture, Hunting and Forestry.

The economy is driven by its abundant natural resources, with mining accounting for nearly half of public sector
revenue and gold representing more than 80 % of total exports, what makes Suriname extremely vulnerable to external
shocks (WBG, 2022a).

5.4.6    Poverty
About one in four people in Suriname, representing 26 % of the population, live on less than US$5.50 a day. The
poverty rate is much higher in the interior region where more than half the population live in poverty. Extreme poverty,
defined as the percentage of the population with an income below US$1.9 a day was estimated at 5 percent (WBG,
2022a).
Suriname was severely impacted by the COVID 19 pandemic, increasing the existing domestic vulnerabilities. Critical
sectors, such as mining and oil, took major hits and many employees in the services and sales sectors experienced
temporary job losses (WBG, 2022a).




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                     Page 113
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL


The Indigenous and Maroon tribal communities in the interior are (materially) the poorest groups in Suriname. For the
Maroon population this represented 74.2% and for the Indigenous population it reached 65.4%, of which another
18.1% was considered semi-poor (VIDS, 2020).

5.4.7       Indigenous and Tribal Peoples

5.4.7.1       Land acquisition
Indigenous villages in the Amazon forest are being affected by deforestation and mercury contamination caused from
small-scale gold mining. Such contamination is not only affecting their health but also the environment, contaminating
rivers and fish41. Mercury contamination, whether from legal or illegal mining, comes mainly from small-scale mining
practices. Large mining companies in Suriname are currently phasing out the use of mercury seeking more
environmentally friendly alternatives. Meanwhile, mercury contamination affects the health of community members
and has a direct impact on their way of life. Fish is the main source of proteins for many Indigenous and tribal
communities and therefore, they are obligated to seek alternative protein sources. In addition, Suriname is alleged to
be selling Indigenous land to gold-mining organizations42.
Along with Guyana and French Guiana, Suriname is the only Amazonian country or territory not to have ratified
Convention 169, a 1989 treaty from the International Labour Organization (ILO) that legally recognizes Indigenous
and tribal peoples’ right to self-determination (Lyons & Espinosa, 2022).
The impacts of gold mining will be reviewed in detail during the Environmental Impact Assessment to be conducted
during the SESA study,

5.4.8       Archaeological and Cultural Heritage
The archaeological record in Suriname extends back at least 10,000 years. In the western hemisphere, archaeological
resources are typically divided into two broad chronological categories. Pre-Contact (also known as Pre-Columbian)
resources are archaeological resources that pre-date the arrival of European explorers and colonizers while post-
Contact resources are Indigenous and/or Euro-American resources that postdate European arrival. The following
sections provide a summary of the types of archaeological resources known to occur in Suriname. Both pre-Contact
and post-Contact archaeological resources can be found in urban and rural settings, with sites in rural and
undeveloped areas as the most susceptible to be impacted from mining projects.
Pre-contact archaeological sites have been identified across Suriname (Figure 5-28). A 2003 synthesis of the
archaeological record identified approximately 109 Pre-Columbian archaeological sites in the country (Versteeg A. H.,
2003). While the distribution of previously recorded sites suggests a greater concentration of Pre-Columbian sites
along the coast plain, this is more likely a result of 20th century agricultural, industrial, infrastructure, and other activities
uncovering sites rather than a lack of or lower number of sites being present in the interior.

During the 19th and early 20th century, the industrialization of the agricultural and mining sectors resulted in the

archaeological site consisting of the ruined sugar factory and the plantation railway, the oldest railway in Suriname
(Kautzor, 2014a); see Figure 5-29.

The most significant built heritage resource in the country is the Historic Inner City of Paramaribo, which is inscribed
on United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage List. This built heritage
resource consists of mainly wooden buildings, many dating from the 17th through 18th centuries, which stylistically
blend European architectural, North American, and local Creole culture architecture (Figure 5-30). Individual buildings
within the district include the Fort Zeelandia Area (18th century military fort), the current Presidential Palace, St. Petrus
en Paulus Roman Catholic Cathedral, and several historic homes (UNESCO, 2002). The listing of these resources by
the Surinamese government demonstrates the historic and architectural significance of colonial period-built heritage
in the country (SEARCH, 2022).




                   Figure 5-30: Example of Built Heritage Resources in Paramaribo - World Heritage Site
Source: (UNESCO, 2022a)
In addition to the Historic Inner City of Paramaribo, the Surinamese government has nominated the settlement of
Joden Savanne and Cassipora Cemetery for listing on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The site is located south of

 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector

 Scoping Report - FINAL


Paramaribo on the Suriname River and is the location of the earliest Jewish community in the western hemisphere.
Jews fleeing the Spanish Inquisition founded the settlement in 1665, a flourishing agricultural community, and built a
synagogue in 1685,owning multiple plantations throughout the 17th and 18th centuries. The site was abandoned in the
early 19th century when the Jewish community relocated to Paramaribo. Today the site consists of the ruins of the
synagogue, several buildings, and two cemeteries (see Figure 5-31) containing 450 marked graves (UNESCO,
2022b).




        Figure 5-31: Ruins at Joden Savanne and Cassipora Cemetery. Synagogue ruins (left) and cemetery (right)
Source: (Jodensavanne Foundation, 2022)
In addition to these two internationally significant sites, the built heritage of Suriname includes diverse statues and
monuments associated with historic events as well as the diverse ethnic groups who emigrated to the country at
various times. While historic buildings, structures, and monuments in urban settings are unlikely to be subject to
impacts from mining development, built heritage resources associated with historic economic and social activity in
rural or areas are more likely to be impacted by mining projects. (SEARCH, 2022). Examples of these types of
resources include historic sugar refineries, historic plantation homes and offices, and historic transportation
infrastructure such as railways and canals, all of which played a significant role in the history and development of
Suriname, and are significant for the historic, architectural, and aesthetic value (Figure 5-32).

Other cultural heritage aspect are the living heritage resources, which include buildings, structures, places, and/or
natural landscape features actively used by stakeholders as part of a living cultural tradition, often associated with
religious beliefs, practices, ceremonies, or rituals; folklore or oral history; and/or mythical or historic events. Living
heritage resources associated with emigrant and Indigenous populations can be found across Suriname. In urban
areas, religious structures such as churches, mosques, synagogues, temples, and cemeteries used by the resident
Christian, Muslim, Jewish, and Hindu populations are an important component of Suriname’s Built Heritage. These
resources are typically located in urban centers or villages, away from mining developments. Cemeteries, however,
can be found in rural settings and typically are significant living heritage resources for local communities, providing a
visible link to their ancestors and providing a sense of belonging to a location or place (SEARCH, 2022).

Living cultural heritage

Living heritage resources of the Indigenous and Maroon populations of Suriname are more likely to be found in rural
areas that could be potentially impacted by mining activities. The Indigenous population of Suriname is typically divided
into five Indigenous groups. The Lokono (Arawaks), Kalinya (Caribs), and Warao peoples are found in the coastal
plain while the Trio (Tiryo, Tareno) and Wayana reside in southern Suriname (ACT, 2015). There are also
descendants of other Indigenous peoples who are no longer present today, among others the Akoerio, the Apalai, the
Wai-Wai, the Okomoyana, the Mawayana, the Katuena and the Tunayana. Of these peoples, only a few remain in
Suriname (VIDS, 2020).




                                            Figure 5-33: Indigenous Territories

   Source: (ACT, 2015)

The Indigenous groups living in the coastal plain are located outside of the areas targeted for goldmine development,
although living heritage sites associated with these peoples could be impacted by associated infrastructure
development. The Wayana peoples in the southeast of Suriname, however, are located within or near potential
goldmining areas. Wayana communities live in small remote villages often lead by a piyai or shaman centered around
a community house referred to as “tukusipan” (Figure 5-34). These traditional community houses are important living
heritage resources that play a central role in community life (Heemskerk et al. 2007). In addition to the tukusipan, local
cemeteries associated with Wayana communities should be considered locally significant/important living heritage
resources (SEARCH, 2022).

The Maroon population of Suriname is divided into six communities: Aluku, Aukan, Kwinti, Matawai,
Paramak, and Saramaka. Figure 5-35 depicts the traditional territorial affiliations of these six
communities relative to the extent of the goldmining industry in 2014, demonstrating that much of the
modern mining industry is found in the traditional territories of the Matawai, Saramaka, Paramaka, Aluku,
and Aukan communities (ACT, 2015). Natural landscape features such as mountains, creeks, rivers,
and forests play a significant role in Maroon oral history, (as locations of former villages or battlefields
during colonial period conflicts), as well as areas of ritual practice and belief. These places and features
function as important living heritage resources as part of the living cultural tradition of these communities
(ACT, 2016).
Based on the above descriptions of Cultural and Archaeological heritage of Suriname, in the rural areas
these are at risk from the impacts of potential mining developments. A critical component of the SESA
will be to develop policies and frameworks for the identification of physical cultural resources that are
targeted and scaled to the risks presented by the development of the gold mining industry in Suriname,
and the development of standard approaches to avoiding, minimizing, and/or mitigating potential
impacts that are informed through stakeholder consultations.

5.4.9   Gender
According to the Global Gender Gap Index for 2018 (WEF, 2018), Suriname scores well in the field of
education with a gender parity of 0.991, and in the field of health with a gender parity 0.973. But in the
economic participation and opportunities the gender parity the score is only 0.638 (GOS, 2022a). Some
of the areas in which women are lagging behind compared to their male peers are: payment, labor
market participation, unemployment, child labor, engagement in sectors with higher wages and
completion of vocational training (GOS, 2022a).
Results from the Living Conditions Survey in Suriname carried out in 2016-2017 show that the women’s
labor force participation is 43% compared to 68% of men within an urban setting. Only 1% of the men’s
labor force (those who have the potential to work, aged 15-64) are engaged in unpaid care and domestic
work, while this represents 19% for their female counterparts. Additionally, about 98% of those engaged
in unpaid care and domestic work are women (GOS, 2022a).

6 OVERVIEW OF THE MINING SECTOR OF SURINAME
The extractive industries play a central role in Suriname’s economy. Bauxite has been the dominant
industry for most of the past century, although extraction and exports have come to a halt recently as
accessible reserves were exhausted. Gold has emerged as the primary extractive industry, including
private industrial gold mines and substantial artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) operations
that represent a significant source of employment. The state oil company Staatsolie has been
successfully extracting low-cost onshore oil for decades, with new prospects for offshore oil recently
identified. (WBG, 2017). In Suriname, the mining of minerals includes (EITI, 2019b):
       Gold and silver based on the Mining Decree 1986 and Mineral Agreements between
        Government and companies;
       Diamond mining (still in the stages of reconnaissance and therefore not commercialized yet);
       Bauxite (production of bauxite ended in 2015);
       Quarry aggregates for building purposes;
       Other ores (such as kaolin, manganese, chromium, tin, phosphate and silica sand).
The extractives sector drives Suriname’s economy, however, it is highly concentrated with potential for
increased revenue generation from mining. Suriname is located on the Guiana Shield geological
formation that has significant mineral resources. One main bauxite extraction operation dominated the
sector for the past 100 years, but operations ended in 2015 after accessible reserves were exhausted.
Two new significant gold mine operations were established in the past decade (2009-2019). The mining
sector also includes significant informal artisanal and small-scale operations and domestic firms
supplying goods and services to extractive operations. Despite its economic importance, however, there
are significant opportunities for the GOS to improve sector governance and revenue generation from
mining, given limitations in sector revenue controls and traceability. (IBRD, 2019)
The majority of mining is taking place in Suriname's Greenstone Belt, which covers 24,000 km2 of
Central-East Suriname (SS, 2017). The location of the Greenstone Belt is shown in Figure 6-1 with other
key spatial features such as the location of the industrial gold mining sites (Rosebel and Merian mines).
The interior of the country is mineral-rich containing a number of important deposits of bauxite, beryl,
copper, diamonds, gold, platinum, iron ore, manganese, pegmatite and tin; exploitation of minerals
mainly concentrates on bauxite and gold. Historically, extraction activities of mineral ores mainly
occurred in the northern parts of the Interior, but mining activities have increasingly been moving further
south over the last decennia. (Berrenstein, 2016)




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                      Page 122
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL




           Figure 6-1:    Greenstone belt, mining titles and current Industrial Mining sites operating
Source: (GOS, 2022b) and (ACT, 2015) adapted by RINA, 2022



Weak legal and regulatory frameworks and limited institutional capacity hinder economic development,
diversification, and sector governance. In mining, the current 1986 decree governing the sector has not
been complemented with implementing regulations. Management of mining titles and licensing
procedures are far from good practice, resulting in lack of clarity, weak transparency, and risks to
property rights. Institutional capacity to monitor the sector and enforce laws and regulations is weak; the
Geological Mining Service responsible for monitoring mining title holders, for example, has almost no
masters-trained geologists. These challenges in sector regulation and monitoring contribute to limited
GOS revenue generation from the sector. (IBRD, 2019)
There are also gaps in the regulatory framework to manage environmental and social impacts of
economic activities, creating risks for sustainable development and for new private investors. Within
mining, this creates risks for deforestation of the country’s vast forest coverage (more than 90 percent
of national territory) due to illegal gold mining, as well as widespread contaminative usage of mercury
for gold extraction by artisanal and small-scale miners. There are Indigenous and tribal populations
living in areas with mineral potential, which often have land rights conflicts with informal (and formal)
mining operations. Lack of transparency and capacity to monitor and enforce environmental and social
regulations can encourage a race to the bottom across sectors, to the detriment of formally established
firms seeking to comply with global standards such as Responsible Agricultural Investment, Global
Sustainable Tourism Criteria, and IFC Performance Standards on Social & Environmental Sustainability
(IBRD, 2019).

A general analysis of macro-economic development outlook of the mining sector in Suriname is
presented in Appendix B. In economic terms the importance of the mining sector in Suriname is
highlighted, providing some economic and business environment data of the country, such as imports
and exports, gross domestic product (GDP), national integration planning and development
mechanisms. In addition, the appendix provides an overview of the resources sectors with focus on
mining and the key main production clusters (industrial and ASM gold mining), and finally a general
analysis of current status and development or relevant infrastructure to the sector (transport and
energy). It is important to note that Appendix B provides the background for the following sections of
this report.

6.1       FUTURE MINING DEVELOPMENT SCENARIOS
Scenarios are stories that may represent the future. Good scenarios are plausible, challenging and
rigorously constructed to address the most critical questions that decision-makers need to face.
One cannot expect any given scenario to come true as it stands. They are not predictions, preferences,
or forecasts. Rather the process of developing and using scenarios is intended to help participants learn
and generate insights, both from exploring each scenario individually and from comparing and
contrasting them.
Based on this precept the following forecast of possible mining scenarios is put forward as a starting
point. There are three main strands to any analysis.
      1. The first is the external, or global, environment faced by Suriname, its mining sector, and the
         different minerals in the world context. These external factors are largely outside of the influence
         of Suriname, and include commodity prices, substitution, climate change, and technological
         developments.
      2. The second is the internal, or Suriname, environment and how it pertains to the mining industry
         and, ultimately, to a particular scenario. These internal factors should be within the ability of
         Suriname to change, or at least modify, given political will and/or a clear action plan as an
         outcome of the strategic options chosen out of the analysis of the potential scenarios. These
         include, political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal.
      3. The third strand is the integration and use of outcomes, conclusions and analysis from previous
         studies and reports put together over the past two decades on Suriname. These sources are
         an important resource that gives detail, depth and source variety to the analysis from the point
         of view of the geology, economics, policy, legal, environmental, social, and other contexts.

6.1.1     Sector 1: Bauxite
Restart of the bauxite industry that closed in 2015. This scenario has significant upsides if it is done in
conjunction with the opportunities presented in the Oil and Gas sector in Suriname or by the significant
gas finds in neighboring Guyana to produce low-cost electricity for the bauxite-alumina-aluminum
processing and smelting. The recent closure of the bauxite industry after more than 100 years of mining
and processing should have left a significant technological legacy in Suriname that could be reengaged
and, since the international aluminum players have left the country, new contracts can be negotiated
with them, if required.
There are significant challenges to this scenario. Startup costs will be high, with new infrastructure such
as a gas-fired power station, refurbishing of railroad infrastructure and the Paranam plant. Environmental
concerns based on the bauxite deposits being in heavily forested areas, will be a significant concern.
And the definition of bauxite reserves and consequent mine feasibility studies and their ultimate
construction will be high cost and will require many years before production could resume.
Reasons for closure in 2015
         Exhaustion of coastal bauxite reserves




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                        Page 124
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL




       High cost of electricity required to produce alumina, and smelting to produce aluminum
       High cost of shipping bulky bauxite
       Decline in world aluminum prices.
Challenges to restarting bauxite industry:
       Exploration would have to be restarted and reserves would have to be defined and restated
       Bauxite deposits are inland from the coastal plain with significant potential for environmental
        impacts (forest, biodiversity, water quality)
       Bauxite deposits are of lower grade
       Infrastructure dedicated to the bauxite industry through 2015 will have to be re-evaluated and
        recommissioned (railways, Paranam plant)
       Cost for restart of industry.
Opportunities in restarting bauxite industry
       Suriname has significant bauxite reserves
       Potential for cheaper electricity from gas because of potentially large offshore gas finds, based
        on finds in neighboring Guyana, hence lower refining and smelting costs
       Suriname has a stated intention to restart the bauxite industry
       Suriname has over 100 years of experience in bauxite mining with the potential to restart without
        major aluminum mining companies
       New contracts can be negotiated with mining companies
       Suriname has deep coastal waters, which is favorable for bulk shipping.

6.1.2   Sector 2: Large-scale Gold Mining
Large-scale mining is currently undertaken by two mining companies, namely, IAMGOLD (Rosebel
mine) and Newmont (Merian mine). Gold discoveries in Greenstone belts are typically low tonnage, with
small reserves, although they can have a long mining life, a result of the geology of these deposits and
complex exploration required to define ore reserves. Although they are typically mines with good grades,
these characteristics make them difficult financing propositions for their owners, and they are typically
owned by mid-tier and small-tier mining companies. The potential for further discoveries of this type of
mines typically requires diligent exploration over a number of years by dedicated exploration teams.
Their compliance with environmental, social and closure, as well as being regulated by the national legal
code, are generally also guided by international reporting guidelines and requirements, frequently driven
by financing or stock exchange disclosure requirements.
These two large-scale mining companies have both been involved with litigation over land rights and
land use issues with local inhabitants (see section 5.3), which highlights a significant challenge for the
government over land use and rights.
Another challenge is the implementation of adequate environmental legislation, including legislation
covering the closure of these facilities at the end of their commercial lives, which is seen as a legacy of
the bauxite mining industry, for example.
The use of gravity circuits instead of mercury potentially holds valuable lessons and requires skills’
development that might well cross over to the small-scall mining sector. Nevertheless, this will likely
require enabling legislation or tax breaks to achieve. The sharing of knowledge and skills in the




Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                      Page 125
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL




management of deforestation, sediments and soils, and better management of water quality may
eventually trickle down to small-scale mining.
This scenario is less guided by external (global) issues than by the implementation of adequate
legislation and its enforcement, and possibly reforms that look to encourage exploration and retain the
geological knowledge base in-country when a company withdraws from its prospecting areas.
This scenario therefore needs to look at its interface with political, economic, social, technological,
environmental and legal factors internal to Suriname.

6.1.3     Sector 3: Formalization of Small-scale and Artisanal Mining
This scenario entails a detailed evaluation of the small-scale and artisanal mining sector from the
perspective of the small-scale miners. As noted by Heemskerk and van der Kooye, 2002, “the socio-
cultural and economic lives of small-scale gold miners merit more attention. Without incorporating the
opinions, beliefs, and life realities of local miners, policy interventions aimed at changing the behavior
of these miners are doomed to fail.”
From this perspective a full business-type analysis should be undertaken to determine the required
strategy for the sector, with the intention -not of achieving perfection- but achieving meaningful progress
in the particularly important social and environmental challenges around this industry sector.
The significant volume of in-country studies and reports, and the international library of case studies
and knowledge base should be utilized for this purpose.
Success will need to be measured on the basis of policy implementation and meaningful key
performance indicators (KPIs). It should be noted that formalization and legality are two different
concepts that need to be clarified and well understood.

6.2       MINING DEVELOPMENT SCENARIOS

6.2.1     Introduction
As stated in the Inception Report, the proposal is that the analysis of the sector development be based
on two scenarios, a base case (conservative) and accelerated (optimistic) scenarios. The analysis will
be undertaken using assumptions (i.e., discoveries, resource studies, exploration results, Suriname’s
macroeconomic development, ease of doing business/export environment, transport infrastructure and
services) and supporting factors (i.e., global demand for minerals, carbon credit opportunities). Once
the scenarios are agreed by the client and validated by the stakeholders, the identification of
environmental and social risks will be developed around these scenarios. These risks will include
cumulative and indirect impacts by studying the possible location of large- and small-scale mining sites,
and transport infrastructure and services:
         Current developments in the infrastructure sector (ports, highways, local roads, possible
          domestic/national aviation);
         Current constraints and opportunities; and
         Infrastructure needed to support the mining development program (capacity, investment costs,
          timing).
RINA has been reviewing existing policies, programs, plans, studies, and public information material,
such as:
         National and sectoral laws and regulations, national or regional plans, future mining
          development;
         Existing public or private programs or initiatives, current projects, plans and trends;

       Contextual information at the country, sub-national or sector levels (based on screening and

6.2.2   Definition and Assumptions
The Base Case Scenario is a conservative scenario where timing is not considered to be a driving
factor, potential outcomes can therefore be more fully considered and associated risks can be managed
with the extra time available.
The Accelerated Case Scenario is where timing is a significant consideration and the integration of
parts of the subsectors is not contingent on the alignment of all aspects before investment decisions are
made. This scenario appears to be contingent on the early availability of cross funding from the Oil and
Gas industry.

  6.3      POTENTIAL CONFLICTS AROUND MINING
  Suriname’s forests provide housing sustenance to local Indigenous and tribal peoples. These peoples
  can be classified as Amerindians and Maroons, respectively (Kambel and MacKay 1999, in Heemskerk
  and van der Kooye, 2002). Maroons are the descendants of runaway African slaves, who established
  independent communities in the rainforest in the 16th and 17th centuries. These Indigenous and tribal
  peoples have maintained relative political, social and economic sovereignty within the nation state.
  However, their access to land, natural resources and self-determination is vulnerable because the
  government has refused to recognize their individual or group property rights (Kambel and MacKay
  1999, Heemskerk and van der Kooye, 2002). Nevertheless, Article 41 of the Constitution of the Republic
  of Suriname (GOS, 2000) clearly states that ,”Natural riches and resources are the property of the
  nation and shall be used to promote economic, social and cultural development. The nation has the
  inalienable right to take complete possession of its natural resources in order to utilize them to the benefit
  of the economic, social and cultural development of Suriname.”
  Conflicts around mining are likely to revolve around some of the same issues that have proved conflictive
  in the past. Examples of conflicts around the issue of mining concessions and the rights of traditional
  communities are the cases of IAMGOLD and the Ndyuka Maroon community of Nieuw Koffiekamp, and
  the Merian and Paramaka traditional territory (WBG, June 2019c).
  In general, some conflicts around gold mining include (GOMIAN, 2011):
       Between LSM and SSM: Multinationals have acquired concessions in the areas of Gros Rosebel
        (Iam Gold) and Meriam (Newmont), where SSM have been –and still are- working first. The SSM
        have been removed with force and threats of force.
       Among local authorities: Some village chiefs allow miners to work on their village lands against
        payment of a fee or other form of material compensation. Not all traditional leaders agree with these
        practices. In the Ndyuka territory, village heads (kapiteins) were reprimanded by the paramount
        chief (granman) for allowing mining in the Mama Ndjuka creek, an important ceremonial ancestral
        site.
       Between local authorities and community members: Local authorities do not equally distribute the
        compensation they receive from miners working on village land to all villagers who are affected. This
        creates tension.
       Among SSM (local-local; local-migrant; migrant-migrant): Non-gold related conflicts (i.e., over
        women) seem to be the most likely causes of physical fights. Yet conflicts also exist over mining
        rights, access to land, payment, etc. For example, in some areas tribal leaders have decided that
        all migrant miners need to leave to allow local men to earn a living.
       Between SSM and park management (Brownsberg national park): Miners are working in the national
        park, which is not in agreement with the park management guidelines: Between SSM and national
        government: related to all of the above, and primarily to access to land and mining rights.

  6.3.1     IAMGOLD and Ndyuka Maroon community of Nieuw Koffiekamp
  In 1992, the Suriname state granted the Canadian exploration firm Golden Star Resources (GSR),
  exclusive rights to the 17,000 ha Rosebel gold concession in Brokopondo district, 85 km south of
  Paramaribo city. The Ndyuka Maroon community of Nieuw Koffiekamp and the lands used by villages




  Doc. No. P0032241-SR Rev. 2 – January, 2023                                                         Page 133
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report - FINAL




for subsistence activities were situated within this concession. The villagers were never consulted and
only informed after the fact. Neither was the community of Nieuwe Koffiekamp mentioned in the
application of Golden Star for an exploration concession, as required by law (IBP US, 2009 in (WBG,
June 2019c)).
It was proposed that the community would be relocated, but for the people from Nieuw Koffiekamp this
was unacceptable. The community had already been relocated from its original community of
Koffiekamp in the early 1960s, to make place for a hydropower dam. That incidence had been very
traumatic, leading to the loss of traditional lands, livelihood, and important cultural heritage sites. The
government constructed “trans-migration villages” that were not constructed in line with the culture and
customs of the Maroon people, and lacked basic infrastructure (drinking water, electricity).
Complicating the matter was that small-scale gold miners were already active in the area, many of whom
from Nieuw Koffiekamp. These gold miners found –and find- it extremely insulting that they are
considered “illegals” in their own home community. After the Rosebel concession was granted to GSR,
even more small-scale miners moved to the area. GSR threatened to abandon the project if the miners
were not removed and in response, the Minister of Justice and Police threatened with violence if the
miners did not immediately vacate the area. Negotiations between the government and the community
did not generate satisfactory results. According to human rights organization Moiwana '86, at least eight
violations of the American Convention on Human Rights were committed due to company action and
government inaction (MacKay, 2002, in (WBG, June 2019c).
In 2001, the Canadian mining company Cambior acquired the Rosebel gold mine and in 2006, IamGold
took over Cambior and thereby became the owner of Rosebel Gold Mines N.V. Since the
commencement of negotiations between the multinational mining companies, the Suriname government
and the community, periods of relative calm have alternated with fierce protests, roadblocks and violent
outbursts by community members -often small-scale gold miners- against Rosebel Gold Mines N.V.
(Theije, et al., 2014). Apart from the fact that people’s livelihoods had been affected, complaints included
that a community forest area that was used to collect wood and Non-Timber Forest Products was
confiscated; dynamite blasting damaged homes and disturbed elders; and the only access road to the
village was regularly blocked by the firm (e.g., during blasting). Grievance mechanisms should have
been set into place.
In late 2014, in an effort to finally resolve the conflict in Nieuw Koffiekamp, the Commission for
Regulation of the Gold Sector (OGS), ordered small-scale gold miners to leave the IAMGOLD
concession by Christmas. As an alternative, the OGS established a “small-scale gold mining reserve”
several km from the village and advised the Koffiekamp miners to apply for a legal concession. However,
the Koffiekamp gold miners soon discovered that the available concession area was about half the size
of the area that had initially been promised, and after prospecting, they were convinced that the area
did not have economically viable gold deposits (Plein, Makamboa board member, pers. com. 24-02-
2015). Moreover, they found the area too far away. As a result, the gold miners did not move to the
small-scale gold mining reserve.
In following years, the cat and mouse game between Koffiekamp small-scale gold miners and Rosebel
Gold Mines N.V. continued. Inhabitants of the village still experience nuisance and damage as a result
of the company’s activities, including dynamite blasting, ever closer to the village. At the same time, the
company faces difficult exploration conditions, with small-scale gold miners running into the exploration
pit after every dynamite blast – creating an extremely hazardous situation.
In November 2017, IamGold and Makamboa signed an agreement that allowed a selected group of
Makamboa members to mine for gold in a specific section of the Rosebel Concession, named Roma pit.
This agreement resolved problems for a small group of small-scale gold miners, but many others
continue to venture onto other areas of the RGM concession. Moreover, the villagers still suffer from
blasting near their community and severe restrictions on their access to the forest and its resources,
including areas for subsistence plots, hunting, and collecting (e.g., medicinal plants) (WBG, June 2019c)

 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector

6.3.2   Merian and the Paamaka traditional territory
The only clause in the Mining Code that refers to people living in tribal communities is Article 25, which
states that applications for exploitation licenses must include a list of all tribal villages located in or near
the requested concession (subsection 1). The inhabitants of the mentioned villages are “obliged to allow
the holder of [a mining] right to carry out mining operations … on land owned or occupied by them: (a)
provided that they have been notified on time … (b) and have been compensated in advance or
been given assurance for such compensation.” (Art. 47). It is not required that affected communities be
consulted about, participate in, or consent to, the allocation of the concession in question (IDB 2004).
Even these minimal provisions are often ignored; mining concessions are frequently granted on tribal
lands without prior “notification.” Compensation is insufficient or non-existent. The limited legal
protection of traditional communities vis-à-vis external mining interests has caused conflict in several
locations, most notably in Nieuw Koffiekamp and the Paamaka traditional territory/Merian.
The Ministry of Natural Resources has indicated that cultural sites are now taken into account in
concession allocations. And advice from the Ministry of Spatial Planning, Land and Forest Management
(ROGB), the Ministry of Regional Development (RO), and the District commissioners (DC), is now
requested prior to any allocation. The DC also conducts a field orientation and delivers a report. Without
these advisory documents, mining concessions are not granted (WBG, June 2019c).

7 IDENTIFICATION OF ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL RISKS AND
  VULNERABILITIES
This section provides a general description of potential impacts centered in themes (water, air, land use,
geology soils, biodiversity, cultural heritage, etc.) and preliminary mitigation measures to be considered
during the SESA.
Typical environmental impacts or effects of a mining projects include (WBG, 2017):
       landscape alteration (erosion, formation of sinkholes, and so forth) and pollution of air, soil and
        water (surface and groundwater),
       development and/or building of related Infrastructure such as roads, railways, port facilities,
        opening of land areas, construction of buildings, etc.
       mining is a water intensive industry, and the utilization of this resource can be particularly critical
        in areas where water is scarce or is heavily used by other local activities, such as agriculture or
        drinking, or is needed by ecosystems.
       decommissioning and closure of mines can also be a source of negative environmental impacts.
In terms of Artisanal and Small-scale Mining (ASM) communities often operate without any
environmental safeguards, due to the country’s lack of resources to manage environmental (and social)
impacts. Therefore, ASM activities contribute either directly or indirectly to environmental degradation,
through deforestation, loss of biodiversity, wildlife poaching for bush meat, soil erosion, dust, noise,
habitat destruction, introduction of invasive species, siltation, and pollution of water bodies or alterations
to rivers’ regimes (WBG, 2017). In terms of ASGM, the activity has associated environmental and
occupational health issues, particularly when practiced informally or with limited technical and material
resources. The health and well-being of miners, their family members as well as nearby communities is
often adversely affected (WHO, 2016). The WHO classifies the main hazards associated with ASGM
as:
       Chemical hazards associated with the use and/or exposure to mercury, cyanide, exposure to
        chemicals contained in dust like silica, and toxic gases from blasting.
       Biological hazards associated with the infections from waterborne and vector borne diseases,
        sexually transmitted infections (HIV/AIDS) and tuberculosis.
       Biomechanical and physical hazards from carrying heavy loads (workers developing
        musculoskeletal disorders) and repetitive tasks (suffering from overexertion, exposure to
        vibrations, loud noises, heat, humidity, and radiation.
       Exposure to other hazards like drug and alcohol abuse, violence, nutritional deficits.
The WHO highlights that woman and children in ASGM must be given special consideration since
women perform many tasks in and around the ASGM process and are subsequently exposed to many
of the environmental and occupational health hazards described previously. The woman can transfer
that risk to children during gestation, not to mention the exposure of woman and kids to other hazards
such as violence from drug and alcohol abuse (WHO, 2016).
The following table provides a general summary of key preliminary environmental and social risks,
impacts and vulnerabilities identified during the Scoping process and literature review. The purpose of
the table is to compile most risks and impacts and discuss these in the workshops and during the
continuous consultation process of the SESA.
