                                                                    underground, but also for surface features, modern topographical 3D
                                                                    deformation measurements and related specific processing and
                                                                    evaluation software should be the standard method for stability
                                                                    monitoring.

8 STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT
During the development of the Inception Report, stakeholders were identified in collaboration with MNR
and based on the literature reviewed.

Key stakeholders include government authorities such as MNR, NIMOS, MRDS, donor agencies (WB,
IDB, USAID and others), local and international NGOs (CI, WWF), CSOs, private companies, mining
companies, and mining communities with special attention to Indigenous and Tribal communities
involved in mining. The Inception Report describing the stakeholder engagement plan is presented as
an Appendix A to this report. In addition, a general display map to be used as reference for the
consultation process is presented in Appendix C. Please note that this map is for reference purposes
and the sources of information used for its development include available spatial information sourced
the National Land Monitoring System of Suriname (GONINI) and other maps identified during the
information review process. The data is not official and, in some instances, due to the lack of available
or updated information, some maps were used and roughly digitized until key reference information such
as mining rights blocks, Indigenous and tribal peoples’ territories, until an official GIS data is provided
by the GOS.

10 MECHANISM TO MONITOR IMPLEMENTATION OF SESA
Based on the analysis conducted, and the recommendations developed, an Action Plan will be
developed by RINA to facilitate the implementation of the SESA. Priorities will be structured into
immediate, short term (1-2 years) and medium term (3-5 years), including the Action Plan Cost Estimate.
The objectives of the SESA Action Plan will be:
    To present a series of recommendations arising from key findings of the SESA;
    To suggest a priority timeline for implementation of the recommendations;
    To identify the GOS Agency responsible for the implementation of the SESA;
    To provide some preliminary costs that will require confirmation and adjustment by applicable GOS
     Authorities.
The Action Plan will contain the preliminary related recommendations organized as follows:
    Findings: refers to a summary of the SESA key finding and forms the basis for the Recommended
     Actions.
    Priorities: organized in three priorities: immediate (2023-2024), short-term (2024-2025) and
     medium to long term (2026-2028). These priorities will define the ideal time span required to follow
     up on the Action Plan, and therefore the implementation of the recommendations.
    Justification: represents the justification for implementing the actions.
    Recommended Actions: a series of action(s) that should be undertaken to implement the
     recommendations.
               Anticipated Outcome: describes the anticipated outcome if the action is fully
                implemented.
               Responsibility: assigns the responsibility for the implementation of the action.
               Cost: presents a preliminary cost estimate that should be re-determined by the
                responsible Suriname authority.
This action plan will include a suggested prioritization of activities or reforms that could be directly
financed or supported by the Suriname Competitiveness and Sector Diversification (SCSD) Project
during its implementation. This would include potential support to MNR/NIMOS or other GOS agencies,
as well as to representatives of social or environmental groups to strengthen their capacity to engage in
future discussions and planning about the mining sector’s development.

1        INTRODUCTION
1.1      GENERAL INFORMATION
RINA Consulting, Inc. (RINA) has been retained by the Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) of the
Government of Suriname (GOS) to conduct a Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA)
of the Mining Sector financed by the World Bank’s International Bank for Reconstruction and
Development (IBRD). The development of this SESA is part of an overarching goal to strengthen the
environmental and social standards and impact management under the Country Partnership Strategy
(CPS) between the World Bank and the GOS.
As part of this consultancy, RINA will prepare the following:

1.2        BACKGROUND
The Suriname Competitiveness and Sector Diversification Project (SCSD) has strong and compelling
links with Suriname’s National Development Plan (Nationaal Ontwikkelings Plan - NOP) 2022-2027
(NDP), which outlines the development trajectory for Suriname for upcoming years.
The NDP presents a vision and a strategy aimed at establishing “a diversified Surinamese economy,
which is competitive in the competitive global market, has significantly more sustainable development,
generates employment and equality, and keeps the environment liveable.” The development vision in
the NDP related to private investment in extractive industries is described below:

1.2.1      PROJECT DESCRIPTION COMPONENT 1: FOUNDATIONS FOR PRIVATE
           INVESTMENT IN EXTRACTIVE INDUSTRIES
This Project Component aims to strengthen foundations for private investment in extractive industries,
by financing a geophysical data collection campaign and a geodata management system. A second




Doc. No. P0032241-IR Rev. 4 – December 5, 2022                                                     Page 7
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Inception Report


objective is to improve the regulatory and institutional framework for managing new investments in
extractives. Foreseen activities under Component 1 include:
    •   Geological data program.
           o Airborne geophysical data collection campaign.
           o Financing of a geodata management system that can be used to manage and promote
               the data and the associated implications for new mining potential. The geodata
               management system will include geospatial information on Indigenous people's areas
               and natural habitats and other protected areas to enhance management of future social
               and environmental impact.

    •   Improving the regulatory framework for new investments in extractives.
           o GOS plans are underway to establish a Minerals Institute that will integrate and
                strengthen mining cadaster, geological data management, and mining inspectorate
                functions. GOS also has plans to establish an independent oil regulator to separate
                production and regulatory functions. The project will support the establishment and
                operationalization of these institutions.
           o The project will also support the development of regulatory frameworks to be
                implemented by these institutions that provide appropriate incentives for future private
                investments including clear mining titles, a level playing field, and compliance with
                transparent social and environmental regulations.

    •   Strengthening institutional capacity to manage social and environmental impacts of future
        private investments.
            o Finance a SESA covering mining and oil as well as the agriculture sector. This report is
                 the Inception Report for the SESA for the mining sector.
            o Finance technical assistance for implementation of some of the recommendations of
                 the SESA. This is expected to include training, advisory support, and other technical
                 assistance to strengthen the capacity of environmental and Indigenous peoples’
                 representative institutions to engage more effectively in managing social and
                 environmental impacts of future investment activities.

2          SCOPE AND OBJECTIVE OF THE SESA STUDY
The SESA will entail a comprehensive mining sector-wide examination of potential impacts, both positive
and negative, of future potential investments in the mining sector, and identify gaps in regulations,
institutional capacity, and public consultation mechanisms that can be strengthened. This will help
address the weaknesses in the current legal and regulatory framework and enable the GOS to integrate
principles of sustainable development both upstream in sector planning efforts and downstream when
specific projects are being prepared or evaluated.
The SESA will also contribute to a more transparent understanding of environmental and social
regulations, creating a more level playing field for future private investors.
Specific objectives of the SESA are:
✓     To identify the social and environmental impacts that could be generated by the mining sector
      development, evaluating the scope and probability of these impacts due to increased activities in
      the sector and related development.
✓     To put forward recommendations to avoid, manage and/or attenuate these impacts.
✓     To facilitate the integration of these measures into a coherent policy and ensure their application;
      and
✓     To help in capacity building and training of the GOS officials in the management of the mining sector
      impacts, in particular, the Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) and the National Institute for
      Environment and Development (NIMOS).
Because this SESA concerns the mining sector and requires a strategic look at environmental and social
aspects, MNR and NIMOS will be particularly important to provide governmental guidance, advice and
input to the expert team that will carry out the SESA:
When completed, the SESA will provide guidance to the MNR and NIMOS on systematically integrating
environmental, socio-economic, health and safety concerns in policy, regulation and planning, project
development, operations, maintenance, and decommissioning of mining sector activities.
The SESA can be the catalyst for the following outcomes:
✓ Increased attention to environmental, Indigenous and tribal community engagement, labor and
  resettlement, health, safety and security priorities associated with mining and development resulting
  in more responsible mining operations;
✓ Strengthened environmental constituencies;
✓ Improved social accountability by making the mining policy process more transparent, especially
  related to Indigenous and tribal communities; and
✓ Enhanced sector capacity for managing environmental, health, safety and socio-political risks
  associated with the development and operation of the mining sector.
Furthermore, the SESA will provide a benchmark for cumulative environmental and social effects with
other ongoing sector programs and plans. The SESA will ensure that the concerns and expectations of
different stakeholders are taken into account in the decision-making process for equity and sustainable
development of Suriname’s mining sector.

2.1        EXPECTED OUTCOMES OF THE SESA STUDY
The expected outcomes of the SESA study are a series of concrete measures for the mining sector to
meet the needs of environmental protection, ensure the well-being of local populations, and identify
clear institutional responsibilities for government, private sector, and civil society. These outcomes
should lead to the growth of the mining sector driven by a more sustainable development process.




Doc. No. P0032241-IR Rev. 4 – December 5, 2022                                                      Page 9

 of Suriname
 Inception Report



2.2      PRIMARY FORESEEN CHALLENGES AND CONCERNS
The substantial number of stakeholders whose participation and contributions to the SESA will be sought
is one of its greatest strengths and the source of a significant challenge given the number of anticipated
groups, diversity of locations, cultural diversity, economic and educational level differences.
The SESA will need to address the specific concerns and expectations raised by these different
stakeholders, which will include the systematic integration of environmental, socio-economic, health and
safety in policy, regulation and planning, project development, maintenance and decommissioning of
mining sector activities, decision-making equity and sustainable development of the mining sector in
Suriname. Other concerns may be raised during consultation with the stakeholders and added to this
anticipated list. All concerns, observations and recommendations will be considered and addressed in
the SESA report to provide transparency and clear information to all stakeholders on the overall process
of the SESA implementation.

2.3      RINA TEAM SAFETY PROTOCOL
RINA will be guided by its approved H&S protocol while in Suriname to ensure the safety of the RINA
team members and that of the stakeholders during meetings and workshops. Likewise, RINA’s travel
procedures will be implemented and followed while traveling to the country interior.
The H&S plan is provided in Appendix A of this Inception Report.

3            SESA METHODOLOGY
The methodology was designed to be consultative and participatory to strengthen institutional capacity,
introduce good global practices, identify and inform specific reform efforts, and raise public awareness
to integrate environmental and social concerns into the mining sector, as to develop the country’s long-
term sustainable development and in alignment with the NDP.
The methodology will ensure the safeguards for the protection of Indigenous and Maroon Peoples’
rights, and their fair and transparent consultation and participation in the SESA in line with the ITPPF
and following the Indigenous and Tribal People the FPIC procedures.
The methodology to be employed in the SESA process was derived from the TOR and from best and
good SEA practice references (Dalal-Clayton and Sadler 2005)1; (OECD 2006)2; (Partidário 2007;
Partidário n.d.)3 and RINA’s experience implementing similar projects.
The overall SESA study will contain three main components:
✓      A technical component underpinning the definition of objectives, targets, and indicators, which
       identify the relevant studies for each of the critical factors for decision-making, allowing necessary
       and sufficient information to be collected from within the available data.
✓      A process component that ensures the linking of a SEA process and the decision-making, planning,
       and programming processes, establishing the governance rules for the integration of the processes.
       This articulation between a SEA process and the strategic decision-making processes is what
       makes the SEA a flexible process adaptable to each scenario.
✓      A communication process, which is crucial for public participation and involvement, which assures
       the exchange of information and the cross-referencing of the multiple perspectives, the opinion
       making, an integrated vision and participative processes suited to the problem and to the critical
       decision moments. The communication component is adjusted to the characteristics of the target
       groups.
The SESA is to be used as a process of sector institutional and governance strengthening that
materializes along with the implementation of mining sector reforms. The development of the SESA will
follow 6 stages and 12 main tasks. The general approach to be used is presented in the Figure below

5.1.2      TASK 2. Desktop Review and Scoping Report
The purpose of this task is to assemble preliminary information relevant to the scope of the SESA
applicable to the mining sector including artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM), forecast future mining
development scenarios to be developed subsequently, identification of the environmental and social
risks and vulnerabilities to be considered and assessed (e.g., potential indigenous and tribal community
land use, water quality, air quality, geology and soils, biodiversity, marine resources, socio-economic,
coastal activities, etc.), and identify the environmental and social characteristics of the areas that are
most likely to be affected by future mining activities, identifying sensitive ecosystems, protected areas,
areas of high biodiversity value, areas inhabited by indigenous peoples, maroons and fishermen, and
the like. The identification will include small, medium and large scales mining activities, along with
mined-out areas.
Two anticipated mining development scenarios in the upcoming years will be presented during our first
meeting (virtual or in person) with the MNR:
    •     Base Case Scenario (Conservative)




Doc. No. P0032241-IR Rev. 4 – December 5, 2022                                                    Page 25
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Inception Report




    •     Accelerated Case Scenario
The analysis of the sector development under these two scenarios will be undertaken using assumptions
(i.e., discoveries, resource studies, exploration results, Suriname’s macroeconomic development, ease
of doing business/export environment, transport infrastructure and services) and supporting factors (i.e.,
global demand for minerals, carbon credit opportunities). Once the scenarios are agreed by the client
and validated by the stakeholders, the identification of environmental and social risk will be developed
around these scenarios. These risks will include cumulative and indirect impacts by studying the
possible location of large and small mining sites and transport infrastructure and services:
    •     Current developments in the infrastructure sector (ports, highways, local roads, possible
          domestic/national aviation);
    •     Current constraints and opportunities; and
    •     Infrastructure needed to support the mining development program (capacity, investment costs,
          timing).
RINA has been reviewing existing policies, programs, plans, studies, and public information material,
such as:
    •     National and sectoral laws and regulations, national or regional plans, future mining
          development;
    •     Existing public or private programs or initiatives, current projects, plans and trends;
    •     Contextual information at the country, sub-national or sector levels (based on screening and
          targeted online searches);
    •     Available remote sensing imagery and geographic data to understand the environmental and
          social constraints. These sites are but not limited to:
              o Integrated Biodiversity Assessment Tool (IBAT) - https://www.ibat-alliance.org
              o KOPI – statistical data for the National Forest Monitoring System – managed by the
                   Foundation for Forest Management and Production Control (SBB) https://kopi.sbb.sr/
              o Suriname Water Resources Information System (WSRIS) - https://www.swris.sr/
              o Global Lithological Map (GLiM) - https://projekte.cen.uni-hamburg.de/lithomap/
              o National Land Monitoring System of Suriname - https://www.gonini.org/
    •     Cultural Heritage;
    •     Scientific literature; and
    •     International mining standards (ICMM, Cyanide Code).
The references collected to date are listed at the end of this report as an Appendix. It should be noted
that a Request for Information (RFI) was place to MNR during the Kick-off call but to date we have not
been provided with the complete information. Likewise, we have requested GIS information from
GONINI, but it has not been provided.

5.1.2.1     Scoping Report
The Scoping Report is the second output of the SESA study and will be presented under separate cover
to be approved by the client and later validated by the stakeholders in conjunction with this Inception
Report. This Inception Report and Scoping Report will be submitted for the consultation and validation
process in the events to take place between October 24 and November 5, 2022. The agenda for the
validation workshop and site visits is included as Appendix B to this Inception Report.
The Scoping Report will use the information from the desktop review and collected during Stage 1 of
the SESA. Preliminary findings based on the document review will be presented, related but not limited
to current project plans and trends in mining, forecast of future mining development scenarios to be
developed subsequently, conflicts around mining, identification of environmental and social risks and
vulnerability to be considered and assessed, Indigenous and tribal community land use, water quality,
air quality, geology and soils. biodiversity, marine resources, socio economics, coastal activities,
identification of environmental and social characteristics of the area’s most likely to be affected by mining
activities, sensitive ecosystems, protected areas, areas of high diversity and areas inhabited by
Indigenous peoples, Maroons and fishermen.




Doc. No. P0032241-IR Rev. 4 – December 5, 2022                                                      Page 26
    Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
    of Suriname
    Inception Report




   The Scoping Report also will include a stakeholder analysis and present key strategic options, key
   restrictions, major interest, and will detail the stakeholder participation process and consultation plan,
   the common vision on environmental, social, occupational safety and health risks, and present a
   proposed monitoring mechanism.

   5.1.3      TASK 3. Stakeholders Mapping

   During the development of this Inception Report, stakeholders were identified in collaboration with MNR.
   Key stakeholders include government authorities such as MNR, NIMOS, MRDS, donor agencies (WB,
   IDB, USAID and others), local and international NGOs (CI, WWF), CSOs, private companies, mining
   companies, and mining communities with special attention to Indigenous People and Maroon and Tribal
   communities involved in mining. This latter group of stakeholders will be described in a separate item.

   The following Table sets forth the identified stakeholders and their relevance to the SESA study.
   However, as we continue to define stakes and relevant parties, the following list may be subject to
   change. If additional stakeholders are identified, they will be included and consulted.

5.1.3.2       FPIC and Engagement
For all projects financed by the WB and that affect Indigenous Peoples, the Bank requires that free, prior
and informed consultations (FPIC) be conducted with potentially affected Indigenous Peoples.
Particularly if the project involves the commercial development of natural resources (such as minerals,
hydrocarbon resources, forests, water, or hunting/fishing grounds) on lands or territories that Indigenous
Peoples traditionally own, or customarily use or occupy, the borrower must ensure that the affected
communities are informed in a culturally appropriate way using their local dialect and in a clear language
to ensure of (a) their rights to such resources under statutory and customary law; (b) the scope and
nature of the proposed commercial development and the parties interested or involved in such
development; and (c) the potential effects of such development on Indigenous Peoples’ livelihoods,
environments, and use of such resources. A local translator will participate in this whole process.
The protocol for meaningful engagement, consultation and grievance redress in this Project thus
requires that Indigenous Peoples and Maroons affected by the project will have the opportunity to
provide their views and feedback in a culturally appropriate manner during Project implementation, as
well as to ensure access to appropriate Project benefits.
When approaching the Indigenous Peoples and Maroons, all Project-related communication will be
executed according to FPIC principles. Guidelines for the practical application of these principles in
Suriname have been described by the he Association of Indigenous Village Leaders (VIDS) and the
Association of Saramaka Dignitaries (VSG) in the “Community Engagement Strategy for the
Government” (2016, version 1.1).4
In line with this document, the ITPPF report proposes the following principles guide engagement with
Indigenous and Maroon communities which will be followed:
       •    Respect;
       •    Capacity building and empowerment - the community should not merely participate as a
            recipient but should be empowered to independently execute and lead projects;
       •    Rights-based - any project or program must respect human rights, including the collective rights
            of Indigenous Peoples and Maroons;
       •    Full information provision, optimal and continuous communication and transparency;
       •    Effective participation, in all phases and at all levels;
       •    Mutual trust, meet commitments made;
       •    Cultural sensitivity - respect for each other’s cultures and way of life, including respect for
            traditional authorities and local decision-making processes;
       •    Gender sensitivity - respect for the differentiated roles and responsibilities of women and men,
            in a way that is both equitable and culturally sensitive; and
       •    Taking different rights, needs and interests into account of different segments of Indigenous and
            Maroon communities, including elderly, youth, and so forth.
To start the engagement process, contact will be made with the traditional authorities of the different
communities to request permission for a first visit to explain the Project. This first contact will be made
by our local coordinator (Salomon Emanuels). In each community, a community contact person may be
appointed to serve as the liaison between the company and the community. These persons may help
schedule follow-up meetings.
Later, RINA’s team will visit the communities according to the agenda and pre-agreed dates to present
the Project, inception, and scoping reports. These meetings will be held in the communities, and
community members will have an opportunity to ask questions and provide feedback, which will later be
integrated into the final reports. Women’s participation will be promoted during the meetings and
separate consultations will be organized is necessary.

To ensure continuous engagement with the IP and Tribal communities, communication will be ensured
through cellular phone communication and WhatsApp. Although not everyone in the community uses
WhatsApp, there is always someone who does. As such, in coordination with the Captain of the
community, we will identify one person in the village that will be responsible for receiving information
that can then be shared with the Captain and with the other members of the community. Considering
the unlikely case that a community does not have anyone using a cell phone or WhatsApp, information
will be hand-delivered by Mr. Salomon Emanuels to community members either in Paramaribo or within
the community itself.



5.1.4      TASK 4. Establishment of SESA Goals and Objectives
During the engagement process, a key series of questions and corresponding desired outcomes related
to sustainable mining development will be raised. Example of preliminary questions are detailed below:
✓   How can the development of mining sector affect artisanal and small-scale (ASM) and informal
    mining?
✓   Is there a desire to transition artisanal miners to other trades or perhaps hire them into the overall
    mining effort? Or perhaps hire them to conduct works that would help preserve the forests of the
    country and its biodiversity? What are the different options these groups have?
✓   How can the mining sector in Suriname be developed while preserving environmental and social
    integrity at the same time? Particular emphasis will be on answering this question as it relates to
    Indigenous Peoples, tribal communities, and other vulnerable populations.
✓   How can effective stakeholder participation and involvement be incorporated into the process of
    sustainable mining development as part of Suriname’s long term strategic planning?
✓   What reforms need to be made to Suriname’s legislative framework to ensure that mining
    development is carried out in accordance with applicable standards and industry best practices?
✓   How can mitigating changes be monitored and responded to in order to allow for immediate
    corrective feedback action?
✓   How can all parties involved in or affected by mining development in Suriname be engaged
    throughout the SESA process?
✓   How can coordination between stakeholders to collaborate in resource exploitation be improved?
✓   How can transparency in decision making in the mining sector be improved?
✓   How can equity in the access/use of resources and distribution of benefits be dealt with?
✓   How can existing and potential conflicts in the sector and with other sectors be addressed?
During the stakeholder engagement process, themes of concern, main risks and impacts, strategic
options, key restrictions, and major interests will be defined through conversations including questions
and answers between RINA and stakeholders. Moreover, consistency of the various sectors objectives
and alternatives will be discussed in meetings, workshops, and site visits. The following Table shows
the anticipated concern themes, risks, and strategic objectives. A finalized Table will be presented in
the consultation.

5.1.5     TASK 5. Conducting the validation workshops
Task 5 aims to ensure the participation of all stakeholders through consultative and validation workshop
and meetings. The first workshop will be held upon the submission of the Inception Report draft version.
The draft will be submitted to MNR and WB for review and comments. After a maximum of five working
days, comments will be returned to RINA for their inclusion in the final Draft Inception Report. Upon
completion of the Draft Inception Report, RINA will present the Draft Scoping Report to MNR and WB
for review and comments. After a maximum of five working days, comments will be returned to RINA for
finalization of the Draft Scoping Report.
The RINA team will then travel to Suriname to present the Inception and Scoping Reports to the
identified stakeholders for consultation and validation. The presentation will include an explanation of
the SESA methodology and its main benefits for Suriname. Invitations will be sent to stakeholders for
their participation in the consultation and validation workshop. RINA will collect all comments,
suggestions, and recommendations from stakeholders for inclusion in the reports.
Field visits to Indigenous and tribal communities will be conducted to better understand the realities of
mining communities, and determine the main interests, concerns, and mitigation measures if required.
These visits will further ensure the contributions of Indigenous and tribal communities to the SESA and
their validation of the Reports. All collected information from the workshop and the field visits will help
RINA define the strategic options to be examined, key restrictions, major interests, and how consistency
of the various sector objectives and alternatives can be ensured. Details for the validation workshops
are presented below. The agenda is included as an Appendix B of this report.

5.1.5.1   First Validation Workshop
The first workshop will be held between October 24 and November 5, 2022, following the submission of
the Draft Inception and Scoping Reports.
The objectives of the first workshop will be to explain to the invited stakeholders what a SESA is, present
the proposed methodology, present the main benefits of the SESA for Suriname, and to collect
comments, concerns and recommendations from the stakeholders for the development of the SESA.
Findings from the Scoping Report will be presented to complete data in the Scoping Report and verify
the data and RINA’s understanding of Suriname’s mining sector. A list of stakeholders attending the
workshop will be prepared.
During the first workshop, RINA will:
✓   Present the Inception and Scoping Reports;
✓   Collect and identify the main interests, concerns, and advice of each stakeholder group regarding
    the SESA work plan;
✓   Define strategic options to be examined, key restrictions, major interests, and how the consistency
    of the various sector objectives and alternatives can be ensured; and
✓   Disclose the process for stakeholder participation throughout the SESA, including Indigenous, tribal
    and Maroons peoples.

5.1.5.2   Second Validation Workshop
The objective of the second workshop will be to:
✓   Present the SESA's main findings and recommendations; and
✓   Record and address doubts, concerns, and recommendations to ensure its applicability in
    Suriname.
The second workshop will be held upon the submission of the SESA draft report which is expected to
take place towards the end of the Project, between the months of August and October of 2023, with the
exact dates to be confirmed.

5.1.5.3        Development of the Workshops
Both workshops will start with an initial expository and informative session and PowerPoint slides
summarizing the main points of the Inception and Scoping Reports during the first workshop, and the
Draft SESA and its results during the second workshop.
Stakeholders will be consulted in various events in large groups or in focus groups based on availability5.
The participation of women during the workshops will be ensured. Anticipated events for consultation
are as follows:
✓      Workshop with Government officials.

       Maroon groups and representatives per FPIC protocol.

5.2            STAGE 2. DESCRIPTION OF THE REGULATORY AND INSTITUTIONAL
               FRAMEWORK OF THE GOS CAPACITY FOR ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL
               AND OCCUPATION HEALTH AND SAFETY ASSESSMENT AND
               MANAGEMENT

5.2.1          TASK 6. Development of an Institutional, Legal and Regulatory Framework and
               GOS Capacity Assessment
The development of an institutional, legal and regulatory framework and the GOS capacity assessment
for the mining sector in Suriname will comprise the following activities:
✓      Identify the institutions responsible for policy, planning, regulating, and enforcing legislation in the
       mining sectors.
✓      Compile and describe the environmental, social, safety and occupational health legal, regulatory,
       and institutional framework. A preliminary compilation of Suriname’s legal framework is presented
       as Appendix C.
✓      Assess existing capacity of the MNR and NIMOS. To assess the capacity of MNR and NIMOS,
       RINA will perform the following activities:
                  o    Design an evaluation methodology for institutional capacity to fulfill mission driven
                       mining sector responsibilities. Relying as a reference on publicly available good
                       practices and methodologies from other entities, propose a capacity assessment tool
                       to be applied to MNR and NIMOS.
                  o    Assessment tool calibration. The designed methodology and tool should be presented
                       to the technical team of mining experts and other international and local consultants
                       designated by RINA evaluation before being implemented in the field.
                  o    Technical assistance for the application of the tool. Orientation will be provided to the
                       RINA consultant team6 that will apply the tool in the field and any questions that arise
                       during implementation will be answered remotely.
                  o    Analysis of information and preparation of evaluation reports. Once the field collection
                       stage is completed, RINA will analyze the information collected and prepare a report
*******

      workshops are to be divided into different focal groups.

                 detailing results and conclusions that shows the main strengths and weaknesses
                 identified, as well as recommendations to improve institutional capacity.
✓   Prepare a compilation of relevant national policies, laws, regulations, guidelines, and contracts,
    including environmental licensing requirements. This will include all relevant WB standards,
    guidelines and policies including all the operational policies as referenced earlier in this report.
✓   Assess the adequacy of the national framework, based on international experience, and the capacity
    of public agencies at national and local levels, governmental organizations at national and
    community levels to address the potential impacts of developments in mining, especially for
    licensing and enforcement of legal ESHS requirement.
✓   Assess mandates, capacity, incentives, and transparency in licensing/permitting, monitoring and
    enforcing environmental, social and occupational health and safety regulations in the above-
    mentioned sectors.
✓   Assess the adequacy of the existing grievance mechanisms to protect landowners and affected
    people, Indigenous and tribal communities; and, if applicable, we will provide recommendations to
    improve such mechanisms.
✓   Assess the adequacy of existing mechanisms for the social distribution of benefits to affected
    people; If applicable, provide recommendations to improve such mechanisms.
✓   Assess the adequacy of the EIA system in Suriname, and identify potential deficiencies in the
    environmental permitting processes, EIA review, EIA follow-up and enforcement in the above-
    mentioned sectors. Recommendations to improve the EIA system, EIAs, EIA follow-up and
    enforcement.
✓   Identify potential gaps regarding international good practices, not only limited to the WB policies and
    safeguards but also practices from ILO, such as ILO 169 and others.
✓   Identify the existing environmental, social, occupational health and safety requirements that are
    included in mining sector contracts with the GOS.
✓   Verify compliance with Suriname’s ratified conventions including all eight ILO fundamental
    conventions (C029, C087, C098, C100, C105, C11, C138 and C182) and three of the four
    governance conventions (C081, C129 and C144).
✓   RINA will evaluate whether mining projects are equipped with appropriate tools to ensure
    compliance with these core labor rights, specifically the prohibitions on discrimination, child labor,
    forced labor, and limitations on freedom of association and collective bargaining. The tools should
    include labor rights policies, work regulations, worker contracts, worker codes of conduct, indirect
    worker policies, among others. For example, one potential labor compliance gap in Suriname mining
    project policies is related to the failure to cover indirect workers. A significant gap in Suriname's
    current legislation is the absence of national legislation on Indigenous and tribal rights and the failure
    to sign ILO Convention 169 - Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989. The absence of
    such legislation allows for tensions to emerge among Indigenous communities and mine operators
    without a framework to mitigate and address conflict.
✓   Finally, RINA will Review of the Mining Sector Contracts with GOS, and will:
    •   Identify the existing environmental, social, occupational health and safety requirements that are
        included in mining sector contracts with the GOS, and assess if additional environmental, social,
        and occupational health and safety safeguards need to be incorporated in such contracts.
    •   Provide the information necessary and specific recommendations on environmental, social,
        occupational health and safety minimum requirements that the GOS should include in the
        Contracts with private sector companies.
    •   Review contracts between mining companies in other countries in the region that can be used
        as a comparison.

5.3        STAGE 3. IDENTIFICATION OF THE GENERAL, STRATEGIC AND SOCIAL
           CONSEQUENCES       RESULTING    FROM   FORECASTED    FUTURE
           DEVELOPMENT OF MINING

5.3.1      TASK 7. Analysis of Future Developments in Mining Environment and Social
           Consequences
During this stage RINA will conduct the following:
✓     Develop forecasts of future expansions in mining sectors, including mapping of potential
      development scenarios. These will forecast developments over a defined period of time and include
      mapping of potential and actual sites that are being explored for mining, or that may be explored.
      Maps will be prepared and presented in the scoping report showing overlap of Mining Exploration
      and Exploitation polygons
✓     Identify and evaluate the environmental and social consequences and risks, including climate
      change risks associated with existing developments and plans for investment in mining, and safety
      and occupational health risks and issues relevant to mining, considering the forecasts and scenarios
      developed. This will include mapping to identify overlapping areas of natural resources/forests/ other
      areas of high biodiversity value, with potential and actual extraction sites.
✓     Include a particular focus on Indigenous and tribal communities and on the possible impacts of
      potential future mining sector developments on social consequences and risks for these vulnerable
      groups.
✓     Evaluate cumulative / synergistic / secondary impacts as well as impacts of individual developments
      in mining should also be included. Coupled with this the consultants should estimate or model the
      potential impacts to the ecosystems and vulnerable populations such as indigenous and tribal
      communities from expansion in the mining sector over a defined period of time.
✓     Investigate, without exclusion, strategic environmental, social and occupational health and safety
      issues related to increased private sector operations in mining and:
      •   Campsites (increased demand for land conversion, potential GHG emissions from land use
          conversion, increased demand for water and potable water, loss of biodiversity; transformation
          of natural ecosystems and consequent loss of environmental services associated with these
          ecosystems; increase in greenhouse gas emissions in the face of possible deforestation of
          forest ecosystems; increase in the consumption and contamination of water; social conflicts
          (IPs and Maroons) over access to local resources; community safety); associated access roads
          and infrastructures (site clearing, loss of biodiversity, fragmentation of habitats, resettlement
          and loss of livelihoods, community safety); processing facilities (discharge of contaminants; air
          and water pollution; impacts of accidental spills; community safety).
      •   Labor influx and associated issues related to gender-based violence, security forces,
          community-level violent conflict, forced and child labor, and human trafficking. This should
          include identification of appropriate mitigation measures, including for example review or
          creation of labor and civil rights protection authorities or regulatory frameworks.
✓     Gather and process information from the informal ASM sector to understand how this sector may
      be impacted by a more formalized set of procedures and approaches; present an overview of small-
      scale mining ASM good practices initiatives in neighboring Latin American countries. Explain
      international certification seals such as Fairmined, Fairtrade, Green Gold and Craft that guide ASM
      formalization processes.




Doc. No. P0032241-IR Rev. 4 – December 5, 2022                                                      Page 44
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Inception Report




✓     Develop criteria to prioritize environmental, social, and occupational health and safety issues in the
      context mining in Suriname. To the extent possible, such criteria will allow for quantification to
      objectively compare and categorize competing issues.
✓ Consider resettlement practices, whether positive or unintentionally negative, as a result of mining
      activities.

5.4         STAGE 4. PROPOSED MITIGATION AND MONITORING MEASURES

5.4.1       TASK 8. Submit Mitigation Measures Including Indicators for Monitoring and
            Evaluation
During this stage RINA will:
✓     Identify potential mitigation measures and monitoring requirements for each potential strategic
      impact on mining. Mitigation measures for strategic impacts may include, among others:
      implementation of appropriate legislation, including legal environmental discharge standards for
      emissions into air, water and soil; measures specifically targeting engagement with indigenous and
      tribal communities, drawing on initial mitigation measures to enable effective benefit sharing with
      such communities identified in the ITPPF and Rapid Social Assessment; revised institutional
      organization, streamlining environmental responsibility, creation of new GOS agency/ies;
      strengthening of specific GOS agencies; review or creation of environmental and social licensing
      agencies or mechanisms; enforcement of international best practices and operational standards
      guidelines for each sector; creation of protected areas or exclusion zones (No Go zones, buffer
      zones); etc. Compensation and sustainable ideas involving the IP communities in mitigating the
      effects of mining through protection of forests and biodiversity with potential cash transfer will be
      addressed in the SESA process.
✓     Select specific indicators to allow for follow up on the effectiveness of proposed mitigation measures.
      Indicators may be individual/stand-alone or combination (complex index), such as established
      indices (representing poverty reduction, migratory bird species, water quality, etc.).
✓     Consider good practice international standards, like the WB Safeguards and ILO policies when
      developing the mitigation and monitoring measures, by proposing how these practices can enhance
      the existing Environmental and Social Framework for mining within the Surinamese context. This
      will draw on lessons learned and good practices, such as effective stakeholder engagements with
      indigenous and tribal communities by existing mining companies such as Newmont.
✓     Consider resettlement practices as part of the mitigation hierarchy resettlement good practices since
      this could help to enhance the Environmental and Social Framework.

5.5         STAGE 5. FORMULATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS AND A SESA
            ACTION PLAN

5.5.1       TASK 9. Development of the SESA Action Plan
Based on the analysis conducted, and the recommendations developed, an Action Plan will be
developed by RINA to facilitate implementation. Priorities will be structured into immediate, short term
(1-2 years) and medium term (3-5 years), including an Action Plan Cost Estimate.
The objectives of the SESA Action Plan will be:
✓     To present a series of recommendations arising from key findings of the SESA;
✓     To suggest a priority timeline for implementation of the recommendations;
✓     To identify the GOS Agency responsible for implementation;




Doc. No. P0032241-IR Rev. 4 – December 5, 2022                                                       Page 45
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Inception Report




✓   To provide some preliminary costs that will require confirmation and adjustment by applicable GOS
    Authorities.
✓   To formulate a policy matrix comprising of concrete policy, institutional and governance
    recommendations (short-term, mid-term and long- term), verifiable indicators as part of a monitoring
    program, action plans, capacity building plans and budgets for its implementation and monitoring.
    The policy matrix, implementation and monitoring plans will also be validated in this national
    workshop.
✓   Organize a consultation workshop in line with FPIC procedures with all stakeholders to validate the
    draft report and action plan.
The Action Plan will contain the preliminary related recommendations organized as follows:
✓   Finding: refers to a summary of the SESA key finding and forms the basis for the Recommended
    Actions.
✓   Priority: organized in three priorities: immediate (2023-2024), short-term (2024-2025) and medium
    to long term (2026-2028). These priorities will define the ideal time span within which to follow up
    on the Action Plan, and therefore the implementation of the recommendations.
✓   Justification: represents the justification for implementing the action.
✓   Recommended Action: a series of action(s) which should be undertaken to implement the
    recommendations.
✓   Anticipated Outcomes: describes the anticipated outcome if the action is fully implemented.
✓   Responsibility: assigns the responsibility for implementation of the action.
✓   Cost: presents a preliminary cost estimate which should be re-determined by the responsible
    Suriname authority.
This Action Plan will include a suggested prioritization of activities or reforms that could be directly
financed or supported by the Suriname Competitiveness and Sector Diversification (SCSD) Project
during its implementation. This would include potential support to MNR/NIMOS or other GOS agencies,
as well as to representatives of social or environmental groups to strengthen their capacity to engage in
future discussions and planning about mining sector development.
RINA will use the interim outputs prepared at the end of each phase to compile the draft SESA report
and Action Plan. Findings, recommendations, and reports will be submitted for consultation to the
various stakeholders. The consultation will include IP and Maroons as guided by the FPIC protocols.
The draft SESA Report and Action Plan will be presented for final consultation and validation.

5.5.2    TASK 10. Realization of the National Consultative Workshop and Validation of
         SESA Action Plan and Report
The objective of the second workshop is to present the SESA's main findings and recommendations
and record and address doubts, concerns, and recommendations. The second workshop will be held
upon the submission of the Draft SESA Report and Action Plan.
A workshop will be organized to validate the Draft SESA Report and Action Plan. Invitations will be sent
to all stakeholders for their participation in the workshop. Stakeholders will be consulted, reviewing the
Draft SESA report and Action Plan, along with its findings and recommendations. All doubts, concerns
and recommendations from stakeholders will be compiled and reported in a stakeholder consultation
report. Field visits will be organized to ensure the equal participation of Indigenous and Tribal
communities that could not attend the national workshop that is to be held in Paramaribo. All comments,
observations and contributions by the stakeholders are to be considered for the preparation of the final
draft SESA report.

5.6        STAGE 6. FINAL CONSULTATIONS, REVIEW AND APPROVAL

5.6.1      TASK 11. Preparation of the Final Report
The final SESA report and Action Plan will be prepared and will include the Stakeholder Consultation

5.7        CONCURRENT            STAGE        -   CAPACITY        BUILDING        AND ADVISORY
           SERVICES

5.7.1      TASK 12. Capacity building and advisory services
The capacity-building program represents an important and critical tool towards the successful
implementation of the SESA. As such, the capacity-building program will be implemented during the
development of the various Stages and Tasks of the Project.

5.7.1.1     Objectives
The general objective of the sector administration capacity-building is to assist the GOS, staff from the
MNR, the Minerals Institute, NIMOS and other relevant ministries including the Ministry of Finance, to
build the required technical skills and managerial capabilities to regulate and monitor the mining sector
in the country.
The specific objective is the transfer of knowledge on SESA to the Project Implementation Units,
implementing ministries, associated agencies, and other GOS officials as appropriate. This includes on-
the-job-training, presentations of international experience, and participatory workshops.
The capacity-building program focuses on the reinforcement of:
✓     Technical understanding of exploration and operation mining activities;
✓     A full grasp of environmental and social issues; and
✓     Capacity to effectively supervise, control and measure potential environmental and social effects.
✓     Cultural competency trainings for GOS staff
The participants will learn how to reach the capacity-building objectives for each Stage and Task of the
Project to develop the SESA.

5.7.1.2     Overview
The purpose of the capacity-building program is to:
✓     Provide advisory services and knowledge transfer to GOS in:
      •   Assessing potential environmental and social impacts, and occupational health and safety risks;
      •   Understanding existing laws and regulations related to the mining sector;
      •   Assisting in the implementation of potential policy, legislative, or regulatory changes under
          consideration.
✓     Monitor the progress of the implementation of the SESA recommendations.
✓     Identify the main difficulties and bottlenecks faced by the implementing officer and advise on how
      to resolve and manage them.

    environmental and social impacts of future mining developments.
✓   Provide technical advice to GOS officials through meetings, video calls and emails, during the
    development of the various Stages and Tasks of the Project. Anticipated activities are as follows:

 Appendix A




                 COVID Protocol for Fieldwork of RINA Teams
The last information by the Suriname Ministry of Health: https://gov.sr/covid-19-update-suriname/
indicates that since March 2022, the Ministry of Health has started phasing out Covid-19 restrictions on
the basis of epidemiological developments. The Ministry of Health strongly recommends wearing a face
mask (surgical mouth-nose mask) in the presence of a large crowd and in poorly ventilated areas. The
use of sanitizer is still highly recommended. RINA will follow the CDC guidelines and those of the
government of Suriname. For visits RINA will use a face maks and utilize alcohol for disinfection.

Based on the best practices and recommendations of the Suriname Ministry of Health, World Health
Organization, and US Center for Disease Control RINA has prepared the following protocol to prevent
transmission of the virus that causes COVID-19. RINA’s team will comply with the following
precautionary measures:

    1. All RINA’s employees and consultants have to be vaccinated with vaccines approved by World
       Health Organization.

    2. The RINA team will bring masks and self-test kits and will be required isolation in the event of a
        positive test
    3. Wear a surgical mouth-nose mask at all times, especially when meeting with stakeholders. Face
        coverings, if used, will be disinfected with 5% bleach, washed, rinsed, and air-dried before being
        used again.
    4. Wash hands frequently, especially before drinking water and after touching surfaces that may
        contain the virus: car handles, door handles, and the like. The field team will carry water for
        hand washing and a container to collect and disinfect liquid waste with bleach after hand
        washing, before disposing of it. Where it is not feasible to carry water, hand sanitizer and
        disinfectant wipes can be used.
    5. The field team will be advised to have a good breakfast before leaving home and not to consume
        solid food while working in the field to avoid removing mask and reduce bathroom stops. If
        deemed appropriate, the afternoon activity could take place at a restaurant on the way back
        where the field team can have a late working lunch.
    6. Maximum occupancy in cars is 4 (four) persons unless a van is provided. If no security risks
        are identified, the windows of the cars should be opened. In case driving with the windows open
        is not feasible, the occupants should wear a mask.
    7. Alert the supervisor when a team member has signs or symptoms that suggest COVID-19.
        Based on test availability and test response times, the supervisor will need to discuss with the
        team member (it is not an option to continue working, although the Suriname Ministry of Health
        informs that people who show mild complaints and are able to work can work with a surgical
        mouth-nose mask) what he or she can do, in accordance with local labor laws; if a reliable rapid
        test is available, take a day of sick leave until a negative COVID-19 test result is reported.
    8. If a field team member has a reliable positive COVID-19 rapid test, this person will need to be
        quarantined. All field team members will be tested for COVID-19 in the event that a field team
        member has a reliable positive COVID-19 test result
    9. In the event of an ongoing outbreak, i.e., several confirmed cases of COVID-19 in this
        community or among field team contacts, the supervisor will immediately contact management
        to discuss the possibility of delaying fieldwork, the same applies to local closures and
        regulations that do not allow the field team to visit the community.
    10. Every person to be interviewed should be asked the following question and if any answer is
        positive, they will not be interviewed:

Have you recently had any of the following symptoms of COVID-19?

✓ Cough




Doc. No. P0032241-IR Rev. 4 – December 5, 2022                                                   Page A-1
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Inception Report
 Appendix A




✓ Fever or chills
✓ Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
✓ Muscle or body aches
✓ Sore throat
✓ Loss of taste or smell
✓ Diarrhea
✓ Headache
✓ Fatigue
✓ Nausea or vomiting
✓ Congestion or runny nose

    11. When performing the interviews with stakeholders and in meetings, maintain a distance of
        approximately two meters from the others and avoid physical contact like greetings with a
        handshake.

       4 LEGAL, REGULATORY AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK IN
         SURINAME’S MINING SECTOR
4.1           INTRODUCTION
This section provides a description of the relevant regulations set by the Republic of Suriname for social
planning and environmental protection relevant and applicable to the mining sector. Therefore, the
legislative, regulatory and institutional requirements guiding the mining sector development project, are
discussed in more detail below.
Suriname is signatory to a number of international conventions that address environmental and social
issues. These international conventions are the key drivers behind for the development of legislation in
most countries, including Suriname.
The Republic of Suriname have different ministries and institutions over which fall the responsibility for
the management of the environment and natural resources, and social themes.

4.2           LEGAL, REGULATORY AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK
The legal and regulatory framework of Suriname is composed of the national regulatory framework
composed from the national constitution, laws, decrees, policies, strategies and plans. The regulatory
framework is also supported by international agreements, treaties, conventions, etc. The following
sections describe in detail the legal and regulatory framework of Suriname.

4.2.1         NATIONAL CONSTITUTION AND LAWS
Suriname is governed in accordance with its National Constitution7 established in 1987 and last
amended in 1992. The Suriname Constitution sets specific social objectives related to environmental
aspects, which include:
       •    Article 6 (a) – “the identification of the potential for development of its own natural environment
            and the augmentation of the capacity to increasingly expand that potential”; and
       •    Article 6 (g) – “creating and improving the necessary conditions for the protection of nature and
            for the preservation of the ecological balance”.
Suriname’s legislation at the national level is exercised through Laws or Acts of Parliament (Wet, also
called Verordening and Landsverordening prior to 1975), Decrees (Decreet)8, Government Decree
(Staatsbesluit), Presidential Decree (Resolutie), Presidential Orders (Presidentieel Besluit) or Ministerial
Orders (Ministeriële Beschikking) targeting various sectors including industry, tourism, nature
conservation, etc. (ERM, 2016)
In 2020, an Environmental Framework Act9 was established (No. 97 of 2020) for the protection and
sustainable management of the environment in Suriname and the implementation and carrying into
effect of obligations deriving from the membership of Suriname to international agreements, notably the
UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, the Paris
Agreement and the Stockholm and Rotterdam (Conventions on POPs and PIC respectively). Another
important matter is the investigation, prosecution and trial of offences defined in this Act as
environmental offences. (UNEP, 2022)
The Act is composed of 77 articles divided into 11 Chapters: General provisions (I); The National
Environment Authority (II); Duty of Care (III); Environmental Strategy (IV); Activities and Environmental
Consequences (V); Control of Pollution – Environmental Pollution and Standards (VI); Waste and
*******

    Decrees date from the period of 1980 – 1986 and have the same status as past or present Laws

 Appendix C



Hazardous Substances (VII); Legal Protection Mechanisms (VIII); Environmental offences and
Sanctions (IX); Provisions on Enforcement and further provisions (X); Transitional and Final Provisions
(XI). (UNEP, 2022)
The Act establishes the National Environment Authority (NMA) as an Independent administrative body.
It shall be the successor to the Environmental Coordination Office of the Presidential cabinet and the
National Institute for Environment and Development in Suriname (NIMOS) shall be placed under it. The
NMA shall prepare the National Environment Strategy and be the main focal point for environmental
protection in Suriname. It shall also ensure that the FPIC principle is applied in decision-making
processes affecting the habitat of the native and tribal peoples. Key chapters include (UNEP, 2022):
    •   Chapter III defines a duty of care for the environment. This duty means that everyone knows or
        can reasonably suspect that his or her actions or omissions shall have adverse consequences
        for the environment, must omit such action insofar as this can be reasonably required.
    •   Chapter IV requires the NMA to elaborate the environmental strategy as incorporated in the
        National Development Plan for Strategy into a national environmental policy plan. The Act sets
        out the priorities of such policy. One priority is the inventory, protection and regulation of
        endemic flora and fauna and traditional and medicinal knowledge. The national plan shall be
        elaborated in environmental programs, which shall also be established at district level. The NMA
        shall publish every four year an environmental report. The Act establishes an Environment
        Fund. Activities for which an environmental impact assessment is required shall be defined by
        a State Decree. This Act sets out the procedures for such environmental impact assessment.
    •   Chapter V, the NMA shall be informed about government activities that may affect the
        environment and shall carry out an environmental impact analyses for such activities or policies
        or a strategic impact analysis for economic sectors such as forestry, water and agriculture.
    •   Chapter VI is about environmental pollution and rehabilitation of the environment. The NMA
        shall define polluting activities and be responsible for environmental authorizations.
    •   Chapter VII indicates that the NMA shall establish standards and procedures for waste
        treatment, reuse and recycling as well as the processing of waste. The NMA establishes rules
        for handling with hazardous substances. It is also charged with monitoring activities in this area
        prevention of environmental pollution.
    •   Chapters VIII and IX are about environmental offences. Penal law shall be the ultimate resort
        for such offences. Article 47 defines environmental offences and for this purpose indicates
        various other laws including, amongst others the Agriculture Act, the Forestry Act and the Water
        Resources Act.
Other relevant environmental legislation in Suriname includes:
    •   The Hindrance Act (Hinderwet, 1930, 1944, and 1972) defines the permit requirements to
        control noise and air pollution for industrial development projects. The permits are issued and
        enforced by local District Commissioners (Buursink, 2005; SRK, 2007); however, the Act’s
        effectiveness has been negatively impacted by outdated and inadequate regulations concerning
        inter alia pollution standards and waste management, and a lack of sufficient resources to
        conduct monitoring inspections (ERM, 2011).
    •   The Nature Conservation Act (Natuurbeschermingswet, 1954) defines the procedures to
        establish and manage conservation areas and protect wildlife. According to the Act, the only
        allowable activities in the protected areas are activities of scientific, educational or cultural
        importance. Conservation areas can be established only by Presidential decree and managed
        by the Nature Conservation Division of the Forest Service (LBB). The Act does not provide for
        the protection of sensitive areas outside the established conservation areas. (ERM, 2011).
    •   The Forest Management Act (Wet Bosbeheer 1992) replaced the Timber Act of 1947 as the
        governing regulation for forest exploitation and conservation. The Act classifies forests in
        Suriname in three ways: permanent, temporary (maintained for the time being), or one-time
        exploitation forest (land intended for other future use where tree cover will be completely
        cleared). Resource exploitation in public forests (domain land) is allowable with a permit or
        forest concession granted by the Ministry of Spatial Planning, Land and Forestry Management

        (RGB), which issued regulations for logging, deforestation, and processing-related activities.
        The Forest management Act also allows the Surinamese government to establish conservation
        forests. (ERM, 2011).

4.2.3        INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK
Suriname’s mining sector is governed by the Mining Decree (1986) and regulated by the Ministry of
Natural Resources, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Regional Development and the Ministry of
Trade, Industry and Tourism. The legal and fiscal framework for the oil, gas and mining sector is also
supported by other legislation, including the Corporate Income Tax Act and Dividend Tax Act. (EITI,
2022). Applications for mining rights are processed by the Geological Mining Service (GMD) and are
reviewed and approved by the Ministry of Natural Resources in accordance with the Mining Decree.
Suriname does not have a public mining license register, however some information about issued
licenses is included in EITI Reports. (GLiM, 2022). EITI Suriname is administered by the Suriname Multi-
Stakeholder Group (MSG), which is hosted by the Ministry of Natural Resources. The MSG is chaired
by the Minister of Natural Resources. (EITI, 2022)




Doc. No. P0032241-IR Rev. 4 – December 5, 2022                                                              Page C-15
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Inception Report
 Appendix C


On the other hand, the environmental approval process is administered under the new Environmental
Framework Act 2022, the National Environment Authority (in Dutch: Nationale Milieu Autoriteit, NMA)
and the National Institute for Environment and Development in Suriname (in Dutch: National Instituut
voor Milieu en Ontwikkeling in Suriname, NIMOS) together form the National Environment Structure in
Suriname. Through this structure the provisions included in the Environmental Framework Act will be
implemented and applied in an efficient and effective manner. (NIMOS, 2022)

4.2.3.1     Ministry of Natural Resources - MNR
The aim of the Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) is to ensure an integral sustainable and efficient
management and development of the production of the natural resources present in Suriname, taking
into account the environment, safety and rights of local communities. The organizational structure of
the MNR has recently changed. The Ministry now consists of four (4) directorates, as further detailed
in the organizational structure, namely (MINR, 2022a):

    1.    Directorate General Administration NH
    2.    Directorate of Water
    3.    Directorate of Energy
    4.    Mining Directorate

The organization has been expanded to include directorate and departmental tasks. The determining
organizational objectives for this are:

    5. Planning, monitoring and control of the spending of the budget and other resources.
    6. The optimization of the operational execution of tasks.
    7. Application of integrated management in the various policy areas.
    8. Application of advancing technology within the various policy areas.
    9. Continuous quality improvement and quality maintenance of the execution capacity.
    10. Entering into regional and international partnerships.
    11. Sustainable professional and personal development of staff.

Based on the objectives described above, the organization chart of the MNR is presented in Figure 4-1.

4.2.3.1.1 Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI) Suriname
EITI Suriname is administered by the Suriname Multi-Stakeholder Group (MSG), which is hosted by the
Ministry of Natural Resources. The MSG is chaired by the Minister of Natural Resources. (EITI, 2022)
Suriname was found to have made meaningful progress in implementing the 2016 EITI Standard in
March 2021, following its first Validation. The Validation identified 19 corrective actions to be addressed
by the country’s next Validation, expected to commence in April 2023. (EITI, 2022)

4.2.3.2    National Council for the Environment – NMR
National Council for the Environment (Nationale Milieuraad – NMR) was established in 1997 with a
mandate to advise the government of Suriname on the development and implementation of national
environmental policies. The NMR consists of a chairperson and 5-10 members representing
government, private sector, Amerindian and Maroon communities, labor unions, consumer rights, and
other Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs). Executive support for the NMR is provided by the
Nationale Instituut voor Milieu en Ontwikkeling in Suriname (NIMOS – the National Institute for
Environment and Development in Suriname).

4.2.3.3    National Environment Authority– NMA
Under the new Environmental Framework Act 2022, the National Environment Authority (in Dutch:
Nationale Milieu Autoriteit, NMA) will be mandated to formulate the Environmental Policy and coordinate
the effective implementation. The State of the Environment Report will be one of the key documents to
support informed policy and decision making. This Report will be developed by NIMOS. (NIMOS, 2022)

4.2.3.4    National Institute for Environment and Development in Suriname (NIMOS)
NIMOS was established on March 15, 1998, as the executive body of the National Environmental
Council (NMR). NIMOS is an autonomous government foundation, supervised by a Foundation Board

and consists of the following seven board members. The board is appointed for two years by the
President of the Republic of Suriname. The day-to-day management and overall coordination of NIMOS
is undertaken by the General Director. Currently NIMOS has 27 staff members, of which 20 are
employed on a permanent basis and the remaining on a project basis. (NIMOS, 2022)

NIMOS consists of several offices, each tasked with specific responsibilities, namely (NIMOS, 2022):
   1. Administration
   2. Environmental & Social Assessment
   3. Environmental Monitoring & Enforcement
   4. Environmental Legal Services
   5. Environmental Education & Public Outreach
   6. Environmental Planning & Information Management
   7. Environmental Funding & Investments (not operational).
   8. Environmental Research (not operational).

The mission of NIMOS is to “initiate the development of a national legal and institutional framework for
environmental policy and management in the interest of sustainable development” and driven by the
following goals (NIMOS, 2022) :
     1. achieving National Environmental Legislation in the broadest sense of the word.
     2. Preparing and implementing Environmental Protection legislation.
     3. Coordination and monitoring of Compliance.
Under the new Environmental Framework Act, NIMOS will be in charge to develop the State of the
Environment Report that will be used to inform policy and decision making of the NMA (NIMOS, 2022).
In addition, the new Act will require the development of Implementation Regulations to facilitate its
implementation. A total of 21 implementation regulations (i.e., Decrees) have been identified, however,
the top six or most important ones were selected to be drafted first and currently under development,
including (NIMOS, 2022):
    1.   EIA Activities,
    2.   EIA Procedure,
    3.   Environmental Permit,
    4.   Hazardous Substances,
    5.   Environmental Fund,
    6.   Rules and Procedures for the Environmental Controllers.
NIMOS has also developed Generic Environmental Assessment Guidelines as well as specific
Guidelines. These Guidelines carefully explain the procedures as how they should be carried out if the
Environmental Framework Law and the Environmental Regulations were in place (NIMOS, 2022).
The EIA process described by NIMOS is divided in five phases, namely (NIMOS, 2022):
    1. Screening phase: This is the phase in the EIA process, in which NIMOS decides whether an
       Environmental Impact Assessment is needed or not. If yes, NIMOS will indicate the nature and
       extent of the analysis. NIMOS acknowledges three categories of EIA:
           a. Category A: an EIA is mandatory
           b. Category B, either:
                       i. An EIA is required (Category B, path 3);
                      ii. Another environmental document is needed (e.g., Environmental Management
                          Plan) (Category B, path 2);
                     iii. No EIA is needed, but some environmental information is required before a
                          decision can be taken (Category B, path 1).
           c. Category C: No EIA is required, but the project proponent will have to keep with the
                minimal guidelines.
    2. Scoping phase: In this phase the Terms of Reference (ToR), sometimes also called Scoping
       report, for the EIA-study has to be prepared.

    3. Assessment phase: In the assessment phase the EIA-study is to be carried out by a qualified
       consultant or consultancy firm by order of the project proponent.
    4. Review phase: During the review process the submitted Environmental Impact Statement (EIS)
       is reviewed by NIMOS
    5. Decision-making phase: After the EIS is reviewed, NIMOS should send the environmental
       advice regarding approval or denial of the project to the permitting agency.

4.2.3.5   Minerals Institute
The government of Suriname wants to promote a regulated and responsible expansion of the mining
industry, including improved control over informal goldmining. However, weak institutional capacity in
the public sector and the absence of an adequate legal and regulatory framework have inhibited
prospects for growth. Moreover, weak corporate governance in the small-scale mining activity and the
lack of social and environmental standards have diminished the sustainability and positive social impacts
of the sector. The current mining policy aims to create a Minerals Institute – through the merger of the
Geological Mining Service (GMD), the Bauxite Institute of Suriname (BIS) and the Suriname Gold Sector
Regulation Commission (OGS) - and to enact a new mining law. Since, these currently are uncapable
to meet legal deadlines for licensing, develop regulations and procedures for their activities, enforce the
regulatory framework for artisanal and small-scale mining. (MINR, 2019)
The government of Suriname by State Decree plans to create the Delfstoffen Instituut Suriname" (DIS)
or Minerals Institute Suriname for the promotion, coordination, regulation, monitoring and inspection of
the mining industry aimed at an optimal contribution to Suriname’s sustainable development. Its creation
is a response to the expected growth of sector activities in the country, the changing focus (from bauxite
to gold and other minerals), the increasing complexity of financial, social and environmental challenges,
and the increased demand for governance and accountability in managing the sector. (MINR, 2019)
In March 2022, the Minister for Natural Resources officially launched the mineral reform for the
restructuring process of the mining sector. The Suriname Competitiveness and Sector Diversification
Project (SCDS-Project) started in December 2021 and should ultimately form a good basis for setting
up the Mineral Institute of Suriname. The Minister indicated that a legal and institutional framework will
be needed to monitor mining areas and restructuring the small-scale gold sector. The Ministry of Natural
Resources is holding workshops with stakeholders and a number of online discussions with various
organizations. (MINR, 2022b)
The Minerals Institute Suriname will be given the functions of Land Registry, Geological Survey and
Inspectorate in order to regulate the mining sector in an efficient and transparent manner. This on the
basis of forms of cooperation and transparent work processes in which technical and capacity issues
are analyzed in a participatory manner, the digitization of the geological survey and capacity
enhancement. (MINR, 2022b).
