1           ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE OF THE MINING SECTOR
In economic terms, Suriname’s economy has traditionally been dependent on extractive industries,
which play a dominant role in driving growth, exports, employment, and government revenues. Gold,
oil, and bauxite resources have historically accounted directly for around 30% of GDP and as much as
90% of exports. About 10% of government revenues are directly linked to gold production in the form of
corporate income taxes, royalties and dividends. More than 30 tons of gold are exported annually,
accounting for about 60% of the country’s exports. The services sector accounts for more than 50% of
the economy and is dominated by construction, retail, trade, and transport activities that are closely
linked to income earned from extractives. The Government of Suriname redistributes extractive
industries revenues through significant public sector employment, accounting directly for about 40% of
total formal employment. (MINR, 2019) However, other extractive industries and sectors for Suriname
include Oil and Gas and agricultural sector. In 2018, the agriculture sector (composed by agriculture,
livestock, and fisheries) contributed 8.1% to Suriname’s GDP and it has been designated by the
government as priority area (ITA, 2022) In terms of the forestry sector, Suriname’s abundant rainforest
contains many valuable hardwood tree species. A sizeable portion of production remains in the local
market as the industry has been unable to compete in quantity, quality, or price with large logging
companies in the region. First Timber N.V. and Houtexploitatie en Verwerkings Onderneming Soekhoe
& Zn N.V. are the largest timber-exporting companies in Suriname. In 2019, the total export value of
timber was US$ 52.2 million, and Suriname exported hardwoods to Europe, Asia, and the Caribbean
region, with Asia (95 percent) representing the largest market (ITA, 2022).

1.1.2     Gross Domestic Product - GDP
In 2021, Suriname had a GDP per capita of US$5,166, below its peak of US$9,350 in 2014 and well
below the Latin America Country (LAC) regional average of US$15,092Suriname had strong economic
growth between 2001 and 2014, averaging 4.4%, mainly due to favorable commodity prices. From 2015,
Suriname’s economy contracted with Government revenue from mining fell sharply (public sector
revenue and gold representing more than 80 percent of total exports), foreign reserves were drained,
and GDP growth contracted. By 2020, a severe fiscal and balance of payments crisis began to unfold
in Suriname, which continued into 2021. Domestic vulnerabilities were exacerbated by the COVID-19
pandemic, leading to a sharp GDP contraction (15.9 percent in 2020) and increasing unemployment
and poverty. In 2021, Suriname had a GDP per capita of US$5,166, below its peak of US$9,350 in 2014
and well below the LAC regional average of US$15,092 (WBG, 2022a). The annual GDP growth (%)
for Suriname if presented in Figure 1.2:   (WBG, 2021). Suriname ranked 87th of 180 countries and
territories on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI) in 2021, putting it on par
with Colombia, Guyana, Ethiopia, Kosovo, Morocco, Tanzania and Vietnam (Transparency
International, 2021).

1.1.3     Short-term development
Suriname’s main short-term challenge relates to improving its macroeconomic performance, particularly
as it relates to fiscal imbalances and increasing debt levels. Thus, addressing energy and water service
provision challenges, along with strengthening the Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) framework, can
help the country realize important benefits in the short to medium term in regard to both fiscal
performance and closing the country’s infrastructure gap in an efficient and cost-effective manner.
Pursuant to these goals, the government’s ongoing fiscal strengthening program calls for the creation
of a PPP Unit, along with improvements to public investment system and strengthening public financial
management.

public investment. Although gross fixed capital formation steadily increased from 38 percent of GDP

1.2           LINKAGES WITH DONOR AND GOS DEVELOPMENT PLANS

1.2.1         Country’s Sector Strategy
The 2006-2011 Development Plan (DP) recognized the importance of physical infrastructure as a means
to facilitate transport and logistics, stimulate development within the coastal areas in the N.E. of the
country and facilitate cross-border links with French Guiana. The 2011-2015 DP continues to emphasize
the east-west corridor and the Government Declaration on infrastructure for the period 2010 to 2015
given to Parliament on October 1, 2010 states that the connections between Paramaribo and
Commewijne will be improved. A later plan is indicated in the section below.
Furthermore, the GOS had included the MACRP as one of the two anchor projects of Suriname in the
Initiative for Regional Infrastructure Integration in South America (IIRSA), within which regional
transportation linkages between the neighbouring countries of Venezuela, Guyana, French Guyana and
Brazil are to be established.

1.2.1.1        Enabling Sectors: The role of Physical Infrastructure in the 2017-2022 Plan2

The physical infrastructure for national and international transactions and transport in the form of roads,
waterways, ports, airports, railways and associated facilities, mostly requires long-term investments,
which usually are of service for decades to the national and international community, in the course of
which in addition to the transport of people, production, export, transit trade, tourism and trade can be
done in an efficient manner. The development of the infrastructure is therefore embedded in long-term
development plans3, which eventually must increase and stabilize the capacity of the economy in a
sustainable manner. However, substantiating the implementation of basic infrastructural works in
Suriname must be linked to the development of the national production, integration of Suriname in the
region and the rest of the world. This is the case, due to the very small size of the population and the
restricted local implementation capacity:
1. Dredging the Suriname River with the development of Paranam as industrial centre with all facilities
   to handle big Panamax ships and oil tankers to forward in transit, products to the South American
   continent.
2. Dredging the Nickerie River with the development of New-Nickerie as industrial centre, facilities
   handling big Panamax ships and all tankers.
3. The bridge over the Marowijne River with the development of Albina as industrial and tourist centre.
   The bridge over the Corantijn River with the development of Apoera as industrial port. Construction
   of a railway between Bakhuis and Apoera or Paranam for the export of oil, gas, alumina, and
   aluminium, timber and agrarian products.
4. Construction of a centre for the gas and oil industry along the Suriname River near Paranam after
   more certainty has been obtained about the gas and oil reserves in the territorial waters.
The decision about the implementation of the aforementioned large-scale projects will be made based
on consensus4.

1.3           NATURAL RESOURCES AND MINERAL POTENTIAL
The Surinamese economy is dominated by natural resources: oil, gold and bauxite (IGF, 2017). In terms
of mineral potential, Suriname’s mineral and oil potential remains largely underexploited. Suriname is
located on the Guiana Shield geological formation and has a very high potential for a range of minerals,
including gold, diamonds, and other metallic minerals in addition to kaolin, rare earth elements and
dimension stones (MINR, 2019).
Suriname is located on the Guiana Shield in the north- eastern sector of South America. Precambrian
rocks make up about 80% of the country, forming a crystalline basement, and the remaining 20%
consists of Cretaceous to Recent sediments that were deposited along the northern fridge of the Guiana
Shield (Coastal Plain) as depicted in Figure 1.6 (Monsels, 2016).Large-scale gold-mining started in
2004, through IAMGOLD’s subsidiary Rosebel Gold Mines, currently expanding its capacity. In the fourth
quarter of 2016, Surgold, a subsidiary of Newmont Mining, opened the Merian mine. In addition to these
two large-scale industrial mines, the small-scale gold sector makes a major contribution to gold
production and exports. A gold refinery - the Kaloti Suriname Mint House (KSMH) – was commissioned
in February 2015, with an annual theoretical processing capacity of 60 tons of gold. (MINR, 2019).

1.3.1      Mining Industry
Suriname’s economy is highly concentrated in the extractive industries (gold, oil, and bauxite), which
play a dominant role in driving growth, employment, and government revenues while also exposing
economic performance to commodity price fluctuations. Historically, extractive industries have
accounted directly for around 30 percent of GDP and as much as 90 percent of exports (IBRD, 2019).
The production clusters in the mining and extractive industry mainly consist of gold, oil, bauxite and
kaolin. The mining sector substantially contributes to the economy in terms of exports, infrastructural
development, creation of employment and economic growth. However, the government revenues are
marginal compared to the export proceeds The gold sector is subdivided in the large-, medium- and
small-scale gold sector. The largescale gold sector develops the economically extractable large gold
ore deposits with foreign capital, in the course of which the government participates as a shareholder.
The medium- and small-scale gold sectors, in which in addition to Surinamese also a large number of
foreigners participate, exploit gold ore deposits with local capital. (GOS, 2017)
The GOS for the 2017 to 2021 planning period, included the following actions related to the mining
sector (GOS, 2017):
    •     The government is in favor of a regulated and responsible expansion of the mining industry,
          including an improved regulation of the informal gold-mining activities. The mining policy is
          aimed at the preparation and adoption of legislation for the minerals institute and the mining act.
          The preparations of the minerals Institute will be substantiated in this planning period. The goal
          is to merge the Geological Mining Department (GMD), the BIS and the Suriname Gold Sector
          Regulation Commission (OGS – Dutch abbreviation).
    •     Increasing the transparency and reporting about the income and expenses from the mining
          sector will also be worked on. In this context, Suriname will join the Extractive Industries
          Transparency Initiative (EITI). The EITI standards will be laid down in the new act.
    •     In this planning period, preparations will be made for the restart of the alumina and aluminum
          industry. In this respect, the exploitation of the bauxite deposits in West Suriname is concerned.
    •     For the coming period, the small-scale gold-mining will be formalized in order to guarantee the
          revenues for the State in the form of royalties and taxes. Efforts will be aimed at eliminating the
          use of mercury to the benefit of the environment and the health of the citizens.

1.3.1.1     Gold Mining
Gold has been a major economic asset for Suriname for more than a century. The long history of gold
mining, concentrated in large parts of a greenstone belt in the northeast of the country, began with small-
scale artisanal extraction activities and has more recently seen the development of major open-pit
operations. Despite the range of mining activities, Suriname’s gold deposits and occurrences are under-
explored from a scientific point of view. Primary gold mineralisations in the greenstone belt occur in
multiple forms, and although their origin is commonly related to the Palaeoproterozoic Trans-Amazonian
orogeny, the controls of ore formation in specific cases often remain obscure (Kioe-A-Sen et.al., 2016).
From the distribution of gold concessions on old maps, Brinck (1955) (in Kioe-A-Sen et.al., 2016)
distinguished three areas of gold occurrences: (1) an E–W-trending area from the Marowijne River to
the Saramacca River (Nassau, Rosebel, Mindrinetti-area), (2) a NW– SE-trending area with the Sara
Creek and Boven-Grankreek prospects and (3) the Drietabbetjekreek and Oelemari area. From recent
exploration and mining activities, gold enrichments appear to follow two major zones: one with an E– W
orientation (including Rosebel, Nassau and Maripaston) and the other with a NW–SE tendency
(including Sara Creek, Lely Mountains and Benzdorp). These areas in the eastern green- stone belt
host the majority of large-, medium- and small-scale operations, but gold also occurs in the Apoera area
in west Suriname (Kioe-A-Sen et.al., 2016).

Since the beginning of the 1990s a new gold rush has developed, involving intensive, often illegal
artisanal mining of lateritic and alluvial deposits in many major creeks in the greenstone belt, as well as
dredging in the Marowijne River and the Afobaka storage lake (Kioe-A-Sen et.al., 2016).
Gold production in Suriname reached its lowest point in the middle of the 20th century and a new stage
of growth driven by the rising gold price beginning in the 1970s was disrupted by the Interior War (1986–
1992). Since the end of the war, jointly with the rise of the price of gold, the now safer gold fields attract
immigrants, foreign prospecting companies and urban Surinamese to the interior of the country (UNEP,
Mercury Release Inventory in Suriname 2016).
There is a long history of gold production in Suriname, which in recent years has culminated in the
development of major mining operations. Although geological research into the origin and setting of gold
mineralisation in the country has made considerable progress, many areas remain virtually untouched
in terms of modern scientific exploration. The apparent diversity of primary and secondary deposits in
the greenstone belt calls for an expansion of research efforts, preferably in a regional context, to better
understand the local complexity of gold-producing processes and the geological controls of ore
formation in the Guiana Shield in general. (Kioe-A-Sen et.al., 2016). In accordance with the NDP (GOS,
2022), the gold mining sector represents the following to Suriname:
    •     Contribution to GDP (gross domestic product) is 21.5%
    •     Contribution to the state treasury in 2020 is USD 125 million
    •     Number of people employed in the (formal) gold sector in 2020 was 2,829
    •     The average gold production from a large mining was about 24,000 kg in 2020 and from small
          and medium-sized mining companies approximately 15,000 kg.
One of the potential impacts associated with the mining sector development in Suriname is associated
with deforestation, the associated Land Use Land Cover (LULC) for post-deforestation in mining is
reported to represent 67% of the post-deforestation from 2000 to 2019 (see Table 1-1), followed by
infrastructure (20%) and Agriculture (5%). The trend of gold mining activity shows a relatively constant
progression of land deforested between 2001 and 2014, however, the level of deforestation was higher
during the period 2008-2014 (around 26,000 ha) compared to 2001-2008 (approximately 19,000 ha).
This seems to follow the annual gold production, which was relatively stable between 2004 and 2013
with a slight increase since 2008 (Rahm, et al., 2014, in UNEP, Mercury Release Inventory in Suriname
2016).

Suriname acceded to the Minamata Convention on 02 August 2018. In its process towards accession,
the Government of Suriname started in 2013 with the legal and institutional analysis of the then current
situation towards the use of mercury and the role of the various actors. Mercury is a persistent heavy
metal, hazardous to human health and the environment, whose release from mining activities is
contaminating lands, rivers and oceans on a global scale and harming human health (UN, 2022). For
Suriname one of the important obligations under this Convention is to formulate a National Action Plan
(NAP) for the Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining (ASGM) (GOS, 2020). The government of
Suriname has yet to act on the project’s findings or implement the Minamata Convention (ITA, 2022).
While the Minamata Convention addresses anthropogenic mercury pollution by regulating trade in
mercury, phasing out mercury-related products and processes and reducing industrial mercury
emissions, it still allows the trade and use of mercury in small-scale gold mining (UN, 2022).

1.3.1.1.1 Industrial Gold Mining
In Suriname, there are two industrialized mining companies namely the multinational IAMGOLD, which
operates at the concession of Rosebel Gold Mines N.V., and Newmont, the majority shareholder of
Newmont Suriname (UNEP, Mercury Release Inventory in Suriname 2016). In addition, a range of
smaller foreign and domestic companies (e.g., Golden Star, Canarc, Wylap, NanaResources, Suparna
Gold, Hunter Bay Minerals) have been active in exploring and exploiting gold mineralisations in many
parts of inland Suriname since the 1990s. (Kioe-A-Sen et.al., 2016).

1.3.1.1.1.1Grassalco state-owned mining company
Grassalco is a 50 year old state-owned company with mining rights to produce crushed stone, gold,
granite and sand (Grassalco, 2022). Grassalco began recovering gold from reprocessed ore in 2014
and started exporting gravel to the Caribbean region (ITA, 2022). Grassalco owns the mining rights to
explore and exploit the Maripaston concession, a gold exploration site located 90 km southwest of
Paramaribo, in the district of Para. Grassalco also explores other sites for gold such Goliath Mountain.
The Goliath concession is located 65 to 90 km south-east of Paramaribo and covers approximately 244
km2 in the Bigi Poika area in Para in the central part of North Suriname (Grassalco, 2022).
Grassalco has begun recovering gold from reprocessed ore since 2014 and has started exporting gravel
to the Caribbean region (ITA, 2022). In 2019, Grassalco exported 102,031 metric tons of gravel (GBS,
March 2020).

1.3.1.1.1.2Merian Mine - Newmont
The Colorado-based U.S. multinational, Newmont, began operations in eastern Suriname in October
2016 (ITA, 2022). Newmont Suriname LLC is a fully-owned subsidiary of Newmont Goldcorp
Corporation, and operates the Merian mine on behalf of Suriname Gold Project CV, a Suriname limited
partnership. Newmont Suriname, LLC (“Newmont Suriname”) is the managing partner, owning a 75%
interest in the limited partnership, and Staatsolie Maatschappij Suriname N.V., Suriname’s State-owned
oil company, the limited partner, owns the remaining 25 % interest (Newmont, 2019)
The Merian gold mine is located approximately 60 kilometers south of Moengo and approximately 150
kilometers southeast of Paramaribo, the capital of Suriname. Commercial production at Merian was
achieved in October 2016. During 2019 the Merian mine produced 393,000 attributable ounces of gold
(Newmont, 2020).
Over the next 10 years (2018-2028) and assuming today’s gold prices, the GOS expects to receive
about o US$1.3 billion from the operations of the Merian mine. This representing back in 2018, an
additional US$4.2 billion in gold over the 10 years period. The Merian contains gold reserves of 400,000

5.2 million ounces and is expected to produce an average of ounces of gold annually over a mine life of

1.3.1.1.1.3Rosebel Gold Mines - IAMGOLD
Rosebel Gold Mines, a subsidiary of the Canadian company, IAMGOLD, started gold production in 2004
(ITA, 2022). IAMGOLD holds 95% of the share capital of Rosebel, while the Republic of Suriname owns
the remaining 5%.The Rosebel gold mine is located in the mineral rich Brokopondo district in
northeastern Surinam, approximately 85 kilometres south of the capital city of Paramaribo. The mining
concession covers 170 square kilometres, with the Suriname River to the east, the Saramacca River to
the west and the Brokopondo reserve to the south. Mining at Rosebel has been carried out by
conventional open pit methods (using excavators and trucks). A total of eight open pits to date: Royal
Hill, Pay Caro, East Pay Caro, Koolhaven, Rosebel, Roma, J-Zone and Mayo have been developed to
date (IAMGOLD, 2022).
In 2016, Rosebel acquired additional property from the Government of Suriname in the Saramacca area,
the Pikin Saramacca project, in which the Surinamese Government participates for 30% and Rosebel
for 70% (RG, 2022). In 2017, IAMGOLD announced that the higher concentrations of gold reserves
at Saramacca will extend the life of the mine until at least 2038 (ITA, 2022). In October 2019, the first
ore from Pikin Saramacca was successfully delivered to the Rosebel mill, using an alternate road. The
new mine was scheduled to begin full production in 2020, with an operation time of 15 years (RG, 2022).
IAMGOLD holds 95% of the share capital of Rosebel, while the Republic of Suriname owns the
remaining 5%. In 2020, Rosebel produced 220,544 troy ounces of gold (ITA, 2022).

1.3.1.1.1.4Gold Refining – Kaloti Suriname Mint House
Dubai-based Kaloti Precious Metals (Kaloti) opened a gold refinery in Suriname in February 2014. The
refinery is part of a joint venture between the Kaloti, the Government of Suriname and local gold traders
(ITA, 2022). The Kaloti Suriname Mint House (gold refinery) opened to promote and enhance the
production of gold within Suriname and the wider Latin American region. It provides a number of key
services and solutions including melting, assaying, evaluation, vaulting, bullion trading, coins,
medallions and investment bars distribution, global logistics, and liability coverage and insurance for the
international transportation of precious metals. The gold will be sourced from Suriname and neighboring
countries like Guyana and French Guiana (GTR, 2015).

1.3.1.1.2 Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining
The international term artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) refers to a wide range of activities,
ranging from the mere use of pans to sift through the soil, to the deployment of modern machinery such
as tractors, hydraulic engines, and sluice boxes. Both forms are prevalent in Suriname, but the latter
makes up the majority of small-scale gold mining production in the country. ASGM is often illegal, but
there are a few Surinamese companies like Sarafina NV, Bishumbar, and Grassalco NV that are working
with a valid exploitation license facilitating small-scale mining operations. Although Maroons have been
mining gold for over 100 years, the modern small-scale mining techniques were introduced to Suriname
by garimpeiros, Brazilian gold miners. It is estimated that up to 60% of miners in Suriname are
garimpeiros; Maroons and indigenous (33%), urban Surinamese (5%) and other foreigners (2%) make
up the remainder (Marieke Heemskerk, personal communication) (ACT, 2015).
Traditionally ASGM has always been a source of income for parts of the community. The negative
impact of mercury on health and environment in Suriname cannot be overlooked and needs to be
addressed. (GOS, 2020).
The actual harm caused by small-scale gold mining to human rights and the environment of countless
individuals, communities, peoples and ecosystems cannot be justified by the economic gains of the
mining industry or the poverty of miners. Everyone has the right to an adequate standard of living, but
no one has the right to harm the health or physical integrity of others to earn a living. The harm caused
by mercury is amplified by its persistence, leading to the proliferation of contaminated sites and




Doc. No. P0032241-SR-AB Rev. 0 – October 18, 2022                                               Page B-15
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report
 Appendix B




accumulated mercury pollution in the food chain that will negatively affect the rights of future
generations. (UN, 2022).
Millions of men, women and children around the world are engaged in ASGM. For most, it provides a
subsistence livelihood based on hard labour in difficult conditions with many hazards. They use hand
tools, panning, sluices, floating dredges and rudimentary mining equipment to extract tiny fragments of
gold from low-grade ore. Those supported by small investors may have excavators. Their activities are
destroying vast areas of jungle, forests and riverbanks, leaving wastelands of tailings and mining pits
(UN, 2022).
The contribution of mercury releases and emissions of mercury from the small-scale gold mining sector
has continued to grow, with grave consequences for millions of miners, vulnerable women and children,
indigenous peoples, ecosystems and aquatic life. There is a growing flow of mercury into the rainforests
of the Amazon basin (UN, 2022).
Small-scale informal gold mining in the interior has increased rapidly since the 1990s. Small-scale gold
miners generally use hydraulic equipment and mercury in their mining with severe consequences to the
environment. According to Suriname’s Planning Office, small scale goldmining produced 14,800 kg of
gold in 2020 (ITA, 2022).




                               Figure 1.8:   Small Scale Gold Mining Areas

Source:   (GOMIAN, 2011)

Virtually all Suriname (not migrant) miners are Maroons; tribal peoples of African descent. Maroons
traditionally live in the Suriname interior where the country’s gold reserves are located. Throughout
history, Maroons have mined for gold when they needed cash to supplement subsistence resources.




Doc. No. P0032241-SR-AB Rev. 0 – October 18, 2022                                             Page B-16

 Appendix B




Today SMGM has become the primary source of subsistence for large share of Maroon households
(GOMIAN, 2011).
One of the most significant environmental aspects of ASGM are the occupational health risks,
environmental contamination of rivers and food sources (fish) and its consequences in public health
from use of mercury. In 2011, GOMIAN (2011) estimated that for 1kg of gold produced, small-scale gold
miners may use up to 1k of mercury, with most of the mercury lost into the environment since there is
little mercury recovery methods (few miners work with retorts. A practical guide fo the use of retorts and
exposure reduction to mercury in ASGM was developed by the Artisanal Gold Council (AGC, 2014) that
is applicable to this risk in Suriname.
Since 2017, the government of Suriname has been working in the developed a National Action Plan
(NAP) for the ASGM in Suriname project (NAP project) with the support and finance of the UNDP and
GEF. The aim of this project was to formulate a NAP to enable the government to determine national
requirements, needs, goals and schemes to limit the use of mercury (Hg) in the small-scale gold mining
sector (ASGM) and processing or stop, as reported by GEF (2016).and NIMOS (2022a).

1.3.1.2   Bauxite Mining
Bauxite, the raw material of aluminum, has been one of the economically vital natural resources for
Suriname. Mining operations started about a century ago, and subsequent development of a refinery
industry and hydro-electric power made Suriname one of the foremost bauxite and alumina producers
worldwide for a prolonged period of time. Alumina dominated the export revenues of Suriname until a
decade ago.
The Surinaamsche Bauxiet Maatschappij (SBM) was established in 1916 after the discovery of the
Moengo bauxite hills in 1915 by the Pittsburg Reduction Company, later renamed the Aluminum
Company of America (Alcoa). In 1939, the N.V. Billiton Maatschappij obtained a concession for bauxite
exploration in the Para district, which led to the discovery of the Onverdacht bauxite deposit. Suriname
was one of the leading bauxite-producing countries in the world during the Second World War (1939–
1945), which generated a boost in bauxite exploration and research on the local deposits. In 1941, the
SBM opened the Paranam bauxite processing plant, named after the Para and Suriname Rivers
bordering the mining concession areas. In 1958, SBM signed the Brokopondo Agreement with the
Surinamese Government to create a fully integrated aluminum industry in the country and became the
Suriname Aluminum Company (Suralco). The most important objectives were the construction of a dam
in the Suriname River and a hydro-electric power facility at Afobakka, and the establishment of an
aluminum smelter and an alumina refinery at Paranam. The smelter operated from 1964 until 1999 and
was dismantled one year later and the refinery closed in November 2015. In 1993, Suralco and Billiton
signed a joint venture about mining and refining activities, but Billiton halted its exploration and mining
activities in Suriname in 2009, while Suralco also later reduced its activities. Suralco finally mining the
remnants of some bauxite deposits in the Moengo area and the Lelydorp 1 deposit before closing in
2015 (Monsels, 2016).
Bauxite deposits of economic interest occur in four districts (see Figure 1.9). The lateritic bauxite
deposits are spread across the northern part of the country and developed on various parent rocks
during Late Cretaceous–Early Tertiary times. Bauxites in the coastal lowlands formed on Cenozoic
sedimentary deposits, whereas plateau bauxites originated on various crystalline rocks in inland regions
of the Precambrian Guiana Shield. The more accessible bauxite deposits in the coastal lowlands are
almost mined out, the areas of economic interest being (Monsels, 2016):
    1. the Paranam–Onverdacht–Lelydorp district (Coastal), which includes the Lelydorp 1, Kankantrie
       and Para bauxite deposits
    2. the Moengo–Ricanau–Jones district (Coastal) with the Coermotibo deepseated bauxite deposit.
    3. The plateau bauxites have been extensively explored but have not been brought into production
       to date. These areas of potential future exploration interest being:
    4. the Bakhuis district (Plateau) with the Bakhuis bauxite deposit




Doc. No. P0032241-SR-AB Rev. 0 – October 18, 2022                                               Page B-17
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report
 Appendix B




    5. the Nassau district (Plateau), which encompasses the Nassau, Brownsberg, Lely bauxite and
       Wintiwaai laterite deposits.
For economic and environmental reasons, the future of the bauxite industry in Suriname is considered
to be uncertain (Monsels, 2016) and will be determined by the quality and size of the reserves, geological
conditions, available production technology, targeted locations in relation to transport facilities, world
market price and political factors. Existing Surinamese bauxite deposits have not been mined yet for
different reasons. The Coermotibo deposit has not been economically attractive due to the high sulfur
content in the bauxite and the 40 m thick overburden. The heterogeneous properties of the bauxite
within the Bakhuis and Nassau bauxite deposits will make it necessary to drill a very close-spaced grid
for mine planning. The remote location of the Nassau Mountains is also an economic and strategic
problem. Political and economic factors have hampered mining of the Bakhuis deposit. A final and most
sensitive obstacle is the environmental impact, as the Nassau Mountains have a unique flora and fauna,
including critically endangered endemic species (Ouboter et al., 2007; Bánki et al., 2008; Alonso & Mol,
2007, in (Monsels, 2016).




              Figure 1.9:   Districts of Coastal- and Plateau-type Deposits of Bauxite in Suriname

Source: (Monsels, 2016)

1.3.1.3    Rare Earth Elements
The mineral monazite—one of the main sources of rare earth elements—occurs in several locations in
Suriname. Also, indications of rare earth elements such as neodymium, cerium, scandium, and yttrium
in Bakhuis have been found (SITA, 2022). No significant exploration is known to have been carried out
for Rare Earth Elements in Suriname.

1.3.1.4    Other resources with potential
Suriname’s Investment and Trade Agency - SITA reports that other resources with potential include
diamonds, crushed stone, sand kyanite, phosphate, and manganese (SITA, 2022), but no significant
deposits of these minerals have been identified.
Except for diamonds, the other minerals and resources used for construction that are mentioned are
required in deposits with large reserves and, if present in Suriname, are unlikely to be discovered and
brought to market in the short term and will require significant exploration effort to identify them.

1.3.2      Oil and Gas Industry
Oil was first discovered in Suriname in 1928 on the coastal plain, close to the western border, but
systematic exploration both onshore and offshore only started in the 1960s, when various international
oil companies became interested. Oil became the primary industry by the mid-1990s, overtaking bauxite.
Total oil production in the last 35 years reached 100 million barrels of crude oil which has boosted the
total value of exports (SITA, 2022).
State-owned entity Staatsolie is the predominant oil company in Suriname. Until 2017, they have been
mainly active in onshore oil production. For offshore exploration, Staatsolie is considered, on behalf of
the Government of Suriname, the contracting party for International Oil Companies (IOCs) and the oil
sector is regulated and supervised by them. The onshore and offshore areas granted to Staatsolie are
shown in the following Figure (EITI, 2017).

Suriname is rapidly growing as a key hotspot in the Caribbean region, as recent discoveries in offshore
Blocks 52 and 58 have detected new wells with excellent oil properties (an API gravity ranging from 27º
to 37º). Moreover, even if three reserves are still under evaluation, the prospections performed until
2021 show reserves accounting for more than 1.300 million barrels.
Suriname produces 16,440 barrels of oil per day (bopd) and 692 thousand cubic feet of gas per day
(Mcfgd) from two mature onshore fields, but with five discoveries over the past two years, the country is
projected to begin offshore production no later than 2025 (Redden, J., 2022). Suriname also has
potentially large oil reserves on-and offshore, which numerous studies have shown, and the discovery
of large reserves in Guyana strengthen the suspicion that there are also large oil reserves in our part of
the Guyana Shield.
Active onshore and offshore exploration has been taken up to compensate the under-exploration of the
Suriname-Guyana Basin. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) ranked in 2000 the Guyana
Suriname Basin as the 2nd in terms of prospectivity among the world’s unexplored basins and estimated
its potential in:

      •   15.2 billion barrels of crude oil

Suriname exploration has primarily focused on Block 58 where two fields (green) have been discovered.
For now, Block 58 is shaping up as Suriname’s version of Stabroek, where operator TotalEnergies SE
is in a 50/50 partnership with Houston’s APA Corp. (Apache). The partners have hit five exploration
discoveries since January 2020 (Redden, J., 2022).
Production costs, at about US$ 30 to US$ 40 dollars per barrel are considered to be low and large
production of oil allows the country to have high levels of primary energy self-sufficiency. The result is a
very low electricity price at around 7 cents per kWh.
There is a significant spin-off industry around oil with types of activity with potential being exploration
companies, prime contractors, subcontractors, service providers, consulting, and investment firms and
there is supportive skills development with the existence of training and management programs and
initiatives such as the Master’s Program in Petroleum Geology in the Anton de Kom Universiteit van
Suriname and Hydrology and Engineering in the Polytechnic College of Suriname (SITA, 2022).

1.4        CURRENT DEVELOPMENT IN THE INFRASTRUCTURE SECTOR
A brief overview of current networks is provided below, by sub-sector (mode). The main transport sub-
sectors include Ports, Roads (Highways, Bridges and Local Roads). Possible secondary sectors might
include Domestic/National Airports, depending on the mine locations, and the volumes and values of
products exported.

1.4.1      Road transport
The main interregional roads are the east-west corridor which links Paramaribo with Nieuw Nickerie, at
the border with Guyana, and Albina, at the border with French Guiana. The major elements of the road
network are this east-west corridor paralleling the coast, and the north –south corridor between
Paramaribo and Brokopondo, the major hydro-electric power station as indicated in the figure below.
The network is linked to the sub region by the ferries across the Corantijn River to Guyana in the west,
and in the east to French Guyana across the Marowijne River at Albina.
The road network in Suriname is comprised of 4,500 km of roads, of which 1,300 km are primary paved
roads. The urban areas of Paramaribo, Albina and New Nickerie, contain 40% of all paved roads, mostly
located within the capital Paramaribo. The primary roads are mainly interregional roads in the coastal
area and forest roads often laterite roads. The vehicle fleet has grown steadily from 148,000 to over
190,000 registered vehicles from 2005 to 2010 contributing to congestion in urban areas and along with
deficiencies in roadway design and maintenance, to a high level of traffic fatalities
The road network is affected by a high motorization rate (303 vehicles/1,000 population in 2015
compared to an average of 204/1,000 population for Latin American and the Caribbean (LAC), relatively
high population density in the coastal area, and capacity and maintenance challenges, which all
contribute to congestion in urban areas. Congestion is also related to an inefficient public transportation
system and parking arrangements for private and public buses in the city. Limited availability of
designated lanes for motorcyclists and bicyclists and a lack of pedestrian walkways, risky practices such
as speeding, and limited capacity for law enforcement are the key factors that contribute to safety issues
and a high fatality rate (19.1 road fatalities/100,000 population in 2013 compared to an average of 16.7
for LAC, as reported by the World Health Organization), with most victims being motorcyclists and auto
drivers.
The road infrastructure in Suriname is characterised by a gradually deteriorating network with a few
rehabilitation programmes under way but generally insufficient maintenance activity on primary and
secondary roads. The tropical climatic conditions, medium to poor quality soils and subgrades, the

unavailability of sufficient first quality road building material and the poor state of maintenance,
contribute to the low quality of the roads, reduced fatigue life of roads and bridges and their rapid
deterioration. The overloading of trucks and poor drainage contributes to a shortened life span.
In 1997 the construction of the bridges across the Coppename and the Suriname river was initiated
with the view to open up the production areas in the east and west completely. The road system is
being destroyed because there are no rules and regulations preventing the transportation of heavy loads
on the roads. Transportation of heavy loads on water, which is environmentally friendly and cheaper
transport, should be stimulated and a policy and strategy should be developed.

investigated later in the SESA study.



1.4.2      Water transport sector
The water transport sector includes the following transport systems:
     •    Sea transport and ports,
     •    Coastal navigation,
     •    Interior waterways and
     •    ferry services.




Doc. No. P0032241-SR-AB Rev. 0 – October 18, 2022                                            Page B-23
 Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment (SESA) for the Mining Sector
 of Suriname
 Scoping Report
 Appendix B




Sea transport is the main mode of transport of goods (import and export). The Harbours of Paramaribo,
Paranam/Smalkalden, Coermotibo/Moengo, Albina and Nw. Nickerie are the main ports for import and
export of goods and produce and serving ocean-going vessels. Of these, only Paramaribo has
significant installations for loading and unloading of ocean freighters. The harbour of Paramaribo is
however not yet optimally equipped to handle containers.
The Paramaribo Harbour also known as the Jules Sedney Harbour, is managed by “N.V. Havenbeheer”
(NVHB), a parastatal. The Harbour is situated along the Suriname River, is a tidal port and the principal
wharf for on and off-loading goods for the domestic economy. The concrete pier is (1815 feet) 600 meter
long and the approximate depth alongside at Low Water At Spring Tide (LWS) is 20 feet (6.10 metres).
The tidal range averages from 8.85 feet (2.70 m) at springs to 5.00 feet (2.00 m) at neaps.
Some of the operations are private sector owned such as the ESSO bunkering facilities and the Suralco
bauxite terminal. Due to the shallowness of the waterway, vessels cannot be loaded to their full capacity.
Dredging of the river is needed to allow bigger vessels to enter the port so port usage can be increased.
indicates the current dredging project. The objective of the dredging project is to achieve a minimum
depth of 4.5 m LWS from the entrance to the Paramaribo Harbour (see following Figure 1.13) also known
as Sedney Harbour, by the end of 2021




                         Figure 1.13: Phase I Suriname River Dredging Project

Source: (MAS, 2020)

There are 4 small ports in the district of Nickerie in the far west of Suriname. One is a government wharf
also managed by NVHB and mostly used to load rice and as an intermediate stop for goods going to
Guyana. The others are a private wharf; an oil jetty; and a private dock of SML for rice loading, which is
currently not in use.
A small private port owned and operated by Suriname Port Services located at La Vigilantia, one of 3
business managed by Integra Marine & Freight Services, mostly used by IAMGOLD, a Canadian
multinational active in gold mining, and a number of construction companies active in the vicinity of this
port. This port is located in the Paranam Harbour area (see Figure below).

The Moengo Port is located in district Marowijne, alongside the Cottica river. For more than 30 years,
Moengo was the center of mining activities performed by then owner, Suralco. The Moengo Port has
played an important role in this part of Suriname’s history as it was known as Suriname’s liveliest Port
for longer than 10 years, exporting one of the country’s valuable commodities as Bauxite. As the years
went by, Suralco decided to move their operations to the Coermotibo river; leaving the Port non-
operational and being purchase by Traymore Moengo Port (TMP, 2022). In October 2015, Coermotibo
bauxite mine operations ceased operation. The port operation supported a mining operation covering
an area of 32,800 hectares and adjacent to and within International Union for Conservation of Nature
protected area; threatened species (International Union for Conservation of Nature listed) (Alcoa, 2019).
Noted that the other modes of water transport have lost importance in economic terms, they are still an
important mode of transportation of people and goods (shipping of sand, crushed stones and timber is
also done by inland water transport. In the past small vessels have been used for the bauxite transport
from East Suriname to Paranam).
The largest port in 2020 is Paramaribo, from where most exports and imports also take place. It concerns
the imported and exported freight since the amount of freight exported in 2018 was;1,200,000 tonnes in
2019; 1,089,000 tons in 2020; 975,000 tons in 202. A decrease every year is observed.

On the other hand, in 2017 the amount of cargo imported was 959,000 and in 2020 1,141,000 tons.
There is an increase of 28% over the period. (2017-2020). There was little change in the number of
vessels docked annually in Surinamese ports between 2017 and 20200 about 884/ 885 in each year.
Details of port imports by commodity will be sought11 . Small-scale gold miners generally use hydraulic
equipment and mercury in their mining with severe consequences to the environment. In particular
details of imports of these commodities will be sought.
There appear to be considerable prospects for Oil and Gas, when the wells are in production, they will
require both imports of materiel inwards and the transport of oil and gas export outwards.
In maritime transportation, challenges relate to port capacity constraints and infrastructure quality.
Moreover, few direct connections and a small number of service providers result in low connectivity.
According to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), in 2018 Suriname
had a liner ship connectivity index of 6.01 (on a 100-point scale), one of the lowest in LAC. Moreover,
the entrance to the Suriname River channel prevents large ships from entering the Jules Sedney Port,
which in part has a draft of only 6.5 meters. Although the country’s internal waterways are already being
used to move people and materials, their use could be formalized and better structured to form a
comprehensive network for accessibility.
It is intended that the rehabilitation and possible new construction of ports for mining support purposes
will be investigated later in the SESA study.

1.4.3          Air transport sector
The air transport sector has an international, regional and domestic dimension. Suriname has one major
airport, the Johan Adolf Pengel International Airport at Zanderij, about 45 km south of Paramaribo. The
route Paramaribo – Amsterdam is the main source of income for the Air transport sector. Air transport
is an important mode of transport of goods and people to the region and to effectively establish regional
integration, one of the main objectives of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM or CC) of which
Suriname is a Member State. The connections by air are however not the most appropriate and a

(integrated) transport/transportation policy and strategy should be developed to reach the objectives of
one single market, regional integration and unity.
The domestic flights have their base at Zorg en Hoop airport and their destination is mainly the interior
where 50 airstrips are present of which 18 are used intensively.
Suriname Airways (SLM) is the national carrier, which frequents the Caribbean and the United States,
but its main route is the Mid-Atlantic to The Netherlands. Apart from passengers, the main cargo
concerns fruit and vegetables from Suriname to cater for almost 342,000 expatriates. Smaller airlines
that mostly offer their services domestically and in the region are Blue Wings, Gonini and Gum Air. Even
though they are not immediately part of the main supply chain, they play an important part in supplying
companies in the extractive sector of investment goods and merchandise, mostly from abroad.
Next to Surinam Airways some small private operators dominate this market as mentioned. The
domestic flights are an important mode of transportation for the gold sector (for staff and materiel). The
“Vliegveld Zorg en Hoop” (VZH), an airstrip in the south-east of the capital, used to transport passengers
and commercial goods into the interior, mostly for entrepreneurs active in gold mining.
Air service is challenged by issues related to terminal and passenger services, plane services, and
ground facilities. Challenges also extend to unreliability and infrequent flights and logistical issues for
both international and domestic flights. It is intended that the rehabilitation and possible new construction
of domestic interior airports for mining support purposes will be investigated later in the SESA study.

1.4.4        Railways
Suriname has two major railways, none of which are currently operational. The first railway (Suriname
Landspooweg SL) was constructed in the beginning of the 20th century and connected Paramaribo with
the gold fields in the District of Sipaliwini. The Lawa railway has not been used from the time the
Blommenstein reservoir was created, around 1965. There are still some remains of the railway visible
in the District of Para but a great deal of the railway has disappeared in the vast Blommenstein hydraulic
lake. In 1995 the Ministry of Transport, Communication and Tourism rehabilitated part of the railway and
some locomotives to provide tourist and citizens a nostalgic trip along the old railway route. The project
did not take off.
The track was lightly-laid, with sand used as ballast. At Kabel, the line was interrupted by the Suriname
River, so a cableway was built to connect both ends. This opened in 1911 and was replaced by a ferry
in 1923. The 86 km section between Onverwacht and Brownsweg remained in use mainly to serve the
small village of Kwakoegron, a gateway to the gold mining camps up the Saramacca River, and the
Dutch military camp at Brownsweg. In May 1986, twice weekly trains still operated to Kwakoegron to
the following schedule: Mo/Fr Onverwacht 08.00 – Kwakoegron 11.00/14.00 – Onverwacht 17.30.
Shortly thereafter, the railway was closed (by 1988). The other railway, which connects Apoera to the
Bakhuysgebergte12, was constructed in the period of 1975-1980 to exploit the (substantial bauxite
reserves in the Bakhuysgebergte. The railway has never been used due to the military conflict and was
subsequently neglected. It appears that some of the original infrastructure remains unutilised. It is
intended that the potential resurrection of the railways for mining support purposes will be investigated
later in the SESA study.

1.4.5        Energy
The National Power System (NPS) of Suriname consists of seven isolated power networks served by
state-owned N.V. Energie Bedrijven Suriname (EBS13) (BID, 2020). Suriname's energy mix comes from
Hydro (Afobakadam) and thermal generation (diesel generated power). The MINR is responsible for the
administration, regulation, monitoring and development of the energy policy in Suriname. The energy

generators of the country are the EBS, the State Oil Company of Suriname (Staatsolie14) and Suralco
LLC (Suralco) (GBS, March 2020).
EBS is responsible for the design, construction, operation and maintenance of the country's electric
transmission and distribution network (GBS, March 2020). EBS provides and sells electricity to 9 districts
in the coastal area and also distributes propane gas through its state-owned subsidiary OGANE.
The electrical energy needs of the country are covered by four generating plants, two of which are
managed by the EBS (i.e., thermal power plants with a generating capacity of 133 MW) and the other
two generating plants (Suralco and Straatsolie) are managed through Power Purchase Agreements
(PPAs). In 2019, the country had an installed capacity of 220.2MW and available capacity of 167.7MW.
(GBS, March 2020).
EBS operates six additional power systems that use Heavy Fuel Oil (HFO) and diesel.
       •    The largest is in Nickerie (also referred as ENIC), which serves around 10,489 customers with
            electricity supplied by a 20.6 MW thermal power plant at Clarapolder running on HFO and
            premium diesel.
       •    The remaining five rural power networks served by EBS are Albina, Apoera, Coronie, Moengo
            and Wagenigen, with an approximate installed capacity of 23 MW of diesel power plants, serving
            roughly 5,857 customers in the coastal zone.
In isolated and remote communities of the Hinterland, where the NPS does not reach customers, the
Electricity Supply Service (DEV15) or Department of Rural Energy, part of the MINR, is responsible for
rural electrification. Approximately 130 villages (close by the Marowijne river, origin of the Suriname
and Saramacca river and the Cottica river) are being intermittently served with small diesel generators.
The electricity service provision is designed for an average time of six hours per day, from 5:00 pm to
11:00 pm, but this is seldom the case due to irregular provision of diesel or, very often, because the
units are out of commission (GBS, March 2020) and (BID, 2020). A 500 kWp solar power generation
and battery storage system was installed in 2018 and integrated with the diesel plant for the Atjoni and
Pokigron villages.
The results of unreliable electricity, or lack thereof, on rural productivity have been widely documented
with impacts on income, employment, school enrollment and firm productivity16 (BID, 2020).

1.4.5.1        Energy generated for the Bauxite sector
The energy that is generated by the Afobaka Hydro Power Plant, the Paranam (thermal) Power Plant
and the Moengo plant was in the first instance intended to facilitate the bauxite sector and in the second
instance for the government (via EBS). The power plants of Paranam and Moengo stopped operation
in 2015 (see table X).

1.4.5.2        Energy generated for the Gold mining sector
The Rosebel Gold Mines Solar Energy Plant has an installed capacity of 5 megawatts and was
commissioned in 2014. This Plant is the first large scale solar energy plant in Suriname. Rosebel uses
the generated energy for its company activities in Brokopondo.
The power supply for the Merian goldmine is provided by a 62.3 MW on-site HFO power plant.
